teile.einleitung: A word is a small unit of language that has a meaning of its own. We build sentences out of words, and whole texts out of sentences. In German you can put words together like building blocks: “Schnee” (snow) and “Mann” (man) become “Schneemann” (snowman).
wichtigste: A word is a unit with a meaning of its own.
In written text there are spaces between the words.
The sentence “I am eating an apple.” is made of five words; in German, “Ich esse einen Apfel.” has four.
Compound words such as the German “Haustür” (front door) are made of two or more words.
Words with the same stem form a word family, such as the German “fahren”, “Fahrer” and “Fahrt” (drive, driver, journey).
“Fruit” is an umbrella term for apple, pear and cherry.
In Switzerland the mid-morning snack is called “Znüni”.

abschnitte.text: A **word** is a series of sounds or letters that carries a meaning. In writing you recognise words by the spaces between them. So the German sentence “Ich esse einen Apfel” (I am eating an apple) has four words. Words can be broken down into smaller parts, for example into syllables or into word building blocks such as prefixes and endings. All the words a person knows make up their **vocabulary**.

Words are divided into **word classes**. The most important are nouns such as “dog”, verbs such as “run” and adjectives such as “red”. Then there are smaller word classes such as articles, pronouns, prepositions, conjunctions and adverbs. In German, nouns, verbs and adjectives change their form, while other word classes such as prepositions always stay the same. In the list “red, blue, dog, yellow”, “dog” does not fit, because it is a noun and not a colour.

One strength of German is its **compounds**, words put together from other words. “Haus” (house) and “Tür” (door) become “Haustür” (front door), and “Schnee” (snow) and “Mann” (man) become “Schneemann” (snowman). The last word is called the base word and decides the article: it is “die Haustür” because it is “die Tür”. The word in front, the modifier, says more precisely what kind of door is meant. This sometimes produces very long words such as “Fussballweltmeisterschaft” (football World Cup).

Words with the same **stem** form a word family. The German “fahren” (to drive) family includes, for example, “Fahrer” (driver), “Fahrt” (journey), “Fähre” (ferry) and “abfahren” (to leave), but “laufen” (to run) does not belong. Words can also be sorted by their meaning. An **umbrella term** such as “fruit” brings together several narrower terms such as apple, pear and cherry. Orders like these help the brain remember words.

Switzerland has many words that are hardly known elsewhere. The **Znüni** is the little break with a snack at about nine o’clock, and the Zvieri the snack in the afternoon. Other examples are “Velo” (bike), “Glace” (ice cream) or “Rüebli” (carrot). New words are always appearing, for example through technology and the internet, while old words slowly disappear. Today the Duden spelling dictionary contains well over 100,000 entries.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the words a person knows or a language has.
A word put together from other words, for example the German “Haustür” (front door).
A group of words with the same stem.
A word that brings together several similar things, such as “fruit”.

gewusst: The German word “Donaudampfschifffahrtsgesellschaftskapitän” (Danube steamship company captain) is often given as an example of a particularly long word.
By the time they start school, a child already knows several thousand words.
The word “Znüni” comes from “z Nüni”, meaning “at nine o’clock”.

t105kt56.t: Capital and small letters in German

teile.einleitung: In German, it is not only nouns that are written with a capital letter. Verbs and adjectives can also turn into nouns and then be written with a capital. The rules on capital and small letters help you spot this.
wichtigste: After “beim” (while) or “zum” (for the), a verb turns into a noun: “beim Essen” (while eating).
After words for “something”, “nothing”, “much” or “all”, adjectives get a capital: “etwas Schönes” (something beautiful).
Times of day after “heute” (today), “gestern” (yesterday) or “morgen” (tomorrow) get a capital: “heute Abend” (this evening).
Words such as “montags” (on Mondays) are adverbs and are written with a small letter.
The polite form “Sie” (you) and its forms are always written with a capital.
In proper names, adjectives also get a capital: “Schweizerisches Rotes Kreuz” (Swiss Red Cross).

abschnitte.text: A verb can turn into a noun. This is called **nominalisation**. A clue is small words in front of it, meaning “while”, “for the” or “the”: “Beim **Essen** spricht man nicht” (You don’t talk while eating) or “Das **Lesen** macht Spass” (Reading is fun). The real verb in the sentence, here “spricht” (talks), keeps its small letter. With the article test you can find nouns like these quickly.

Adjectives can also turn into nouns. After words such as **“etwas”, “nichts”, “viel” or “alles”** (something, nothing, much, all), they get a capital letter: “etwas Schönes” (something beautiful), “nichts Neues” (nothing new). Colours get a capital after a preposition: “ein Kleid in **Blau**” (a dress in blue). Before a noun, though, the colour stays an adjective: “ein blaues Kleid” (a blue dress). Since the spelling reform, fixed phrases such as “im **Allgemeinen**” (in general) or “im Voraus” (in advance) are also written with a capital.

With times you have to look closely. After “heute”, “gestern” or “morgen”, times of day are written with a capital: “heute **Abend**” (this evening), “gestern Morgen” (yesterday morning). Words with an s at the end such as **“montags”** (on Mondays) or “abends” (in the evenings) are adverbs. They mean “every Monday” or “every evening” and are written with a small letter. In the sentence “Wir haben montags Turnen” (We have PE on Mondays), only the school subject “Turnen” (PE) is a noun.

The polite form of address **“Sie”** (you) is always written with a capital, as are “Ihnen” and “Ihr”. This sets it apart from “sie” meaning “they”. In **proper names**, adjectives are written with a capital: “Schweizerisches Rotes Kreuz” (Swiss Red Cross) or “Vierwaldstättersee” (Lake Lucerne). Words formed from place names ending in **“-er”**, such as “Basler” or “Zürcher”, also get a capital: “Basler Läckerli” (Basel gingerbread biscuits), “Zürcher Geschnetzeltes” (Zurich-style sliced veal).

gewusst: In letters you may write “du” and “dich” (you) with a small letter, or with a capital as a sign of friendliness.
German is one of very few languages in which all nouns are written with a capital letter.

teile.einleitung: A proverb is a short, fixed sentence that contains a piece of wisdom about life or a piece of advice. Almost everyone knows German proverbs such as “Übung macht den Meister” (Practice makes perfect) or “Morgenstund hat Gold im Mund” (The morning hour has gold in its mouth). Proverbs have been handed down from generation to generation for centuries.
wichtigste: A proverb is a whole sentence with a lesson; that is what makes it different from an idiom.
“Morgenstund hat Gold im Mund” means that getting up early pays off.
“Übung macht den Meister” (practice makes the master) means that you get good by practising.
“He who digs a pit for others falls into it himself” warns against harming others.
“The apple does not fall far from the tree” means that children are like their parents.
“Speech is silver, silence is golden” praises wise silence.
“Too many cooks spoil the broth” means things go wrong when everyone has a say.

abschnitte.text: A **proverb** is a well-known sentence that expresses a general truth or a piece of advice. It is usually short, easy to remember and often uses an image. Unlike an **idiom**, a proverb forms a complete sentence with a lesson. So “to put your foot in it” is an idiom, while “practice makes perfect” is a proverb. You can quote proverbs in a conversation to back up an opinion.

Many proverbs sound especially catchy. Some rhyme, such as the German “Ohne Fleiss kein Preis” (No effort, no prize). Others work with opposites, such as “Speech is silver, silence is golden”. They often use vivid **images** from everyday life, such as apples, cooks or broth. It is precisely this short, catchy form that has made people remember them over generations.

Proverbs come from very different sources. Some go back to the **Bible**, for example “He who digs a pit for others falls into it himself”, which appears in a similar form in the Book of Proverbs. Others come from Latin: “Morgenstund hat Gold im Mund” is often traced back to a Latin saying that the dawn is a friend of the Muses. But many simply arose among ordinary people, from the experience of farmers, craftsmen and traders.

Scholars began collecting proverbs early on. The famous scholar **Erasmus of Rotterdam** published a large collection of Latin and Greek proverbs. He lived in Basel for many years and died there in 1536. In the 19th century, Karl Friedrich Wilhelm Wander put together a German dictionary of proverbs in several volumes. In 1559 the painter Pieter Bruegel even painted a picture that shows more than a hundred proverbs.

Almost every language has its own proverbs, which often say something similar with different images. For “Morgenstund hat Gold im Mund”, English says that the early bird catches the worm. Swiss **dialects** also have many proverbs. Some proverbs even contradict each other: “Birds of a feather flock together”, but also “Opposites attract”. That is why they are pieces of wisdom and not fixed laws.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fixed sentence with a piece of wisdom or advice.
A fixed group of words with a figurative meaning but without a lesson of its own.
Experience that many people have had in their lives.
Language as it is spoken by many people in everyday life.

gewusst: Pieter Bruegel’s painting “Netherlandish Proverbs” hangs in Berlin today.
The game Chinese whispers shows why proverbs have to be short: long sentences quickly get changed as they are passed on.
Some proverbs are twisted for fun, such as the German joke version: “He who digs a pit for others has a pit-digging machine”.

teile.einleitung: One dog, two dogs: when there is more than one of something, you need the plural. In grammar the form for one is called the singular, and the form for more than one the plural. German has several different ways of forming the plural.
wichtigste: The form for one is called the singular, the form for more than one the plural.
In German you often add an ending: “Hund” (dog) becomes “Hunde”, “Blume” (flower) becomes “Blumen”.
Sometimes a, o or u becomes ä, ö or ü: “Vogel” (bird) becomes “Vögel”.
With some words you add “-s”: “Velo” (bike) becomes “Velos”.
Some words stay the same: ein Lehrer, zwei Lehrer (one teacher, two teachers).
In the German plural, the article is always “die”.

abschnitte.text: If a word means exactly one thing, it is in the **singular**, for example “ein Stuhl” (a chair). If it means several, it is in the **plural**, for example “viele Stühle” (many chairs). To find the singular, you ask: what is it called when there is only one? “Viele Kühe” (many cows), but only one **“Kuh”** (cow).

In German the plural is often formed with an ending. With **“-e”**: ein Hund, zwei Hunde (one dog, two dogs). With **“-n”** or **“-en”**: eine Blume, viele Blumen (one flower, many flowers). With **“-er”**: ein Ei, zehn Eier (one egg, ten eggs). With **“-s”**: ein Velo, zwei Velos (one bike, two bikes). You have to learn which ending fits for each word. If in doubt, a dictionary helps.

abschnitte.titel: A, o, u become ä, ö, ü
abschnitte.text: With some German words, the vowel gets two little dots in the plural. These dots are called an **umlaut**. Ein Vogel, viele **Vögel** (one bird, many birds): the o becomes ö. Ein Baum, viele **Bäume** (one tree, many trees): au becomes äu. Often an ending is added too, as with “Hut” and **“Hüte”** (hat, hats). Here the u becomes ü, and an e is added.

Some German words look the same in the singular and the plural. Ein **Lehrer**, zwei Lehrer (one teacher, two teachers). Ein Messer, drei Messer (one knife, three knives). Then only the **article** shows what is meant: “der Lehrer” (the teacher) or “die Lehrer” (the teachers). This is because in the plural the article is always **“die”**, even if in the singular it is “der Baum” (the tree) or “das Velo” (the bike).

gewusst: Some German words only exist in the plural, for example “Ferien” (holidays), “Eltern” (parents) and “Leute” (people).
Other words are used almost only in the singular, such as “Milch” (milk) or “Glück” (luck).

teile.einleitung: Prepositions are small words such as “on”, “with”, “for” or “between”. They show how things, people or events relate to each other, for example where something is or when something happens. Although they are so small, in German they often decide which case the following word is in.
wichtigste: In German, prepositions are also called “Verhältniswörter” (relation words).
They show place, time, reason or manner.
Prepositions never change their form.
In German every preposition needs a particular case, for example “with” takes the dative and “for” the accusative.
In standard German, “trotz” (despite) takes the genitive.
Two-way prepositions such as “on” or “in” take the dative or the accusative.
One example of a preposition is “between”.

abschnitte.text: A **preposition** is a word that expresses a relationship between two things. In the sentence “The cat is sitting on the roof”, “on” says where the cat is. The word comes from the Latin “praepositio”, which means “placing in front”. This is because prepositions usually come before the word they belong to. Together with this word they form a group of words, for example “on the roof” or “after school”.

In German every preposition decides the **case** of the following noun. Prepositions that take the dative include aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von and zu (out of, at, with, after, since, from, to). Prepositions that take the accusative include durch, für, gegen, ohne and um (through, for, against, without, around). In standard German, wegen, trotz, während and statt (because of, despite, during, instead of) need the genitive. In spoken German you often hear the dative with “wegen” and “trotz” too.

Nine German prepositions can take two cases: an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor and zwischen (at, on, behind, in, next to, above, under, in front of, between). They are called **two-way prepositions**. If you ask “Where?”, the dative follows: “The book is lying on the table” (in German with the dative “dem Tisch”). If you ask “Where to?”, the accusative follows: “I am putting the book on the table” (in German with the accusative “den Tisch”). With this question trick you almost always find the right case.

Prepositions can express very different relationships. Prepositions of place say where something is, for example “in the woods” or “next to the school”. Prepositions of time give the time, such as “since Monday” or “before dinner”. Causal prepositions give a **reason**, for example “because of the rain”. Prepositions of manner describe how something is done, such as “with joy” or “without help”.

Many verbs, nouns and adjectives need one particular preposition. In English you say “be interested in”, “wait for” or “be afraid of”. You simply have to learn these **fixed combinations**, because they cannot be worked out logically, and they differ from language to language. In German, the preposition and the article often merge into one word: “in dem” becomes “im” and “zu der” becomes “zur”. Some German prepositions even come after the noun, as in “meiner Meinung nach” (in my opinion).

begriffe.erklaerung: The German name for the preposition (Verhältniswort), because it shows a relationship between things.
The form a noun is in: nominative, genitive, dative or accusative.
A German preposition that takes the dative or the accusative depending on whether you ask “Where?” or “Where to?”.
A preposition and an article merge into one word, for example “zum” from “zu dem”.

gewusst: German has more than a hundred prepositions, but most of them are rarely used.
People learning German as a foreign language often find prepositions especially difficult, because every language uses them differently.
A German word such as “zuliebe” (for the sake of) always comes after the noun: “dem Hund zuliebe” (for the dog’s sake).

teile.einleitung: Pronouns are words that stand in place of a noun or go with it. Instead of saying “Tim” again and again, you can simply say “he”. This makes texts shorter and much less boring.
wichtigste: In German, pronouns are also called “Fürwörter” (for-words).
The word comes from the Latin “pro nomine”, which means “for a noun”.
Personal pronouns such as “I”, “you” or “we” stand for people and things.
Possessive pronouns such as “our” show who something belongs to.
Relative pronouns introduce a subordinate clause, like “that” in “the dog that barks”.
Demonstrative pronouns such as “this” point to something particular.
Question pronouns such as “who” or “what” come at the beginning of questions.

abschnitte.text: A **pronoun** replaces a noun or goes with it. In the sentence “I’m giving the children an ice cream”, you can replace “the children” with “them”. In German, pronouns are declined like nouns, so they change their form depending on case, number and gender. That is why German says “er”, “ihn” or “ihm” (he, him, to him), depending on how the word is used in the sentence.

The German **personal pronouns** are ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr and sie (I, you, he, she, it, we, you, they). With them you talk about yourself or others, or speak to someone directly. The polite form “Sie” (you) is written with a capital letter. **Reflexive pronouns** refer back to the subject, for example “I wash my hands” or “She is pleased”, which in German use “mir” and “sich”. In Bernese German, adults are often addressed politely with “Dir”, the plural “you” form.

**Possessive pronouns** show ownership or belonging: my, your, his, her, our, your. Demonstrative pronouns point to something, for example “this”, “that” or “the same”. They help when you want to stress something or tell things apart precisely: “I’ll take this jumper, not that one.” In German, possessive pronouns match the noun they go with, which is why it is “mein Velo” (my bike) but “meine Tasche” (my bag).

Question pronouns, or **interrogative pronouns**, are who, what, which and what kind of. With them you ask about people or things. **Relative pronouns**, in German der, die, das or welcher (who, which, that), introduce a relative clause. In the sentence “The dog that is barking belongs to Tim”, the relative clause explains more precisely which dog is meant. In German there is always a comma before a relative clause.

Sometimes you do not know exactly who is meant. Then you use **indefinite pronouns** such as someone, nobody, one, all, something or nothing. “Someone knocked at the door” says that a person knocked, but not who. The German “man” (one, people) is a pronoun like this too, as in “Man soll nicht über die Strasse rennen” (You shouldn’t run across the road). Altogether, grammar distinguishes about seven kinds of pronoun.

begriffe.erklaerung: The German name for the pronoun (Fürwort), because it stands for a noun.
A pronoun for people and things, for example I, you, we.
A pronoun that shows who something belongs to, for example our.
A pronoun that introduces a subordinate clause and refers to a word before it.
A pronoun for people or things that are not specified, for example someone or nothing.

gewusst: Depending on the sentence, the little German word “sie” can mean “she”, “they” or, written as “Sie”, a polite “you”.
Children often only learn the word “I” at about the age of two; before that, many talk about themselves using their own name.
In English there is now only one single word for both the familiar and the polite “you”: “you”.

teile.einleitung: A noun is a word that names people, animals, things, places or feelings. In German it is also called a “Namenwort” (naming word) or “Substantiv”. In German, nouns are easy to recognise, because they are always written with a capital first letter.
wichtigste: Nouns name living things, objects, places and also feelings or ideas.
In German, nouns are written with a capital first letter.
In German a noun often has an article in front of it, such as der, die or das (the).
Every German noun has a grammatical gender.
Nouns come in the singular and in the plural.
Table, hammer, sun and joy are nouns.
Other German names for nouns are “Namenwort” and “Substantiv”.

abschnitte.text: A **noun** gives everything a name. It can name people such as child or teacher, animals such as cat, things such as **table** or hammer, and places such as Bern. Things you cannot touch are nouns too, for example feelings such as **joy** or ideas such as friendship. In German they are also called naming words (Namenwörter) or substantives.

In German, all nouns are written with a **capital first letter**. This is special, because in almost all other languages nouns are written with a small letter. A trick for recognising nouns in German: you can put an article in front of them, such as “der Hammer” (the hammer) or “die Freude” (the joy). Words of other word classes also become nouns when they are used like this: “Lachen” (laughing), “Schwimmen” (swimming).

Every German noun has a grammatical **gender**. Masculine nouns have the article “der”, as in “der Löffel” (the spoon). Feminine ones have “die”, as in “die Sonne” (the sun), and neuter ones “das”, as in “das Haus” (the house). These little words are called **articles**. You often just have to learn the gender, because it has nothing to do with real-life sex: for example, the German word for girl, “Mädchen”, is neuter.

Most nouns come in the **singular** and the plural: one table, many tables. In German the article in the plural is always “die”. In a sentence, German nouns also change their form depending on the case: der Hund, des Hundes, dem Hund, den Hund (the dog). This change is called declension.

In German you can very easily join nouns to make new words. “Haus” (house) and “Tür” (door) become **“Haustür”** (front door), and “Schule” (school) and “Tasche” (bag) become “Schultasche” (school bag). The gender always follows the last part: “die Tür”, so “die Haustür”. This sometimes produces very long words, such as “Bundesverfassungsgericht” (Federal Constitutional Court).

begriffe.erklaerung: A word that names living things, objects or ideas.
Another word for noun.
A little word that goes with a noun, such as “the” or “a”; in German der, die, das or ein, eine.
The grammatical division of nouns into masculine, feminine and neuter.

gewusst: German is one of very few languages in the world in which all nouns are written with a capital letter.
Some German nouns have a different meaning depending on their gender, such as “der See” (the lake) and “die See” (the sea).
In Switzerland some nouns have a different gender from in Germany; people often say “das Tram” rather than “die Tram” (the tram).

teile.einleitung: A commentary is a newspaper or media piece in which someone gives their view on a current event. Unlike a report, it puts forward an opinion and backs it up with arguments. Commentaries help readers to form their own judgement.
wichtigste: The commentary is one of the opinion-based forms of journalism.
It judges a current event from a personal point of view.
Commentaries are usually signed with the writer’s name.
The Swiss Press Council requires facts and comment to be clearly kept apart.
Special forms are the leading article, the satirical sketch and the column.
A review discusses and judges a book, a film or a concert.

abschnitte.text: Journalistic texts are divided into **informative** and **opinion-based** forms. A **report** gives the facts as objectively as possible. A **commentary**, on the other hand, judges what has happened and puts forward a reasoned opinion. Because it is a personal view, the person’s name usually appears underneath. That way readers know who holds this opinion.

A commentary usually begins with the **occasion**, the current event. First it briefly explains what it is about. Then come the **judgement** and the **arguments**. At the end there is often a conclusion or a demand. A good commentary is clear, well reasoned and understandable even for people who hold a different opinion.

The **Swiss Press Council** has drawn up rules for journalism. One important rule is that facts and comment must be clearly **kept apart**. Readers should be able to tell what is fact and what is opinion. That is why commentaries are labelled as such. This keeps the reporting trustworthy.

abschnitte.titel: Leading article, satirical sketch and column
abschnitte.text: The **leading article** expresses a newspaper’s position on an important topic and often appears in a prominent place. It is frequently written by the editor-in-chief. The **satirical sketch** (Glosse) is short, sharp and ironic, often with a surprising twist at the end. The **column** appears regularly, by the same person, in a fixed place. The name originally refers to a column in the page layout.

A special form of judgement is the **review**, also called a critique. It gives information about a book, a film, a play or a concert and judges it with reasons. Reviews often appear in the **arts section** of a newspaper. They help the public decide whether a work is worth it.

gewusst: The Swiss Press Council is run by the media industry itself and rules on complaints about newspaper articles and broadcasts.
The word “column” comes from the Latin “columna”, which means pillar.

teile.einleitung: A word field is a group of words with similar meanings. The word field “go”, for example, includes walk, stroll and run. Word fields help you write texts that are varied and precise.
wichtigste: A **word field** is made of words with related meanings from the same word class.
The words in a word field mark out each other’s meanings.
The **word field theory** was founded by the linguist **Jost Trier** around 1931.
If one word in the field changes, the others shift too.
At school, word fields are used to find more fitting words.

abschnitte.text: The word field **go** includes walk, stroll, run, creep, hurry and wander. They all describe moving on foot, but each word means something different. Someone who **creeps** is quiet and slow. Someone who **hurries** is in a rush. There is also a large word field for **say**: whisper, shout, answer, explain or mumble.

Jost Trier imagined the words of a field like the pieces of a **mosaic**. Each word covers part of the meaning, and together they fill the field. If a word drops out or a new one is added, the others have to share out their space again. That is why you can best understand the meaning of a word if you know its neighbours in the field.

If you keep writing “said” or “went” in an essay, the text becomes monotonous. A look at the word field helps you find the right word. “He whispered” shows at once that someone is speaking quietly. That way the text becomes more precise and more exciting. You can also find word fields in dictionaries of synonyms.

gewusst: In his book of 1931, Jost Trier studied the words to do with the mind, such as words for knowledge and cleverness.
A word field and a word family are not the same thing: a word family is made of words with the same stem, such as drive, driver and driving.

teile.einleitung: In principle, the same German spelling applies in Switzerland as in Germany and Austria. But there is one important special feature: the Eszett (the sharp S) is not used, and people always write ss instead.
wichtigste: In Switzerland and Liechtenstein the Eszett is not used.
Instead of the Eszett, people always write ss, for example in “Strasse” (street) and “gross” (big).
From 1938 the canton of Zurich no longer taught the Eszett in its state schools.
In 1974 the Neue Zürcher Zeitung was the last Swiss daily newspaper to give it up.
Since 2017 a capital Eszett has been part of official spelling.
After a short vowel, ss is written everywhere, as in “Fluss” (river).

abschnitte.text: Where an **Eszett** is written in Germany, Switzerland has **ss**. So it is “Strasse” (street), “gross” (big), “Fuss” (foot) and “heissen” (to be called). **Liechtenstein** does without the Eszett too. In Germany, Austria and Luxembourg it is used. The umlauts ä, ö and ü, on the other hand, are a completely normal part of Swiss writing.

The **Zurich education department** decided that from 1 January **1938** the Eszett would no longer be taught in the canton’s state schools. Other cantons followed. For a long time some newspapers still went on using the Eszett. On 4 November **1974** the **Neue Zürcher Zeitung** gave it up, as the last Swiss daily newspaper to do so. To this day there is no key for the Eszett on the Swiss keyboard.

After a **short vowel**, ss is written everywhere, in Germany too: “Fluss” (river), “Kuss” (kiss), “essen” (to eat). After a **long vowel** or a double vowel sound, Germany uses an Eszett, for example in the words for street and to be called. Switzerland makes no difference here. Since 29 June **2017** there has also been a **capital Eszett** in official spelling. Like the small one, it is not used in Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: When two words look the same
abschnitte.text: Without the Eszett, some words look the same. In Switzerland “in Massen” can mean **“in large amounts”** or **“in moderation”**. In Germany, “Massen” (masses) is told apart from the form with an Eszett that comes from “Mass” (measure). In Switzerland only the **context** shows what is meant. But cases like this are rare and hardly ever lead to misunderstandings.

gewusst: The Eszett originally developed from two letters joined together.
As well as ss, Switzerland also has its own words, the Helvetisms, such as “Velo” (bike), “parkieren” (to park) or “Znüni” (mid-morning snack).

teile.einleitung: The German language has developed over many centuries and is still changing today. From an ancient parent language came, by way of Germanic, Old High German, Middle High German and finally the German of today. In Switzerland this development has led to a special situation: people speak dialect and write Standard German.
wichtigste: German belongs to the family of Indo-European languages.
The second sound shift separated High German from Low German.
Through it, for example, “Appel” became the word “Apfel” (apple).
In the 16th century, Martin Luther’s Bible translation helped to unify the written language.
Words such as “Fenster” (window), “Mauer” (wall) and “Strasse” (street) come from Latin.
The spelling reform agreed in 1996 came into force in 1998.
German-speaking Switzerland has diglossia: dialect in everyday life, Standard German in writing.

abschnitte.text: German belongs to the **Indo-European languages**, a huge family that also includes English, French, Italian, Russian and Hindi. All these languages go back to a shared parent language that was spoken many thousands of years ago. Within this family, German is one of the Germanic languages, like English, Dutch and the Scandinavian languages. That is why words such as “Haus”, “house” and “huis” are similar.

With the first sound shift, the Germanic languages split off from the other Indo-European languages. The **second sound shift** took place roughly between the 6th and 8th centuries and affected only the south of the German-speaking area. In it, p became pf or ff, t became z or ss, and k became ch. So “Appel” became “Apfel” (apple) and “Water” became “Wasser” (water). In the north the old sounds were kept, and Low German is still spoken there today.

The oldest German texts were written around 750 in **Old High German**, for example the Song of Hildebrand. Around 1200 people wrote **Middle High German**, the language of the Song of the Nibelungs. After that, Early New High German developed. In the 16th century Martin Luther translated the Bible into a German that was understood in many regions. Together with printing, this did a great deal to create a shared written language.

Languages are always borrowing words from each other. The Romans already brought many **loanwords** into the Germanic area, for example “Fenster” (window) from the Latin “fenestra”, “Mauer” (wall) from “murus” and “Strasse” (street) from “strata”. Later many words came from French, in Switzerland for example “Velo” (bike) or “Trottoir” (pavement). Today German mainly takes on words from English, such as “Computer” or “Team”.

In German-speaking Switzerland, people speak **Swiss German**, Alemannic dialects, in everyday life. Writing, on the other hand, is mostly in Standard German, and you also hear it at school and on the news. This division is called **diglossia**. Spelling has also developed in its own way: from 1938 the canton of Zurich led the way in no longer teaching the Eszett in its state schools. In 1996 the German-speaking countries agreed on a joint spelling reform, which came into force in 1998.

begriffe.erklaerung: The name of the large language family that German belongs to.
A regular change of sounds in a language over a long time.
A word taken over from another language.
Two forms of a language used side by side for different purposes, such as dialect and Standard German.

gewusst: In many Swiss dialects people say “Chind” instead of “Kind” (child), because the sound shift went even further here than in Standard German.
The English “apple” still shows the old form that was also usual in the south before the second sound shift.
A text from around 800 is hardly understandable to German speakers today without a translation.

teile.einleitung: Hyperbole is a stylistic device in which you deliberately exaggerate a lot. If someone says “I’ve rung you a thousand times”, they do not mean it literally, but want to stress something. We come across hyperbole in everyday life, in poems and in advertising.
wichtigste: Hyperbole is a strong, deliberate exaggeration.
It is not meant literally but is supposed to make a statement stronger.
Examples are “waiting for ages” or “ringing a thousand times”.
The opposite is litotes, an understatement.
Litotes often denies the opposite, as in “not bad”.

abschnitte.text: The word **hyperbole** comes from Greek and means “exaggeration”. You deliberately say more than is really true. Nobody really rings a thousand times or waits for an eternity. But the exaggeration shows how strong a feeling is, for example impatience or anger. That is why everyone understands what is meant.

In everyday life we use hyperbole all the time, often without noticing. “I’m dying of hunger”, “I’ve told you a hundred times” or “It’s freezing in here” are examples. Words such as “dead tired”, “ancient” or “snail’s pace” exaggerate too. They make language lively and vivid. But if you use them too often, you soon seem hard to believe.

Poets use hyperbole to express feelings especially strongly. In fairy tales and legends there are giants who move mountains and heroes of enormous strength. **Advertising** likes to exaggerate too, for example with “the best ice cream in the world”. In a text analysis you describe what effect the exaggeration has.

**Litotes** is seen as the opposite of hyperbole. It **understates**, often by denying the opposite. “Not bad” usually means “very good”. “That wasn’t entirely without danger” means “That was dangerous”. It is precisely the restraint that sometimes makes the statement stronger.

gewusst: The curve called a “hyperbola” in maths has the same Greek name, which means something like “throwing beyond”.
Many hyperboles with numbers like “thousand” or “hundred” are so everyday that you hardly notice them as exaggerations any more.

t1433z14.t: Writing German words separately or together

teile.einleitung: Do you write two words apart or join them into one word? In German, the rules on writing words separately or together help with this question. They were reorganised in the spelling reform.
wichtigste: A noun and a verb are usually written separately, for example “Rad fahren” (to ride a bike).
Two verbs are written separately, for example “spazieren gehen” (to go for a walk).
Separable verbs such as “teilnehmen” (to take part) are written as one word in the infinitive.
Combinations with “irgend” (some) are written together, such as “irgendetwas” (something).
Numbers below a million are written as one word, such as “dreizehn” (thirteen).
When three identical letters meet, all three stay: “Schifffahrt” (shipping).

abschnitte.text: When a noun is combined with a verb, the two are usually written **separately**. That is why it is “Rad fahren” (to ride a bike), “Ski fahren” (to ski) or “Auto fahren” (to drive a car). The noun keeps its capital letter. Two verbs also stand separately side by side: “spazieren gehen” (to go for a walk), “schwimmen gehen” (to go swimming) or “lesen lernen” (to learn to read). For “kennenlernen” (to get to know), both spellings have been allowed since 2006.

Some verbs are made of an add-on and a verb, for example **“teilnehmen”** (to take part) or **“stattfinden”** (to take place). In the infinitive they are written **together**. In a sentence, however, the parts are split up: “Ich nehme am Lager teil” (I am taking part in the camp) or “Das Fest findet morgen statt” (The party takes place tomorrow). A trick: if the first part moves to the end of the sentence, it belongs to the verb.

Words with **“irgend”** are always written together: “irgendetwas” (something), “irgendwann” (sometime), “irgendwo” (somewhere). The adverb **“zurzeit”** means “at the moment” and is also written as one word. It is only written apart in a phrase like “zur Zeit der Römer” (in Roman times), where “Zeit” (time) is a noun. **Numbers** below a million are written as one word and in small letters, for example “dreizehn” (thirteen) or “zweihundertvierzig” (two hundred and forty).

In compounds, three identical letters can meet. Since the **spelling reform**, all three stay: “Schifffahrt” (shipping), “Balletttänzer” (ballet dancer) or “Kaffeeersatz” (coffee substitute). If you find it clearer, you may use a hyphen: “Schiff-Fahrt”. Today the **Council for German Orthography** watches over the rules. Experts from several countries work together in it, including from Switzerland.

gewusst: Before the spelling reform, “Schiffahrt” was written with only two f’s.
The number 999,999 is one single long word in German: neunhundertneunundneunzigtausendneunhundertneunundneunzig.

teile.einleitung: Rhetoric is the art of speaking well and persuading others. It was already being taught more than 2000 years ago in ancient Greece and Rome. We still need it today, for example for a presentation at school, in politics or at work.
wichtigste: Rhetoric means the art of speaking and comes from Greek.
Aristotle named three means of persuasion: ethos, pathos and logos.
Ethos is based on the speaker’s credibility.
Marcus Tullius Cicero is regarded as the most important speaker of Roman antiquity.
A rhetorical question does not expect an answer.
With the “captatio benevolentiae”, a speaker tries to win the audience’s goodwill.
A tricolon is a series of three similar parts.

abschnitte.text: **Rhetoric** arose in Greece in the 5th century BC. In cities such as Athens, citizens had to speak for themselves in court and in the people’s assembly. Anyone who could speak well had great advantages. In the 4th century BC, the philosopher **Aristotle** wrote a famous textbook on rhetoric. Later the Romans took over this art and developed it further.

According to Aristotle, there are three ways to persuade. **Ethos** is based on the speaker’s credibility: you believe someone who seems honest and competent. **Pathos** appeals to the audience’s feelings, for example pity, joy or outrage. **Logos** persuades through arguments, evidence and logical thinking. Good speeches usually combine all three.

The Roman **Marcus Tullius Cicero** lived from 106 to 43 BC and is regarded as Rome’s greatest speaker. His speeches in court and in the Senate are still read in Latin lessons today. Later the teacher Quintilian wrote a long textbook on training to be a speaker. The Romans divided the preparation of a speech into five steps: finding the material, arranging it, putting it into words, learning it by heart and delivering it.

Speakers use special language devices to make an impact. A **rhetorical question** such as “Who wants to lose?” does not expect an answer but makes a statement. A tricolon such as “Liberty, equality, fraternity” sticks in the memory because it is in three parts. A parenthesis is an insertion in the middle of a sentence. A euphemism makes something sound nicer, such as “pass away” instead of “die”.

A speech often begins with the captatio benevolentiae, the attempt to win goodwill, for example with thanks or a compliment to the audience. For good presentations, voice, posture, eye contact and pauses also matter. In Switzerland, for example, politicians give speeches on the national holiday, 1 August. If you know about rhetoric, you can also spot more easily when someone is trying to manipulate you with tricks.

begriffe.erklaerung: Persuading through the speaker’s credibility.
Persuading through the feelings a speech stirs up.
Persuading through arguments and logic.
A question to which no answer is expected.
An expression that makes something unpleasant sound nicer.

gewusst: The Greek speaker Demosthenes is said to have practised with pebbles in his mouth to speak more clearly.
In the Middle Ages, rhetoric was one of the seven liberal arts taught at schools and universities.
Many famous speeches in history use groups of three, because audiences can remember three things well.

teile.einleitung: The Walser are a people who originally came from the Upper Valais. From the 13th century many of them moved away to other Alpine valleys. In some places their special dialect has survived to this day.
wichtigste: The Walser come from the German-speaking **Upper Valais**.
From the **13th century** they founded settlements in other Alpine areas.
There are Walser settlements in the **Grisons**, in **Ticino**, in **Piedmont** and in **Vorarlberg**.
They speak **Highest Alemannic** dialects.
The name Walser comes from “Walliser” (people from the Valais).

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages, families from the Upper Valais moved over the Alpine passes into other valleys. They often settled in high areas that had hardly been inhabited until then. In return, the local rulers gave them special rights, such as more personal freedom. These rights are called the **Walser law**.

In the Grisons, for example, **Davos**, **Vals**, the **Rheinwald** and **Avers** are Walser areas. In Ticino, **Bosco/Gurin** is the only municipality where German is traditionally spoken. Other Walser places are in Piedmont and the Aosta Valley in Italy, at **Triesenberg** in Liechtenstein, and in the **Kleinwalsertal** and the **Grosses Walsertal** in Austria.

The Walser took their **Valais dialect** with them. In the remote valleys it survived for a long time and sometimes sounds very old-fashioned. That is why language researchers are especially interested in it. Today, in some Walser villages in Italy, only a few people still speak the old dialect, and associations are working to preserve it.

gewusst: Typical of Walser settlements are single farms and wooden houses spread out widely across the slope.
By car, the Kleinwalsertal in Austria can only be reached through Germany.

teile.einleitung: Konrad Duden was a German teacher and language scholar. He worked hard to make German spelt the same way everywhere. His dictionary from 1880 became the basis of standard German spelling.
wichtigste: Konrad Duden lived from 1829 to 1911.
He was a grammar school teacher and head teacher in Germany.
In 1880 his “Complete Orthographic Dictionary of the German Language” came out.
Before that, there was no standard spelling in the German-speaking world.
Today the name “Duden” stands for a whole series of dictionaries.

abschnitte.text: Konrad Duden was born in 1829 and worked as a **grammar school teacher** and later as a head teacher. He saw that words were spelt differently depending on the region and the school. That made teaching difficult. Duden wanted everyone in the German-speaking world to write by the same rules. He died in 1911.

In **1880** Konrad Duden published his “**Complete Orthographic Dictionary of the German Language**”. Orthography means spelling. The book quickly became very popular and the most important basis for standard German spelling. Around 1900, Germany, Austria and Switzerland agreed on shared rules, which Duden had helped to work out.

The **Duden** still comes out in new editions today. In many schools, offices and newsrooms it is an important reference book. New words are added when they are used often. Switzerland uses the same spelling, with a few special features: the Eszett (the special letter for a sharp s) does not exist here, and people always write ss, as in “gross” (big) and “Strasse” (street).

gewusst: Many people say “I’ll look it up in the Duden”, even when they are using a different dictionary.

teile.einleitung: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing was a German writer and thinker of the Enlightenment. He lived from 1729 to 1781 and wrote plays, fables and essays about art and religion. His best-known work is “Nathan the Wise”.
wichtigste: Lessing lived from 1729 to 1781 and belongs to the age of the Enlightenment.
“Miss Sara Sampson” from 1755 is regarded as the first important middle-class tragedy.
“Minna von Barnhelm” from 1767 is a famous comedy.
From 1770 Lessing ran the ducal library in Wolfenbüttel.
“Nathan the Wise” is set in Jerusalem at the time of the Crusades.
At its heart is the parable of the rings, which argues for tolerance.

abschnitte.text: Lessing was born in **Kamenz** in Saxony in 1729. He studied in Leipzig and later worked as a critic, writer and dramaturge. Lessing belongs to the **Enlightenment**, a time when people relied on reason and thinking for themselves. He also wrote **fables**, short animal stories with a lesson. In his writings he liked to argue cleverly for his ideas.

Until then, the heroes of tragedies had mostly been kings and nobles. With “**Miss Sara Sampson**” in 1755, Lessing put middle-class characters on stage as tragic heroes for the first time. This form is called **middle-class tragedy**. Later came “Emilia Galotti”. With “**Minna von Barnhelm**” he wrote a **comedy** in 1767 that is set shortly after the Seven Years’ War.

From **1770** Lessing ran the famous ducal library in **Wolfenbüttel**. There he had access to a great many old books and manuscripts. During this time he wrote “Emilia Galotti” and “Nathan the Wise”. Lessing died in Brunswick in 1781. The library in Wolfenbüttel still remembers him today.

abschnitte.titel: Nathan and the parable of the rings
abschnitte.text: “**Nathan the Wise**” is set in **Jerusalem** at the time of the Crusades. There the Jewish merchant Nathan, a Christian Knight Templar and Sultan **Saladin** meet. Saladin asks Nathan which religion is the true one. Nathan answers with the **parable of the rings**, a story about three identical rings. It argues that Judaism, Christianity and Islam should treat each other with **tolerance**.

gewusst: Lessing’s friend, the philosopher Moses Mendelssohn, is thought to be the model for Nathan.
“Nathan the Wise” was only performed on stage for the first time after Lessing’s death.

teile.einleitung: A subordinate clause is a clause that cannot stand on its own but depends on a main clause. It adds to the main clause and says, for example, why, when or for what purpose something happens. Together, main and subordinate clauses form a complex sentence.
wichtigste: A subordinate clause depends on a main clause.
A main clause and a subordinate clause together are called a complex sentence.
In a German subordinate clause with a joining word, the finite verb normally comes last.
In German, subordinate clauses are separated from the main clause by a comma.
A causal clause gives a reason, a final clause a purpose.
A concessive clause typically begins with “although”.
Relative clauses begin with a relative pronoun such as “who”, “which” or “that”.

abschnitte.text: A **main clause** can stand on its own: We are staying inside. A **subordinate clause** such as “because it is raining”, on the other hand, does not make complete sense by itself. It depends on the main clause and gives extra information. If you join the two, you get a **complex sentence**: We are staying inside because it is raining.

An important feature in German is where the verb goes. In a subordinate clause with a joining word, the **finite verb**, the form of the verb that changes with the person, normally comes last. Compare: “Es regnet heute” (It is raining today) and “Wir bleiben drinnen, weil es heute regnet” (We are staying inside because it is raining today). In German, subordinate clauses are also always separated from the main clause by a **comma**.

Subordinate clauses are often named after their meaning. A **causal clause** gives a reason, usually with “because” or “since”. A final clause gives a purpose with “so that”: She speaks loudly so that everyone can hear. A **concessive clause** with “although” gives a counter-reason, and a consecutive clause gives a result: He told the story so funnily that everyone laughed. There are also temporal clauses for time and conditional clauses for conditions.

A **relative clause** describes a noun more precisely. In German it begins with a relative pronoun such as der, die, das, welcher or dessen (who, which, whose). Example: The book that you lent me is exciting. In German, if the relative clause is in the middle of the sentence, it is marked off with a comma in front and behind.

abschnitte.titel: Subordinate clauses as parts of a sentence
abschnitte.text: A subordinate clause can also take on the role of a whole part of the sentence. In the German proverb “Wer wagt, gewinnt” (Who dares, wins), “Wer wagt” is a **subject clause**, because it stands in the place of the subject. In “I know that you are right”, the subordinate clause is an object clause. If you use subordinate clauses skilfully, you can link ideas precisely and write in a varied way.

begriffe.erklaerung: A clause that can stand on its own.
A combination of a main clause and at least one subordinate clause.
The form of the verb that changes to match the person.
A subordinate clause that describes a noun more precisely.
A subordinate clause that gives a reason.

gewusst: A subordinate clause can also come before the main clause; then in German the verb of the main clause moves to the front: “Weil es regnet, bleiben wir drinnen” (Because it is raining, we are staying inside).
Most technical names of subordinate clauses come from Latin; “causa”, for example, means reason.
Some writers, such as Thomas Mann, built sentences with a great many subordinate clauses nested inside one another.

teile.einleitung: Weimar Classicism is a period of German literature. It is closely linked with Johann Wolfgang von Goethe and Friedrich Schiller, who lived in the town of Weimar. Their works are still read and performed today.
wichtigste: Weimar Classicism lasted from about **1786 to 1805**.
It begins with Goethe’s **journey to Italy** and ends with **Schiller’s death**.
Its model was the art of **ancient Greece**.
Important ideals were **harmony**, **balance** and **humanity**.
1797 is called the **year of ballads**.
Schiller’s “William Tell” from 1804 is set in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: In 1786 Goethe travelled to Italy and was deeply impressed by the art of the ancient world. The writers of Classicism sought **harmony** and **balance**. People were to develop into good, well-balanced and humane beings. This aim is called the **ideal of humanity**. In Goethe’s play **“Iphigenia in Tauris”**, the priestess Iphigenia solves a conflict by giving up a trick and telling the truth.

Goethe and Schiller became close friends and worked closely together. They wrote each other many letters and discussed their works. In **1797** they competed in writing ballads, which is why it is called the **year of ballads**. Goethe’s **“The Sorcerer’s Apprentice”** and Schiller’s **“The Glove”** were written then. This collaboration ended with Schiller’s death in 1805.

Goethe worked on his **“Faust”** for decades. The first part came out in **1808**, the second only after his death. In it, the scholar Faust makes a pact with the devil **Mephistopheles**. Faust promises him his soul if he ever wants to hold on to a single moment. “Faust” is regarded as one of the most important works of German literature.

In 1804 Schiller wrote the play **“William Tell”** about the people of Central Switzerland fighting for their freedom. It tells of the Rütli oath and the shooting of the apple. Schiller himself never went to Switzerland and relied on old chronicles. The play later became a Swiss national drama.

Ludwig van Beethoven set Schiller’s poem **“Ode to Joy”** to music in the final movement of his **9th Symphony**. Today the melody is the anthem of the European Union. In Weimar, Goethe and Schiller stand side by side as a monument in front of the theatre.

gewusst: Goethe lived in Weimar for more than fifty years.
Together with Wieland and Herder, Goethe and Schiller are often called the great four of Weimar.
Weimar Classicism is now part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site “Classical Weimar”.

teile.einleitung: Word classes are groups into which all the words of a language can be divided. Whether a word is a noun, a verb or an adjective depends on how it changes and what job it does in the sentence. If you know the word classes, you understand sentences better and make fewer mistakes with capital and small letters in German.
wichtigste: Every word in German belongs to a word class.
In German, nouns such as “die Freiheit” (freedom) or “der Hund” (the dog) are written with a capital letter.
Verbs can be conjugated, that is changed by person and tense.
Adjectives describe qualities and can be compared, for example “gross, grösser, am grössten” (big, bigger, biggest).
The German der, die, das and ein (the, a) are articles and come before nouns.
Words such as “yesterday” or “here” are adverbs and always stay the same.
The same word shape can belong to a different word class depending on the sentence, such as “laufen” (to run) and “das Laufen” (running).

abschnitte.text: A **word class** is a group of words with similar features. The main question is whether a word **can change** or not. The German verb “lesen” (to read), for example, can become “liest” (reads) or “las” (read), whereas the word “gestern” (yesterday) always stays the same. You also look at what job a word does in the sentence.

The **noun** (naming word) names living things, objects and ideas, such as “bike” or “freedom”. The **verb** (doing word) says what someone does or what happens, for example “play”. The **adjective** (describing word) describes what something is like, such as “fast” in the sentence “The bike is fast.” These three word classes make up most of our words.

**Articles** such as the German der, die, das and ein (the, a) go with nouns. **Pronouns** such as I, you or she can replace nouns. Prepositions such as “on” or “under” show relationships, and conjunctions such as “and” or “because” link words and sentences. Adverbs such as “yesterday”, “there” or “gladly” say more about time, place or manner.

In many Swiss schools pupils learn a system with **five word classes**, following the linguist Hans Glinz. It distinguishes verb, noun, adjective, pronoun and **particle**. In this system the articles count as pronouns, and all words that cannot change, such as adverbs, prepositions and conjunctions, are called particles. In Germany pupils often learn ten word classes, but they mean the same words.

Many words can change their word class. If you put an article in front of the German verb “laufen” (to run), it becomes a noun: “Das Laufen macht Spass” (Running is fun). This process is called **nominalisation**, and in German the new noun is written with a capital letter. Adjectives can also become nouns, for example “das Gute” (the good) or “etwas Schönes” (something beautiful).

There are simple tests for working out word classes. If you can put an article in front of it, it is usually a noun. If you can combine the word with “I”, “you” or “we” and put it into the past, it is a verb. If a word can be compared, it is usually an **adjective**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A word for living things, objects or ideas; in German it is written with a capital letter.
A word for an activity or an event; it can be conjugated.
A word that describes what something is like, for example fast or blue.
The basic form of a verb as it appears in the dictionary, for example the German “lesen” (to read).
To change a verb by person and tense, as in the German ich lese, du liest, er las (I read, you read, he read).

gewusst: More than 2000 years ago, Greek scholars were already dividing the words of their language into word classes.
In English nouns are written with small letters, but in German with capitals, which is a rare feature in Europe.
The German word “Laufen” can be a verb or a noun, depending on the sentence.

teile.einleitung: Every story has characters. The most important of them is the main character; everything revolves around them. There are also opponents and minor characters who make the story exciting.
wichtigste: The main character is the most important character in a story.
The opponent fights against the main character or wants to harm them.
Minor characters appear but are not at the centre.
Pippi Longstocking lives with the monkey Mr Nilsson and the horse Little Old Man.
Pinocchio’s nose grows longer when he lies.
Ronia the Robber’s Daughter’s father is called Matt.

abschnitte.text: The **main character** is at the centre of a story. They have most of the adventures and often have to solve a problem. Experts also call them the **protagonist**. You usually learn a lot about their thoughts and feelings. That way you are on the edge of your seat with them as you read.

The **opponent** makes life difficult for the main character. They want to harm them or stop them reaching their goal. This creates **tension**. **Minor characters** are friends, family or helpers. They appear in the story but are not at the centre.

The Swedish writer **Astrid Lindgren** invented many famous main characters. **Pippi Longstocking** lives in Villa Villekulla with the little monkey **Mr Nilsson** and the horse **Little Old Man**. Pippi is so strong that she can lift her horse. **Ronia the Robber’s Daughter** lives in Matt’s Fort in the forest. Her father **Matt** is the chief of a band of robbers.

**Pinocchio** is a wooden puppet that comes to life. He comes from a book by the Italian Carlo Collodi. Every time Pinocchio lies, his **nose grows longer**. **Peter Pan** lives in Neverland, can **fly** and never wants to grow up. Switzerland has well-known main characters too, for example Heidi or Ursli with his bell.

gewusst: Pippi Longstocking has a suitcase full of gold coins and can therefore buy everything herself.
The word “protagonist” comes from Greek and means something like “first fighter”.

teile.einleitung: The comma is a small punctuation mark with a big effect. It structures sentences, separates lists and makes texts easier to read. Sometimes a comma even changes the whole meaning of a sentence.
wichtigste: The comma separates parts of a sentence from each other.
In lists there are commas between the items, but not before “and” or “or”.
In German there is always a comma before “aber” (but) when it introduces a contrast.
In German, subordinate clauses, for example with “weil” (because), are separated from the main clause by a comma.
Relative clauses are marked off with a comma in front and behind.
After a form of address such as “Lukas” there is a comma.
Insertions such as “our teacher” go between two commas.

abschnitte.text: The **comma** is a punctuation mark that looks like a little hook. It shows the reader where one part of a sentence ends and a new one begins. When reading aloud, you often make a short pause at a comma. The word comes from Greek and originally meant “section”.

When you list several things, you separate them with commas. In the sentence “I’m buying apples, pears and bananas”, there is therefore a comma after “apples”. In a list there is normally **no comma** before “and” and “or”. That is why “Do you want tea or coffee?” does not need a comma either. In German, however, there is always a comma before words that introduce a **contrast**, such as “aber” (but), “sondern” (but rather) or “doch” (yet).

In German, a **subordinate clause** is always separated from the main clause by a comma. So it is correct to write: “Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil es regnet” (I’m staying at home because it’s raining). This also applies to clauses with “dass” (that), “wenn” (if), “obwohl” (although) or “damit” (so that). **Relative clauses** are marked off with commas on both sides when they are in the middle of a sentence. An example: “The bike, which is in the cellar, is new.”

When you speak to someone directly, you separate the **form of address** with a comma: “Lukas, come here, please!” Exclamations such as “Oh”, “Yes” or “No” at the start of a sentence also often get a comma. An **insertion** that explains something more precisely goes between two commas. So it is correct to write: “Mr Meier, our teacher, is ill.”

A missing or wrongly placed comma can completely change the meaning of a sentence. A famous example is “Come on, let’s eat, Grandpa!” and “Come on, let’s eat Grandpa!” In the first sentence Grandpa is being called to dinner; in the second he is on the menu. That is why people jokingly say: commas save lives. The exact German rules are in the Duden dictionary and in the official rules of German spelling.

begriffe.erklaerung: Marks such as the full stop, comma or question mark that structure a text.
A series of several similar words or parts of a sentence.
A clause that cannot stand on its own and usually begins with a conjunction.
An extra part in the middle of a sentence that explains something.

gewusst: In Switzerland a point rather than a comma is often used for decimals in numbers, for example in prices such as 3.50 francs.
In English, a comma is used before subordinate clauses much less often than in German.
In the past, a slanted stroke called a virgule was often used instead of a comma.

teile.einleitung: If you use other people’s texts for a presentation, a project or your Matura paper, you have to say where they come from. This is called citing your sources. That way others can check where a piece of information comes from, and the work of the authors is recognised.
wichtigste: A source reference shows where a quotation or a piece of information comes from.
For internet sources you give the date you accessed them as well as the address.
In the author-date system, only the author, year and page appear in brackets in the text.
The APA style comes from the American Psychological Association.
“Et al.” means “and others”; the German “vgl.” means “compare” (like “cf.”).
You can identify a book by its ISBN and a digital academic article by its DOI.
Primary sources come directly from the period being studied; secondary sources interpret them.

abschnitte.text: If you pass off other people’s ideas as your own, you are committing **plagiarism**. This is unfair to the authors and is marked severely at school and university. With a **source reference** you show honestly where something comes from. That way others can check whether it is right. A word-for-word **quotation** also goes in quotation marks, and when you take over an idea in your own words, you mark it with **“cf.”** (in German “vgl.”), meaning “compare”.

There are different **citation styles**. In the **author-date system**, also called the Harvard system, a short reference such as “(Müller 2020, p. 15)” appears in the text. It points to the full entry in the **bibliography**. The **APA style** of the American Psychological Association works this way too and is widely used in the social sciences around the world. Other subjects prefer **footnotes** at the bottom of the page.

For a book you usually give the author, title, year of publication, place and publisher. If a source has several authors, people often shorten it with **“et al.”**, Latin for “and others”. For **internet sources**, the **date you accessed them** belongs with the address. Websites change or disappear, and this way it stays clear which version you read.

Books have an **ISBN**, the International Standard Book Number, which today has 13 digits. Magazines and journals have an **ISSN**. Academic articles on the internet often carry a **DOI**, a permanent identifier that keeps them findable. People also distinguish between **primary sources** such as diaries, letters or official documents and **secondary sources** such as textbooks, which interpret this evidence later.

gewusst: The ISBN has existed since the 1970s; it used to have only 10 digits.
Pictures, graphics and videos from the internet also need a source reference.

teile.einleitung: A conjunction is a joining word that links words, parts of sentences or whole sentences. Well-known conjunctions are and, or, but, because and that. Without conjunctions we could only make short, choppy sentences.
wichtigste: In German, conjunctions are also called “Bindewörter” (joining words).
Coordinating conjunctions such as “and” link two main clauses.
Subordinating conjunctions such as “because” introduce a subordinate clause.
In a German clause with “weil” (because), the conjugated verb goes at the end.
“But” expresses a contrast, “because” a reason.
“So that” expresses a purpose or an aim.
Conjunctions never change their form.

abschnitte.text: A **conjunction** is a small word that links other words or sentences. The word comes from the Latin “coniungere”, which means to join. That is why in German it is also called a **Bindewort** (joining word). Conjunctions do not change, which means they always have the same form.

**Coordinating conjunctions** link parts of equal rank, for example two main clauses. The most important ones are and, or, but, for and but rather (in German “sondern”). Example: I am reading a book, and my sister is painting a picture. The word order in the second clause stays normal; in German the verb stays in second place.

**Subordinating conjunctions** introduce a subordinate clause; they are also called subjunctions. Examples are because, that, whether, if, although and so that. In German, the conjugated verb slides **to the end** of the subordinate clause: “Ich bleibe drinnen, weil es regnet” (I’m staying inside because it’s raining). In “I know that you are right” and “I don’t know whether he is coming today”, the German verb also goes at the end.

Each conjunction gives the sentence a particular meaning. “Because” and “for” give a **reason**; “but” and “but rather” a contrast. “So that” expresses a purpose or an aim: I practise so that I get better. “If” gives a condition, and “although” expresses that something happens despite an obstacle.

With conjunctions you can link ideas and make texts flow better. Instead of “It’s raining. We’re staying inside.” it is better to write: We’re staying inside because it’s raining. In German, there is always a comma before subordinating conjunctions. In simple lists, on the other hand, no comma is needed before “and” and “or”.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for conjunction.
A clause that can stand on its own.
A clause that depends on a main clause.
A conjunction that introduces a subordinate clause.

gewusst: The German word for “and” is one of the most common words in the German language.
In spoken German you often hear “weil” (because) with the verb in second place, but in standard German this counts as wrong.
Some conjunctions are made of two parts, such as “either ... or” and “both ... and”.

teile.einleitung: A false anglicism is a word that sounds English but is not used in English at all, or is used with a different meaning. The best-known example is the German word “Handy” for a mobile phone.
wichtigste: False anglicisms sound English but were made up in German.
A “Handy” is called a “mobile phone” or “cell phone” in English.
A German “Beamer” is a “projector” in English.
A German “Oldtimer” is a “vintage car” in English.
If you use false anglicisms abroad, you are often not understood.

abschnitte.text: German has many words from English, for example “Computer” or “Team”. There are also words that only **look** as if they came from English. They are called **false anglicisms**. The word **“Handy”** for a mobile phone is one such example. In English, “handy” actually means “practical” or “easy to use”.

The device that projects pictures onto the wall in the classroom is called a **“Beamer”** in German. In English it is called a **“projector”**. An old car is called an **“Oldtimer”** in German, while in English people speak of a “vintage car” or “classic car”. **“Smoking”** for a formal evening suit is also unknown in English, where people say “tuxedo” or “dinner jacket”.

To many people, English-sounding words seem modern. That is why they like to invent them in advertising and in everyday life. Sometimes they also arise when an English word is shortened or given a new meaning. For travelling and talking with English speakers, it is good to know the **real English words**. Otherwise misunderstandings happen quickly.

gewusst: False anglicisms also exist in other languages, for example in French or Japanese.
In English, “public viewing” does not mean watching football together; it means something quite different, such as viewing a body before a funeral.

teile.einleitung: A back-formation is a special way of making new words. A shorter word is created by leaving out part of a longer word.
wichtigste: In a back-formation, a word-building element is left out.
The longer word came first; the shorter one was formed later.
One German example is “notlanden” (to make an emergency landing), formed from “Notlandung” (emergency landing).
Other examples are “staubsaugen” (to vacuum) from “Staubsauger” (vacuum cleaner) and “bergsteigen” (to climb mountains) from “Bergsteiger” (mountaineer).
Many verbs formed this way are used almost only in the infinitive.

abschnitte.text: Normally words get longer when new ones are formed: “landen” (to land) becomes “Landung” (landing). In a **back-formation** it works the other way round. First there was the noun **“Notlandung”** (emergency landing). Only afterwards did people form the verb **“notlanden”** from it by leaving out the ending “-ung”. So you have to know the history of a word to recognise a back-formation.

The word for the appliance, **“Staubsauger”** (vacuum cleaner), existed before the verb **“staubsaugen”** (to vacuum). It is similar with “Bergsteiger” (mountaineer) and “bergsteigen” (to go mountaineering), or with “Uraufführung” (premiere) and “uraufführen” (to premiere). Verbs like these often feel a bit odd when you conjugate them. People happily say “Wir gehen bergsteigen” (We’re going mountaineering), but rarely “Ich steige berg” (I mountain-climb). That is why many of these verbs are used mainly in the **infinitive**.

You cannot tell from the outside whether a word is a back-formation. If you want to know, you look in an **etymological dictionary** to see which word is recorded first. English has them too, where they are called **back-formations**: “to edit”, for example, came from “editor”. Back-formation shows that language is always changing and that new words arise in surprising ways.

gewusst: Many German verbs formed this way are written as one word, for example “schlafwandeln” (to sleepwalk) from “Schlafwandler” (sleepwalker).
Back-formation is a kind of word formation that linguists count as a form of derivation.

teile.einleitung: Every complete sentence needs a predicate. It says what someone does or what happens. The predicate is always made of one or more verb forms.
wichtigste: The predicate is the part of the sentence that says what happens.
It is always formed by a verb.
In a German statement, the finite verb comes in second place.
A predicate can be made of several parts, such as the German “fährt ab” (leaves).
The parts can form a sentence bracket: “Ich habe Fussball gespielt” (I played football).
The predicate matches the subject in person and number.

abschnitte.text: The **predicate** is the core of the sentence. It says what someone does or what happens. It is always formed by a **verb**. In the sentence “Lena reads”, “reads” is the predicate. Together with the **subject**, which says who does something, it forms the simplest complete sentence. You find the predicate by asking: what does someone do, what happens?

In a German **statement**, the **finite verb** is always the second part of the sentence. Example: “Morgen spielen wir Fussball” (Tomorrow we are playing football). Even if you move the parts of the sentence around, the verb stays in second place: “Wir spielen morgen Fussball.” In a yes/no question, on the other hand, it comes first: “Spielen wir morgen Fussball?” In a subordinate clause it moves to the end.

The predicate is often made of several parts. With **separable verbs** such as “abfahren” (to leave), you say: “Der Zug **fährt** um acht Uhr **ab**” (The train leaves at eight o’clock). Both parts together form the predicate. Tenses such as the perfect are also made of two parts: “Ich **habe** gestern Fussball **gespielt**” (I played football yesterday). The same goes for sentences with modal verbs: “Ich **muss** heute **lernen**” (I have to study today).

When the parts of the predicate are far apart, they enclose the other parts of the sentence. This is called the **sentence bracket** or **verb bracket**. It is typical of German. The finite verb matches the subject: “ich spiele” (I play), but “wir spielen” (we play). This matching is called **agreement**.

gewusst: In long sentences the second part of the predicate can come right at the end, which is why in German you sometimes have to listen until the very last word.
Sentences without a predicate, such as “Watch out!” or “Thanks!”, are called ellipses or exclamations.

teile.einleitung: A unique morpheme is a part of a word that only occurs in one single word. On its own it no longer has any recognisable meaning. A well-known German example is “Him-” in “Himbeere” (raspberry).
wichtigste: A **morpheme** is the smallest part of a word that has a meaning or a job.
A **unique morpheme** only occurs in one single word combination.
Examples are “Him-” in **“Himbeere”** (raspberry) and “Brom-” in **“Brombeere”** (blackberry).
On their own, without the whole word, these parts cannot be understood.
They are also called **blocked morphemes**.

abschnitte.text: In the word “Himbeere” you recognise the part **“Beere”** (berry) straight away, because it is a word of its own. But the part **“Him-”** does not exist anywhere else. Even so, you notice that it turns the berry into one particular berry. It sets the raspberry apart from, for example, the blackberry (Brombeere) or the bilberry (Heidelbeere). That is why it counts as a morpheme of its own.

Unique morphemes are often the remains of words that used to exist. The independent word disappeared over time and only survived in one compound. Other German examples are “Lind-” in **“Lindwurm”** (dragon) or “-gall” in **“Nachtigall”** (nightingale). In English technical language they are also called **cranberry morphemes**, after the word “cranberry”.

gewusst: Other languages also have unique morphemes, for example “cran-” in the English word “cranberry”.

teile.einleitung: Some German words are spelt wrongly especially often. Many mistakes happen because two words sound the same or because a word is linked to the wrong related word. With a few tricks you can avoid most spelling mistakes.
wichtigste: “seid” comes from “sein” (to be); “seit” (since) gives a time.
“wider” means against, “wieder” means again: so “widersprechen” (to contradict).
“tot” (dead) is an adjective; “der Tod” (death) is a noun.
“endlich” (finally) comes from “Ende” (end) and is written with a d.
“nämlich” (namely) is written without an h, and “Standard” with a d at the end.
The eyelid is spelt “Lid”; a song you sing is a “Lied”.

abschnitte.text: Many mistakes happen with words that sound the same. **“seid”** is a form of “sein” (to be): “Ihr seid fröhlich” (You are cheerful). **“seit”** gives a time: “seit gestern” (since yesterday). The eyelid, **“Lid”**, is written with just an i, even though it is pronounced long. The song, **“Lied”**, with ie, is something you sing. Here the only help is to know the meaning and read carefully.

**“wider”** means “against”, **“wieder”** means “again”. If you **“widersprechen”** someone, you speak against them (contradict them), so it is written without an e. The same goes for “Widerstand” (resistance). If, on the other hand, you **“wiederholen”** something, you do it again (repeat it). A good test: if you can put in “gegen” (against), you write “wider”.

It often helps to look for related words. **“endlich”** (finally) comes from “Ende” (end) and is therefore written with a d. The prefix “ent-” as in “entscheiden” (to decide) has nothing to do with it. **“Reparatur”** (repair) comes from “reparieren” (to repair), so it has two a’s. With **“tot”** and **“Tod”**, the word class helps: the fish is **“tot”** (dead, an adjective), but **“der Tod”** (death, a noun). Making the word longer helps too: “tot” becomes “die Toten” (the dead).

**“nämlich”** (namely) is written without a lengthening h and with one m. Many people wrongly write it with an h, like “nehmen” (to take). **“Standard”** comes from English and ends in d; spelling it with a t is a common mistake. In Switzerland there is also the rule: always **ss**, never the sharp S (Eszett). A **dictionary** or the spellchecker on the computer can help, but the program often does not catch words like seid and seit.

gewusst: A computer spellchecker only finds words that do not exist, not necessarily the wrong one of two real words.
German spelling was changed in a big reform in 1996 and revised again in 2006.

teile.einleitung: The Luther Bible is the translation of the Bible into German by Martin Luther. It came out from 1522 onwards and was read very widely. As a result it helped a shared written German language to develop.
wichtigste: In 1522 Martin Luther first translated the New Testament into German.
The whole Bible in German came out in 1534.
Luther translated from the original languages, Greek and Hebrew.
He wanted a language that ordinary people could understand.
Thanks to printing, the translation spread quickly.
The Luther Bible strongly shaped the New High German written language.
It is still read today, in revised versions.

abschnitte.text: Martin Luther was a monk and theologian and is regarded as the most important founder of the **Reformation**.
