Because he was being persecuted by the emperor and the Church, he hid at the **Wartburg** castle in Thuringia in 1521 and 1522. There he translated the **New Testament** in only about eleven weeks. It came out in September 1522 and is therefore also called the **September Testament**. The whole Bible followed by 1534.

Luther wanted everyone to be able to read the Bible themselves, not just scholars who knew Latin. So he looked for words that people used in everyday life. He wrote that you had to ask the mother in the home, the children in the street and the ordinary man at the market. This gave rise to the well-known German saying “dem Volk aufs Maul schauen”, which means listening closely to how ordinary people talk. His language was lively and full of images.

At that time there were many German dialects, and there was no shared written language. Luther based his work on the language of the Saxon chancery, the administration, which was understood in many areas. **Printing** made his Bible available in large numbers in a short time. So people in many regions read the same text. This encouraged a **written language used across regions**, from which today’s Standard German developed.

Luther was not the first to translate the Bible into German, but his version had the greatest effect. In Zurich, under the reformer **Huldrych Zwingli**, a separate translation was made, the **Zurich Bible**. It was available in full in print in 1531. The language of the Luther Bible has been revised again and again, most recently for the 500th anniversary of the Reformation in 2017.

gewusst: Many words and sayings became known through Luther, for example “Lückenbüsser” (stopgap) or “sein Licht unter den Scheffel stellen” (to hide your light under a bushel).
There were printed German Bibles even before Luther, such as the Mentelin Bible of 1466, but they were hard to understand.

teile.einleitung: We mostly use language to describe the world. But some sentences do more than that: when you say them, an action happens as a result. This quality is called performativity.
wichtigste: Performative statements do not describe anything; they carry out an action themselves.
One example is “I name this ship Helvetia”.
The term was coined by the British philosopher John L. Austin.
Constative statements, on the other hand, are statements that can be true or false.
Performative statements are not true or false; they succeed or fail.

abschnitte.text: If you say “I name this ship Helvetia”, you are not describing a naming ceremony. You name the ship by saying this sentence. Statements like this are called **performative**, from the English “to perform”, meaning to carry out. Other examples are “I promise to come tomorrow”, “I bet you” or “I apologise”. Often you can add the word **“hereby”**: “I hereby open the meeting.”

The British philosopher **John L. Austin** studied these statements closely. His lectures were published as a book after his death, in 1962, with the title “How to Do Things with Words”. Austin distinguished **performative** from **constative** statements. A constative sentence such as “It is raining” can be true or false. A performative sentence, on the other hand, can **succeed** or **fail**.

For a performative statement to succeed, the circumstances have to be right. Only someone who has been chosen to do so can name a ship, and only at the right moment. If a spectator shouts it out, the ship has not been named. Austin called such requirements **felicity conditions**. His ideas gave rise to **speech act theory**, which shows that almost every statement is also an action.

gewusst: Austin later noticed himself that performative and constative sentences cannot always be clearly separated.

teile.einleitung: Poems are often divided into stanzas. A stanza is a group of verse lines, that is lines of a poem, separated from the next group by an empty line.
wichtigste: A single line of a poem is called a verse line.
Several lines together make a stanza.
There is usually an empty line between two stanzas.
Many poems and songs have several stanzas.
A refrain is repeated after every stanza.

abschnitte.text: A single line in a poem is called a **verse line**. Several lines together make a **stanza**. There is usually an **empty line** between two stanzas. That way you can see at first glance how a poem is divided up. A stanza is a bit like a paragraph in an ordinary text.

Stanzas can be of different lengths. A stanza of **four lines** is especially common, for example in folk songs. Some forms of poem have fixed stanzas: the **sonnet** is made of two stanzas of four lines and two stanzas of three lines. There are also poems without stanzas, which simply consist of many lines one after another.

Within a stanza the lines often rhyme. In **couplets**, two lines in a row rhyme; in **alternate rhyme**, every second line does. Songs often have a **refrain**, also called a chorus. It is repeated after every stanza, while the words of the stanzas change. That is why you can often join in with a song quickly.

gewusst: The word “stanza” comes from Italian, while the German word “Strophe” comes from Greek and means “turn”.
The Swiss national anthem, the Swiss Psalm, also has several stanzas.

teile.einleitung: The history of literature tells how stories, poems and plays have changed over the centuries. It is divided into periods, for example the Enlightenment, Storm and Stress, Classicism, Romanticism and Realism. Swiss authors such as Gottfried Keller, Max Frisch and Friedrich Dürrenmatt have also strongly shaped German-language literature.
wichtigste: The history of literature divides texts into periods with typical features.
The Enlightenment in the 18th century put reason at the centre.
Storm and Stress lasted from about 1765 to 1785 and stressed feeling and genius.
Goethe and Schiller are the main figures of Weimar Classicism.
The blue flower from Novalis’s novel is the symbol of Romanticism.
During Realism, Gottfried Keller from Zurich wrote the novel “Green Henry”.
Expressionism, from about 1910 to 1925, was shaped by the big city and a sense of the end of the world.
Max Frisch and Friedrich Dürrenmatt are the best-known Swiss authors of the 20th century.

abschnitte.titel: From the beginnings to the Baroque
abschnitte.text: The oldest German texts date from the early Middle Ages and were written down by monks. Around 1200, heroic epics such as the **Song of the Nibelungs** and the songs of the minstrels were created. Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg invented printing, which made books much cheaper. In the Baroque period of the 17th century, the Thirty Years’ War and thoughts about how everything passes away shaped many poems.

The **Enlightenment** in the 18th century put reason at the centre and called on people to think for themselves. One important author was Gotthold Ephraim Lessing with “Nathan the Wise”. As a counter-movement, **Storm and Stress** arose from about 1765 to 1785, celebrating feeling, nature and genius. During this time the young Goethe wrote “The Sorrows of Young Werther” and Schiller his play “The Robbers”.

In **Weimar Classicism**, Goethe and Schiller strove for harmony, balance and beauty. In 1804 Schiller wrote the play “William Tell”, which is set in Central Switzerland. **Romanticism**, on the other hand, sought the mysterious, dreams and nature. Its symbol is the **blue flower** from Novalis’s novel “Heinrich von Ofterdingen”, which stands for longing. The Brothers Grimm also collected their fairy tales during this time.

In the 19th century, **Realism** wanted to show life as true to reality as possible. **Gottfried Keller** from Zurich wrote the novel “Green Henry” and the novellas “The People of Seldwyla”. Conrad Ferdinand Meyer also came from Zurich, while Jeremias Gotthelf described life in the Emmental. Johanna Spyri published “Heidi” in 1880, which is still world famous today.

**Expressionism**, from about 1910 to 1925, was shaped by the big city, war and a sense of the end of the world; many poems sound like a cry. After the Second World War, two Swiss writers became world famous. **Max Frisch** wrote the novel “Homo Faber” in 1957 and the play “Andorra”. **Friedrich Dürrenmatt** wrote the comedy “The Physicists”, which had its first performance in Zurich in 1962, and “The Visit”.

begriffe.erklaerung: A stretch of time with typical features.
A play for the theatre.
A medium-length story about one special event.
The very first performance of a play.
A period that shows life as true to reality as possible.

gewusst: Goethe’s “Werther” started a real fashion: young men dressed like the character in the novel, in a blue tailcoat and a yellow waistcoat.
Schiller never went to Switzerland himself, even though with “William Tell” he wrote the best-known play about Switzerland.
Alongside his writing, Gottfried Keller worked for 15 years as state secretary of the canton of Zurich.

teile.einleitung: If someone shouts “Watch out, the dog bites!”, the listeners may get a fright. This effect of a statement is called perlocution. The term comes from speech act theory.
wichtigste: Perlocution is the effect of a statement on the listeners.
The term comes from John L. Austin’s speech act theory.
Austin divided a speech act into three parts.
A warning is the illocution; getting a fright is the perlocution.
You cannot always control the effect.

abschnitte.titel: Three sides of a speech act
abschnitte.text: The philosopher **John L. Austin** showed that we act with language. He distinguished three parts. The **locutionary act** is the saying itself, speaking words that have a meaning. The **illocutionary act** is the action you carry out by doing so, for example warning, asking or promising. The **perlocutionary act** is the effect on the other person.

If someone shouts “Watch out, the dog bites!”, that is a **warning**, the illocution. If someone gets a fright or stops, that is the **perlocution**. Other perlocutionary effects are convincing, comforting, annoying, calming or making someone laugh. So perlocution does not happen in the saying, but **through** the saying.

A speaker can intend an effect but cannot force it. A joke can make someone laugh or hurt their feelings. Good advice can convince or make someone stubborn. That is why perlocution also depends on the listeners and the situation. This shows how important it is to pay attention to the other person when speaking.

gewusst: The word perlocution comes from the Latin “per” for through and “locutio” for speaking.

teile.einleitung: The West Germanic languages are a group of related languages. They include German, English and Dutch. They have a common origin in Germanic.
wichtigste: The Germanic languages are divided into **West**, **North** and **East Germanic**.
German belongs to the **West Germanic** languages.
Other West Germanic languages are **English**, **Dutch** and **Frisian**.
North Germanic languages include **Swedish** and **Icelandic**.
East Germanic was the extinct language **Gothic**.

abschnitte.text: Languages, like families, have a **family tree**. The Germanic languages belong to the great family of **Indo-European** languages. Three branches developed out of Germanic. The West Germanic branch is the largest today, because it includes English, which has a great many speakers all over the world.

The West Germanic languages include **German**, **English**, **Dutch**, **Frisian**, **Afrikaans**, **Luxembourgish** and **Yiddish**. **Swiss German** belongs too, because it is a dialect of German. You can see the relationship in many similar words: Wasser, water, water (German, English, Dutch), or Hand, hand, hand.

Although the languages are related, they have developed differently. In High German, for example, the **second sound shift** took place. That is why German says “Apfel”, but English and Dutch say “apple” and “appel”. English has also taken over many words from French and Latin.

gewusst: Frisian is regarded as one of English’s closest relatives.
Afrikaans developed out of Dutch in South Africa.

teile.einleitung: In a loan rendering, a foreign word is carried over into German, but not quite literally. A well-known example is “Wolkenkratzer” (cloud-scraper) for the English “skyscraper”. Literally it would be “Himmelskratzer” (sky-scraper).
wichtigste: A loan rendering translates a foreign word freely.
One part is translated literally, another is chosen freely.
“Wolkenkratzer” renders the English “skyscraper”.
Instead of “Himmel” (sky), “Wolken” (clouds) was chosen.
Loan renderings, like loan translations, belong to the borrowings.

abschnitte.text: In a **loan rendering**, a foreign word serves as a model but is **only partly translated literally**. The English “skyscraper” is made of “sky” (Himmel) and “scraper” (Kratzer). So literally it would be “Himmelskratzer”. In German, people chose “**Wolkenkratzer**” (cloud-scraper) instead. The part “Kratzer” is translated literally, while the part “Wolken” (clouds) was chosen freely.

The loan rendering is closely related to the **loan translation**. In a loan translation, every part is carried over exactly, as with “Gehirnwäsche” from “brainwashing”. In a loan rendering you are freer. An older example is “**Vaterland**” (fatherland) based on the Latin “patria”, which comes from the word for father. Both kinds belong to the **borrowings**, in which one language takes inspiration from another.

gewusst: The French “gratte-ciel”, on the other hand, is a literal translation of “skyscraper”, so it is a loan translation.

teile.einleitung: Cue cards help you give a presentation without reading it out. They only have the most important words on them, which remind you of your thoughts, and no whole sentences.
wichtigste: On cue cards you only write the most important key words.
Whole sentences tempt you to read aloud.
The writing should be big and easy to read.
Index cards are numbered so that the order is right.
Colours and symbols make the card clear.
Names, numbers and quotations are written down exactly.

abschnitte.text: **Cue cards** only have **key words** on them. They remind you of the next thought, which you then tell in your own words. A good key word contains the most important information in short form. For the sentence “At around 1230 kilometres, the Rhine is one of the longest rivers in Europe”, for example, **“Rhine, approx. 1230 km long”** fits well. The word “river” on its own would be too vague.

If you write down **whole sentences**, you usually just read them out. Then you hardly look at the audience and speak in a flat voice. With key words you speak **freely** and in a lively way. You can look at your listeners and notice whether they are following you. It is worth practising the presentation with your cue cards a few times.

During the presentation you only have a moment to glance at your card. So you write **big and clearly** and leave enough space. **Colours**, arrows, underlining and **symbols** highlight what is important and show the structure at a glance. Many people use **index cards**, which are easy to hold in your hand.

Index cards are **numbered**. If they fall on the floor or get mixed up, you can quickly put them back in the right order. There is one exception to the key word rule: **difficult names**, exact **figures** and word-for-word **quotations** are written out exactly. They are easy to forget or to say wrongly.

gewusst: Experienced speakers use cue cards too, for example in parliament or on television.
If you have practised your presentation well, you often hardly need your cue cards any more.

teile.einleitung: Storm and Stress (Sturm und Drang) is a period of German literature from about 1765 to 1785. Young writers such as Goethe and Schiller rebelled against strict rules and put feeling, freedom and the creative genius at the centre.
wichtigste: Storm and Stress lasted from about 1765 to 1785.
The name comes from a play by Friedrich Maximilian Klinger from 1776.
The highest ideal was the creative genius.
Goethe’s “The Sorrows of Young Werther” (1774) is a novel in letters.
Schiller’s “The Robbers” had its first performance in Mannheim in 1782.
Johann Gottfried Herder is regarded as a pioneer of the movement.

abschnitte.text: The age of the **Enlightenment** stressed reason. Young writers felt that feeling, passion and freedom were being neglected. They celebrated the **genius**, who creates from his own strength and feeling without sticking to rules. The movement got its name from a play by **Friedrich Maximilian Klinger** from 1776. It was first called “Wirrwarr” (Confusion) and was renamed **“Sturm und Drang”** (Storm and Stress). **Jean-Jacques Rousseau** from Geneva, with his love of nature, also influenced the young writers.

In **Strasbourg** in 1770 the young **Goethe** met **Johann Gottfried Herder**. Herder drew his attention to **Shakespeare**, to folk songs and to the language of feeling. This meeting is regarded as the starting point for Storm and Stress. In 1773 Goethe wrote the play **“Götz von Berlichingen”** about an imperial knight with an iron hand. The play deliberately breaks the classical rules of the theatre.

In 1774 Goethe’s novel **“The Sorrows of Young Werther”** came out. It is a **novel in letters**: it is made up almost entirely of letters from Werther to his friend Wilhelm. That way readers experience his feelings directly. The book made Goethe famous overnight. In his hymn **“Prometheus”**, the Titan rebels against **Zeus**, the father of the gods. The poem stands for the self-confidence of the genius.

**Friedrich Schiller** became famous with the play **“The Robbers”**. At its first performance in **Mannheim in 1782**, the very different brothers Karl and Franz Moor face each other. The audience was thrilled. In 1784 came the middle-class tragedy **“Intrigue and Love”**. It was first called **“Luise Millerin”**, after the musician’s daughter. The actor **Iffland** suggested the later title.

gewusst: The Zurich pastor Johann Kaspar Lavater was a friend of the young Goethe and was close to Storm and Stress.
After Storm and Stress, Goethe and Schiller turned to the calmer Weimar Classicism.

teile.einleitung: A dictionary is a book in which words are collected and explained. You look things up in it to find out how a word is spelt or what it means. So that you can find things quickly, the words are arranged in alphabetical order.
wichtigste: In a dictionary the words are in **alphabetical order**, that is in ABC order.
Words beginning with A come right at the front, words with Z right at the back.
If the first letters are the same, the **next letter** decides.
In German you look up verbs in the **basic form**: “rannte” (ran) under “rennen” (to run).
You look up nouns in the **singular**: “Bücher” (books) under “Buch” (book).
You look up adjectives in the **basic form**: “grösser” (bigger) under “gross” (big).

abschnitte.text: All the words are arranged by their first letter. “Affe” (monkey) comes before “Ente” (duck), “Igel” (hedgehog) and “Uhu” (eagle owl). If two words begin the same way, you look at the **second letter**: “Milch” (milk) comes before “Mond” (moon), because i comes before o. With “Ball” and “Bank” (bench), only the **third letter** decides: l comes before n.

At the top of each page there are often **guide words**. They show the first and last word on the page. That way you can quickly see whether your word is on this page. A tip: open the dictionary roughly in the middle, where the words beginning with M are.

Not every form of a word appears in the dictionary. You find verbs in the **basic form**, for example “rennen” (to run) instead of “sie rannte” (she ran). Nouns are in the **singular**, so “Buch” (book) instead of “Bücher” (books). With adjectives you look for the simple form: “gross” (big) instead of “grösser” (bigger). That is why you sometimes have to think about what the basic form is before you search.

The best-known German spelling dictionary is the **Duden**. It goes back to Konrad Duden, who published a spelling dictionary in 1880. In 1838 the **Brothers Grimm** began a huge German Dictionary, which was only finished in 1961. Today there are also many dictionaries on the internet and for foreign languages.

gewusst: In German dictionaries the umlauts ä, ö and ü are usually sorted as if they were a, o and u.
People worked on the Brothers Grimm’s German Dictionary for more than 120 years.

teile.einleitung: The second sound shift was a change in sounds that took place in the early Middle Ages. It separated High German from Low German and from English. That is why German says “Wasser” but English says “water”.
wichtigste: The second sound shift is also called the **High German sound shift**.
It took place roughly in the **6th to 8th centuries**.
It started in the **south** and grew weaker towards the north.
After a vowel, **t became ss**: water, Wasser.
In some positions, **p** became **pf**: apple, Apfel.
Most Swiss dialects also shifted **k at the beginning of a word to ch**: Chind (child).

abschnitte.text: In the second sound shift, the sounds **p**, **t** and **k** changed. After a vowel they became friction sounds: “water” became **“Wasser”**, “make” became **“machen”** and “open” became **“offen”**. At the beginning of a word, p and t became **affricates**, which are a stop sound and a friction sound together. That is why German says “Pfund” instead of “pound” and “zehn” instead of “ten”.

abschnitte.titel: A difference from south to north
abschnitte.text: The shift began in the south of the German-speaking area and spread north. The further north, the fewer sounds were shifted. In the north of Germany, people still say “maken” instead of “machen” (to make) in Low German today. The boundary of this sound shift is called the **Benrath line**. English and Dutch were not affected by this change and kept the old sounds.

The **High Alemannic** dialects in Switzerland carried the sound shift furthest. They even shifted the **k at the beginning of a word** to **ch**. That is why in Swiss German people say **“Chind”** (child), **“Chäs”** (cheese) and **“Chuchichäschtli”** (kitchen cupboard). A well-known exception is the **Basel dialect**, which says “Kind”.

There was also a **first sound shift**, which happened much earlier. It separated the Germanic languages from other Indo-European languages such as Latin. That is why Latin says “pater”, but English says “father” and German “Vater”. Among those who researched these sound laws was **Jacob Grimm**, one of the Brothers Grimm.

gewusst: The word “Chuchichäschtli” shows the shift from k to ch several times over.
Because of the second sound shift, German often sounds very different to English speakers, even though the languages are closely related.

teile.einleitung: The subject is one of the most important parts of a sentence. It says who or what does something or is something in a sentence. Together with the verb it forms the core of the sentence.
wichtigste: In German the subject is also called the **“Satzgegenstand”** (sentence object of attention).
You find it by asking “Who or what?”.
In German the subject is in the **nominative**, the first case.
The finite verb matches the subject in person and number.
The subject does not have to come at the beginning of the sentence.
Even a small word like “it” can be the subject.

abschnitte.text: First you look for the verb in the sentence. Then you ask “Who or what” and add the verb. In the sentence “The dog barks loudly” you ask: “Who or what barks?” The answer is **the dog**. That is the subject.

In German you can rearrange the parts of a sentence. In the sentence “Den Kuchen hat meine Tante gebacken” (My aunt baked the cake, literally “The cake has my aunt baked”), the subject **“meine Tante”** (my aunt) only comes after the verb. With the **moving test** you can check which words together form a part of the sentence. They always stay together when you rearrange it.

The verb adapts to the subject. This is called **agreement**. It is “the child plays” but “the children play”. And it is “I laugh” but “she laughs”. If you know the subject, you can find the right verb form this way.

With weather verbs such as “rain”, “snow” or “thunder” there is often an impersonal **it**. In the sentence “It is raining hard today”, “it” is the subject, even though it does not mean a person or a thing. The subject can also be a pronoun such as “she” or “we”, or even a whole subordinate clause. In the sentence “Whoever is late misses the beginning”, the subordinate clause is the subject.

gewusst: In commands such as “Come here!” the subject is often missing altogether.
The word subject comes from the Latin “subiectum” and means roughly “what lies underneath”.
In some languages, such as Italian, the subject is often left out, because the verb form already shows who is meant.

teile.einleitung: A poem is a short text that often sounds especially beautiful. Many poems have rhymes and a rhythm you can clap along to. There are poems to make you laugh, to dream to and to learn by heart.
wichtigste: Someone who writes poems is a poet.
A line in a poem is called a verse line, and several lines make a stanza.
Two words rhyme when they sound the same at the end, like “tree” and “sea”.
In rhyming couplets, two lines rhyme one straight after the other.
Many poems have a regular rhythm.
With a counting-out rhyme you decide who starts a game.

abschnitte.text: A poem looks different from a story. It is made up of short lines, the **verse lines**. Several lines together form a **stanza**, a bit like a paragraph. A line is often left empty between the stanzas. Someone who writes poems is called a **poet**.

In a **rhyme**, the ends of two words sound the same, for example “house” and “mouse”. If two lines rhyme one straight after the other, this is called a **rhyming couplet**. In many poems, stressed and unstressed syllables take turns regularly. This creates a **rhythm** that you can clap or stamp along to. That is why poems are good for reciting.

Some verses are there for playing. With a **counting-out rhyme** such as the German “Ene mene muh” (like “Eeny, meeny, miny, moe”), you point at a different child on each syllable. Whoever is chosen on the last word has to seek or catch. A **tongue twister** such as the German “Fischers Fritz fischt frische Fische” (Fisher’s Fritz fishes fresh fish) is hard to say quickly. If you try, you easily trip over the words and have to laugh.

A very well-known book in rhyme is “**Max and Moritz**” by Wilhelm Busch. It came out in 1865 and uses rhymes and pictures to tell of the pranks of two cheeky boys. At school you often learn a poem **by heart**. Then you can recite it without a sheet of paper. This trains your memory, and the rhyme helps you remember.

gewusst: “Max and Moritz” is more than 150 years old and has been translated into a great many languages and even into dialects.
Because rhymes help you remember, they are also used for rules, for example weather sayings.

teile.einleitung: Not every sentence wants the same thing. With some sentences we tell something, with others we ask, tell someone to do something or show a strong feeling. These kinds of sentences are called sentence types.
wichtigste: There are four kinds of sentence: statement, question, command and exclamation.
A statement tells something and ends with a full stop.
A question ends with a question mark.
A command says what someone should do.
An exclamation shows a strong feeling and ends with an exclamation mark.
In a yes/no question in German, the verb comes right at the front.

abschnitte.text: With a **statement** you tell or report something. Examples are “The cow is eating grass.” or “The train is leaving.” At the end there is a **full stop**. In a German statement the verb comes in **second place**. Most of the sentences we write are statements.

With a **question** you want to find something out. At the end there is a **question mark**. Many questions begin with a **question word** such as who, what, where, when or why: “Where is my bike?” Other questions can be answered with yes or no. In these **yes/no questions** the German verb comes right at the front: “Hast du Hunger?” (Are you hungry?) or “Kommst du mit?” (Are you coming along?)

A **command** tells someone what they should do. Examples are “Tidy your room!” or “Please shut the door!” The verb usually comes at the beginning, in the imperative form. At the end there is often an **exclamation mark**, sometimes a full stop. With the word “please” the command sounds friendlier.

With an **exclamation** you show a **strong feeling**, for example joy, amazement or anger. “What a great day!” is an exclamation. At the end there is an **exclamation mark**. When reading aloud you can often hear the kind of sentence in the voice: with questions the voice often goes up, with exclamations it gets louder.

gewusst: A sentence can be very short: “Come!” is already a complete command.
The punctuation marks at the end help you recognise the kind of sentence straight away when reading.

teile.einleitung: “Heidi” is a children’s book by the Swiss writer Johanna Spyri. It tells the story of a girl who lives with her grandfather on an Alpine pasture. Heidi is one of the best-known Swiss books in the world.
wichtigste: Johanna Spyri wrote Heidi; the two volumes came out in 1880 and 1881.
The story is set in the mountains of the Grisons above Maienfeld.
Heidi’s grandfather is called the Alm-Uncle.
Heidi’s friend is Peter the goatherd.
In Frankfurt am Main, Heidi lives with Clara Sesemann, who cannot walk.
The book has been translated into a great many languages.

abschnitte.text: **Johanna Spyri** came from Hirzel in the canton of Zurich. She wrote many stories for children. In 1880 “**Heidi’s Years of Learning and Travel**” came out, and a year later “Heidi Makes Use of What She Has Learned”. Both volumes were popular straight away. Soon there were translations into other languages.

The orphan Heidi is taken to her grandfather by her aunt Dete. He lives alone on the Alpine pasture above the village and is called the **Alm-Uncle**. At first he is grumpy, but Heidi wins his heart. With **Peter the goatherd**, Heidi looks after the goats. She loves the mountains, the flowers and the wind in the fir trees.

One day her aunt fetches Heidi and takes her to **Frankfurt am Main**. There she is to become a companion to **Clara Sesemann**, who uses a wheelchair. The strict housekeeper **Fräulein Rottenmeier** is often unhappy with Heidi. Heidi learns to read but becomes terribly **homesick**. In the end she is allowed to go back to the mountains.

In the second part, Clara visits Heidi on the Alpine pasture. Thanks to fresh air and good care, she learns to walk again there. Heidi has been translated into a great many languages and filmed several times. A Japanese cartoon series from the 1970s also made Heidi famous in Asia. Today the area around Maienfeld promotes itself to visitors as “Heidiland”.

gewusst: Heidi is one of the most translated books in Swiss literature.
Many people abroad still imagine Switzerland today as it is in Heidi.

teile.einleitung: Some words begin with a capital letter, others with a small one. In German, it is mainly nouns, names and the beginning of a sentence that get a capital. With a few simple tests you can find out which words these are.
wichtigste: Nouns are always written with a capital, for example “Tisch” (table), “Hund” (dog) or “Freude” (joy).
Names of people, places and countries get a capital, such as “Anna”, “Bern” and “Schweiz” (Switzerland).
The first word of a sentence gets a capital.
Adjectives like “schnell” (fast) and verbs like “singen” (to sing) are usually written with a small letter.
The article test helps you find nouns: does “der”, “die” or “das” (the) fit in front?

abschnitte.text: **Nouns** are words for people, animals, plants, things and also feelings. Examples are “Hund” (dog), “Baum” (tree), “Tisch” (table) and “Freude” (joy). In German, all nouns begin with a **capital letter**. The article in front of them stays small in the middle of a sentence: “der Hund” (the dog). Words such as “schnell” (fast) or “laut” (loud) are not nouns and are written with a small letter.

**Names** are also written with a capital. This applies to people such as “Anna” or “Luca”. It also applies to cities such as “Bern” or “Genf” (Geneva) and to countries such as “Schweiz” (Switzerland). Names are nouns too. They stand for one particular person or place.

How do you find out whether a word is a noun? You put **“der”, “die” or “das”** (the) in front of it. If it sounds right, as with “der Baum” (the tree) or “die Katze” (the cat), it is usually a noun. “Der schnell” (the fast) does not fit, so “schnell” is not a noun. This test is called the **article test**.

abschnitte.titel: At the start of a sentence
abschnitte.text: The **first word** of a sentence is always written with a capital, even if it is not a noun. In the sentence “Wir gehen nach draussen” (We are going outside), “Wir” (we) has a capital because it comes first. In the middle of a sentence, “wir” is written with a small letter. In the sentence “Der Vogel singt im Garten” (The bird sings in the garden) there are three words with capitals: “Der” at the beginning and the nouns “Vogel” (bird) and “Garten” (garden).

gewusst: In almost all other languages nouns are written with small letters; only in German do they all get a capital.
Words for feelings such as “Angst” (fear) or “Mut” (courage) are nouns too, even though you cannot touch them.

teile.einleitung: Children’s and young adult literature means books that are written for young readers or that young readers especially like to read. They include adventures, fantasy stories, detective novels and picture books. Many of these books are world famous and have been read for generations.
wichtigste: Michael Ende wrote “The Neverending Story” (1979) and “Momo”.
Erich Kästner wrote “Emil and the Detectives” and “Lottie and Lisa”.
“Pippi Longstocking” is by the Swedish writer Astrid Lindgren; the first book came out in 1945.
Otfried Preussler published “Krabat” in 1971.
Some classics such as “Robinson Crusoe” or “Treasure Island” were originally written for everyone.
“The Little Prince” by Antoine de Saint-Exupéry came out in 1943.

abschnitte.text: Michael Ende is one of the best-known German children’s authors. In “**The Neverending Story**”, the boy Bastian reads a book about the realm of **Fantastica** and ends up inside it himself. In “**Momo**”, the **grey gentlemen** steal people’s time. They talk them into “saving” time and then rob them of it. The girl Momo brings the stolen time back. Both books have been filmed.

Erich Kästner wrote funny and exciting stories about children’s everyday lives. In “**Emil and the Detectives**” (1929), Emil is robbed on the train to **Berlin**. With a gang of Berlin children, he catches the thief. In “**Lottie and Lisa**”, the twins **Luise and Lotte** meet by chance at a holiday camp. They swap places so that their separated parents will get back together.

The Swedish author **Astrid Lindgren** invented Pippi Longstocking, the strongest girl in the world. Pippi lives on her own with her horse and the monkey Mr Nilsson in **Villa Villekulla**. Her neighbours are Tommy and Annika. “**Krabat**” by Otfried Preussler is quite different: a boy learns black magic in a sinister mill. In the end, with the help of friendship and love, he frees himself from the evil master.

Some books were written for adults and later became favourite books of young people. Daniel Defoe published “**Robinson Crusoe**” in 1719. Robinson is shipwrecked on an island and calls his companion **Friday**, because he rescued him on a Friday. In Robert Louis Stevenson’s “**Treasure Island**” (1883), **Long John Silver** is the one-legged ship’s cook who secretly leads the pirates’ mutiny.

In “**The Little Prince**”, a boy travels from planet to planet. On Earth he tames a **fox**, who tells him: “It is only with the heart that one can see rightly.” Switzerland has famous children’s books too. Johanna Spyri wrote “Heidi”. “**A Bell for Ursli**” by Selina Chönz, with pictures by Alois Carigiet, came out in 1945 and is set in the Engadine.

gewusst: “The Little Prince” is one of the most translated books in the world.
Astrid Lindgren originally made up Pippi Longstocking as a story for her daughter, who was ill.

teile.einleitung: Samnaun is a municipality in the canton of the Grisons on the border with Austria. It is special when it comes to language: it is the only place in Switzerland where people speak a Bavarian-Tyrolean dialect.
wichtigste: Samnaun lies in a side valley in the far east of the Grisons.
The valley borders the Austrian state of Tyrol.
In the past, people in Samnaun spoke Romansh.
Through close contacts with Tyrol, the people adopted a Tyrolean dialect.
This dialect belongs to Bavarian and not to Alemannic like the rest of Swiss German.

abschnitte.text: Samnaun lies in a high valley in the Lower Engadine, very close to the border with **Austria**. For a long time the valley was hard to reach from the rest of Switzerland. The easier route went through **Tyrol**. That is why the people had a lot of contact with their neighbours across the border, in trade, at work and in everyday life.

Originally people in Samnaun spoke **Romansh**, as in many parts of the Grisons. But because of the close links with Tyrol, people switched to a **Tyrolean dialect**. This belongs to the **Bavarian** group of dialects. Almost all the other dialects of German-speaking Switzerland, on the other hand, are **Alemannic**. So Samnaun is the only place in Switzerland with a Bavarian dialect.

Today Samnaun is known above all as a **holiday resort**. Its ski area is linked to Ischgl in Austria. Samnaun is also a **duty-free area**: many goods can be bought here without customs duty. This too has to do with the difficult connection to the rest of Switzerland in the past.

gewusst: Samnaun shows that language borders do not always match national borders.
Three national languages are spoken in the Grisons: German, Romansh and Italian.

teile.einleitung: Bittersweet, eloquent silence, love-hate: here two ideas stand together that really contradict each other. This figure of speech is called an oxymoron. It makes you curious and gets you thinking.
wichtigste: An oxymoron joins two contradictory ideas into one unit.
Examples are “bittersweet”, “eloquent silence” and “love-hate”.
The word comes from Greek and combines “sharp” and “foolish”.
So the name is itself an oxymoron.
A pleonasm is the opposite: it repeats a meaning, as in “free gift”.

abschnitte.text: An **oxymoron** is a **figure of speech**, a language device that gives a text a special effect. It joins two ideas that logically exclude each other. Silence cannot really speak, and yet an **“eloquent silence”** says a lot. This creates a tension that makes the reader sit up. An oxymoron often describes mixed feelings, such as **“bittersweet”** or **“love-hate”**.

abschnitte.titel: A word with its own contradiction
abschnitte.text: The word comes from **Greek**. “Oxys” means sharp and “moros” means foolish. Together that gives roughly “sharply foolish”. So the name of the figure of speech is itself an oxymoron. Other everyday examples are “old boy” or “open secret”.

The counterpart of the oxymoron is the **pleonasm**. It repeats a meaning that is already contained in the word, as in the German **“weisser Schimmel”** (white grey horse, since a Schimmel is always white) or “round ball”. Similar to the oxymoron is the **antithesis**, which, however, sets opposites against each other in separate parts of a sentence, such as “The day is bright, the night is dark”. In a **paradox**, a whole statement seems contradictory but contains a deeper truth.

gewusst: Advertising and song lyrics love oxymorons too, because contradictions stick in your head.

teile.einleitung: In sentence analysis you examine how a sentence is built. You identify the parts of the sentence, that is subject, predicate, objects and adverbials, and look at what job each part does. If you can analyse sentences, you understand grammar better and make fewer mistakes with commas and cases.
wichtigste: Sentence analysis breaks a sentence down into its parts.
You find the parts of a sentence with the moving test, also called the shifting test.
In the German “Die Schülerin schenkt dem Lehrer ein Buch” (The pupil gives the teacher a book), “dem Lehrer” is a dative object.
“Auf den Zug” in “Wir warten auf den Zug” (We are waiting for the train) is a prepositional object.
“Since the morning” is an adverbial of time; it gives the time.
In “My uncle is a good doctor”, “a good doctor” is a predicative.
Attributes such as “of the neighbour” are not parts of the sentence in their own right but parts of other parts.

abschnitte.text: **Sentence analysis** is a grammar method for exploring how a sentence is built. First you look for the predicate, the verb, then the subject and after that the other parts of the sentence. For each part you decide its function, for example object or adverbial. Finally you can also examine subordinate clauses and attributes. Sentence analysis is practised mainly from the middle years of primary school and at secondary school.

There are several **tests** for finding the parts of a sentence. In the moving test you shift words around: whatever stays together is one part. In the replacement test you replace a part with a pronoun, for example “the teacher” with “him”. The deletion test shows which parts you can cross out without making the sentence wrong. With the question test you ask about the part, for example “To whom?” or “When?”.

Objects complete the verb. In German there are accusative objects (Whom or what?), dative objects (To whom?) and the rare **genitive object** (Whose?), for example in “Wir gedenken der Opfer” (We remember the victims). With a **prepositional object**, the verb needs a fixed preposition, as with “wait for”. After verbs such as be, become and remain there is a **predicative**, which describes the subject more closely. That is why in the German “Mein Onkel ist ein guter Arzt” (My uncle is a good doctor), “ein guter Arzt” is in the nominative.

Adverbials give the circumstances of an action. An **adverbial of time** says when or for how long something happens, for example “since the morning”. An adverbial of place names the place, an adverbial of reason the reason and an adverbial of manner the way something is done. Unlike objects, adverbials can usually be left out without the sentence becoming ungrammatical.

The predicate can be made of several parts. In the German “Ich habe das Velo gestern repariert” (I repaired the bike yesterday), “habe” and “repariert” together form the predicate. The two parts wrap round the rest of the sentence, so this is called a **sentence bracket**. Attributes, on the other hand, describe a noun more precisely and stay with that noun in the moving test. In “the neighbour’s car”, in German “das Auto des Nachbarn”, “des Nachbarn” is a **genitive attribute**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part of a sentence that can only be moved as a whole.
A test in which you move words around to find the parts of a sentence.
A part of the sentence after be, become or remain that describes the subject.
An addition that describes a noun more precisely.
A two-part predicate that encloses other parts of the sentence.

gewusst: The moving test was made known by the Swiss linguist Hans Glinz.
The genitive object is becoming rarer and rarer: instead of “sich eines Freundes erinnern” (to remember a friend, with the genitive), people today usually say “sich an einen Freund erinnern”.
In theory a sentence can get as long as you like, because you can always add new subordinate clauses.

teile.einleitung: Conjunctions are joining words. They link words, parts of sentences or whole sentences, for example “and”, “but”, “because” or “although”. Conjunctions cannot be changed; they always have the same form.
wichtigste: In German, conjunctions are called “Bindewörter” (joining words).
Coordinating conjunctions such as “and”, “but” and “for” link parts of equal rank.
Subordinating conjunctions such as “because”, “that” and “although” introduce a subordinate clause.
After “nicht” (not), German corrects with “sondern” (but rather).
After a comparative, German uses “als” (than); for equality, “so ... wie” (as ... as).
Conjunctions in several parts include “either ... or”.

abschnitte.text: The word **conjunction** comes from Latin and means “connection”. Conjunctions link words (“apples and pears”), parts of sentences or whole sentences. They are **unchangeable**, so you cannot conjugate or decline them. Depending on the conjunction, a different relationship is created: a list, a contrast, a reason, a time or a condition.

**Coordinating conjunctions** link parts of equal rank, for example two main clauses. They include and, or, but, but rather and for. After a negative with “nicht” (not), German makes the correction with “**sondern**” (but rather): “That isn’t my bike, but my brother’s.” “**Denn**” (for) also gives a reason, but in German the verb then stays in second place, as in a main clause: “I’m staying at home, for I’m ill.”

**Subordinating conjunctions** introduce a **subordinate clause**; in German the verb then goes at the end. “**Nachdem**” (after) shows time: “After we had eaten, we went outside.” “**Wenn**” and “**falls**” (if, in case) give a condition. “**Obwohl**” (although) expresses a contrast: “We’re going outside although it’s raining.” Clauses like this are called concessive clauses. Other examples are because, that and so that. In German there is a comma before the subordinate clause.

There is an important rule for comparing in German. For **equality** you say “so ... **wie**” (as ... as): “He is as tall as his father.” For **inequality**, that is after a comparative, you use “**als**” (than): “Lisa is taller than Tom.” The form “grösser wie” is often heard, but it counts as colloquial and not correct.

Some conjunctions are made of **two parts** that belong together. Examples are “either ... or”, “both ... and” and “neither ... nor”. “Either we go swimming or we go cycling” means that only one of the two happens. With “both ... and”, both apply; with “neither ... nor”, neither does.

gewusst: The German word for “and” is one of the most common words in the German language.
Between two main clauses, no comma is needed in German before the words for “and” and “or”, but you may put one.

teile.einleitung: A sentence is a unit of language that expresses a complete thought. In writing it begins with a capital letter and ends with a punctuation mark such as a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark. We build all texts out of sentences, from a short chat message to a thick novel.
wichtigste: A sentence always begins with a capital letter.
At the end there is a full stop, a question mark or an exclamation mark.
Almost every sentence needs a verb, for example “The cat is sleeping”.
“I live in Bern.” is a statement.
“Come here at once!” is a command.
Questions often begin with a question word such as “where” or “who”.
A distinction is made between main clauses and subordinate clauses.

abschnitte.text: A **sentence** joins words so that they make complete sense. “The cat is sleeping” is a sentence, but “Cat the sleeping” is not. Most sentences contain a **subject**, who or what does something, and a **predicate**, the verb. Even the very short sentence “It is raining” has both. “It is raining. I’ll take my umbrella.” is two sentences, because two full stops close two thoughts.

Depending on the purpose, there are different **kinds of sentence**. A statement tells something and ends with a full stop: “I play football.” A question wants to know something and ends with a question mark: “Where do you live?” A command gives an order or makes a request, often with an exclamation mark. An exclamation expresses a strong feeling, such as “How beautiful that is!”

In German, the position of the verb tells you a lot about the kind of sentence. In a statement, the finite verb comes in **second place**: “Heute spiele ich Fussball” (Today I am playing football). In yes/no questions and commands it comes right at the front: “Kommst du mit?” (Are you coming along?) In subordinate clauses the verb slides to the end: “weil ich müde bin” (because I am tired). These rules are among the biggest challenges for people learning German.

A **main clause** can stand on its own, but a subordinate clause cannot. Subordinate clauses often begin with words such as “because”, “that”, “if” or “although”. In German there is a comma between the main clause and the subordinate clause. If you join several main clauses, you get a compound sentence. A main clause with one or more subordinate clauses is called a complex sentence.

For essays and stories it is worth building your sentences in a varied way. If every sentence begins with “Then”, a text soon becomes boring. In German you can keep the verb in second place and still put different parts of the sentence at the beginning. Short sentences seem exciting and clear; long sentences can explain things more precisely. A good **mix** makes texts pleasant to read.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sentence that tells something and ends with a full stop.
A sentence that asks something and ends with a question mark.
A sentence that expresses an order or a request.
A part of a sentence that cannot stand on its own, for example “because it is raining”.

gewusst: Some writers have written sentences that go on for several pages.
The sentence “Go!” is made of just one word and is still complete.
In maths and in music, the German word for sentence, “Satz”, means something quite different from in grammar: a theorem or a movement.

teile.einleitung: Grammaticalisation is a kind of language change. In it, a word with a full meaning gradually turns into a small grammatical tool. Changes like this often take many centuries.
wichtigste: In grammaticalisation, a content word becomes a grammatical element.
In the process the word loses part of its original meaning.
One example is the German “werden” (to become), which is used for the future tense.
Endings such as the German “-heit” and “-lich” used to be words of their own.
Grammaticalisation happens in all languages.

abschnitte.text: Some words carry a lot of meaning, such as “house” or “go”. Other words mainly have a grammatical job, such as auxiliary verbs or endings. In **grammaticalisation**, a word moves from the first group to the second. It is used more often, loses part of its meaning and often becomes shorter. The term was coined at the beginning of the 20th century by the French linguist **Antoine Meillet**.

The German verb **“werden”** actually means “to become something”. Today it is also used to form the **future**: “Ich werde morgen kommen” (I will come tomorrow). In a similar way, “haben” (to have) has become the auxiliary verb for the perfect: “Ich habe gegessen” (I have eaten). The suffix **“-heit”** in “Freiheit” (freedom) was a separate word in Old High German, meaning “kind” or “nature”. The “-lich” in “freundlich” (friendly) also goes back to an old word.

Grammaticalisation happens everywhere. In English, “going to” literally means moving towards something, but today it often expresses the future. In French, the future forms grew out of a Latin combination with the verb for “to have”. Experts compare many languages and find similar paths. This shows that people change language in similar ways.

gewusst: The word “heit”, which used to stand alone, has become one of the most common suffixes in German.

teile.einleitung: Swiss literature is written in four languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. On top of that there are texts in dialect. Many Swiss authors are known far beyond the country’s borders.
wichtigste: There is Swiss literature in all four national languages.
Friedrich Dürrenmatt and Max Frisch are classics of the 20th century.
The Swiss Book Prize has been awarded since 2008.
Pedro Lenz wrote the novel “Der Goalie bin ig” (I’m the Goalie) in Bernese German.
Lukas Bärfuss received the Georg Büchner Prize in 2019.
Joël Dicker from Geneva became famous around the world with a crime novel.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century, **Jeremias Gotthelf**, **Gottfried Keller** and **Conrad Ferdinand Meyer** wrote important works. Carl Spitteler received the **Nobel Prize in Literature** in 1919. In the 20th century, **Friedrich Dürrenmatt** (“The Visit”) and **Max Frisch** (“Homo Faber”, “Andorra”) became world famous. Their works are still read in many schools today.

Since 2008 the **Swiss Book Prize** has honoured a German-language work from Switzerland every year and is presented at the Buch Basel book festival. In 2010 **Melinda Nadj Abonji** received both the German and the Swiss Book Prize for “Fly Away, Pigeon”. The novel tells of a family from Vojvodina who run a café in Switzerland. **Christian Kracht** won the Swiss Book Prize in 2016 with “The Dead”. **Lukas Bärfuss**, known for “One Hundred Days” about Rwanda, received the **Georg Büchner Prize** in 2019, the most important literary prize in the German-speaking world.

**Martin Suter** writes very successful novels. In “Small World” (1997), the main character Konrad Lang loses his memory through **Alzheimer’s disease**, and old memories reveal a family secret. **Peter Stamm** became known in 1998 with the novel **“Agnes”**, which is often read in schools today. **Joël Dicker** from Geneva wrote “The Truth About the Harry Quebert Affair” (2012) in French, a crime novel that has been translated into many languages.

Switzerland has a lively **dialect literature**. In 2010 **Pedro Lenz** wrote the novel **“Der Goalie bin ig”** (I’m the Goalie) in Bernese German. It tells of the outsider Goalie in the invented village of Schummertal, who gets mixed up in shady deals. The novel was filmed in 2014. Songs, poems and stage texts in dialect, the so-called **spoken word** scene, are popular too.

gewusst: The Geneva philosopher Jean-Jacques Rousseau is also one of the famous authors from Switzerland.
The term “Swiss literature” covers works in four languages, which often hardly know each other.

teile.einleitung: The haiku is a very short form of poem from Japan. It has only three lines and often captures a small moment in nature. Today people all over the world write haiku, in English too.
wichtigste: The haiku comes from Japan.
It has three lines with, traditionally, 5, 7 and 5 syllables.
It is often about nature and the seasons.
The best-known haiku poet is Matsuo Bashō.
A haiku usually does not rhyme.

abschnitte.text: The **haiku** is a Japanese form of poem. It is made up of **three lines**. Traditionally the first line has 5 syllables, the second 7 and the third 5 again. Strictly speaking, Japanese counts sound units that do not quite match our syllables. The most famous haiku poet is **Matsuo Bashō**, who lived in the 17th century.

Many haiku describe a **moment** in nature: a shower of falling leaves, a frog, the first snow. The poem often contains a word that points to a **season**. The haiku explains nothing; it just shows a picture. The reader does the thinking about it. Precisely because it is so short, every word has to be well chosen.

Anyone can have a go at a haiku. You look closely, for example on your way to school or in the woods. Then you count the syllables and shape three lines: 5, 7, 5. An example: “By the brook stones gleam / the trout leaps away from there / rings on the water.” You do not need any rhymes for it.

gewusst: One of Bashō’s best-known haiku is about a frog jumping into an old pond.

teile.einleitung: Gottfried Keller is one of the best-known Swiss writers. He lived from 1819 to 1890, mostly in Zurich, and wrote novels, novellas and poems. For many years he also worked as state secretary of the canton of Zurich.
wichtigste: Gottfried Keller was born in Zurich in 1819 and died there in 1890.
At first he wanted to become a painter and went to Munich for this.
His main work is the novel “Green Henry”.
From 1861 to 1876 he was First State Secretary of the canton of Zurich.
The novella “Clothes Make the Man” belongs to the collection “The People of Seldwyla”.
Keller is regarded as an important writer of poetic realism.

abschnitte.text: Gottfried Keller was born in **Zurich** in 1819. His father died early, and his mother brought him up on her own. As a teenager he was expelled from school. He wanted to become a **painter** and went to **Munich** in 1840, but had no success there. Back in Zurich he began writing poems and realised that his talent lay in writing.

Keller’s main work is the novel “**Green Henry**”. It first came out in the 1850s, and later Keller wrote a heavily revised version. Young Heinrich Lee wants to become a painter and fails. Keller put a lot of his own life into it. A novel like this, which shows how a person grows up and learns, is called a **coming-of-age novel** (Bildungsroman).

In his novellas Keller invented the small town of **Seldwyla**, where headstrong people live. The best-known story is “**Clothes Make the Man**”. In it, the townspeople of Goldach take the poor tailor **Wenzel Strapinski** for a Polish count because of his fine coat. Another well-known novella is “A Village Romeo and Juliet”. Later came the “Zurich Novellas” and the novel “Martin Salander”.

In 1861 Keller was elected **First State Secretary** of the canton of Zurich. He ran the office of the Zurich government and was responsible for many documents. During these years he had little time for writing. After he retired in 1876, he devoted himself fully to literature again. Keller remained closely connected with Zurich all his life.

gewusst: The title “Clothes Make the Man” is still a well-known saying today.
Keller spent a few years in Heidelberg and Berlin on a grant from the canton of Zurich.

teile.einleitung: In German, vowels are also called “Selbstlaute” (self-sounds). They are called this because they sound by themselves, without help from other sounds. The other letters are called “Mitlaute” (sounds that go along) or consonants.
wichtigste: Without the umlauts there are **five** vowels: **A, E, I, O, U**.
In German there are also the **umlauts** ä, ö and ü.
All the other letters are **consonants**, for example B, H or N.
Every syllable needs a vowel.
Double vowels as in the German “Boot” (boat) are pronounced long.
Sounds such as **ei**, **au** and **eu** are called diphthongs (double sounds).

abschnitte.text: When you say a vowel, the air flows freely through your mouth. That is why you can sing an **A** or an **O** for a long time. With a consonant such as **B** or **T**, the air is briefly stopped by your lips or tongue. Consonants only really sound right together with a vowel, which is why in German they are called “Mitlaute”, sounds that go along.

abschnitte.titel: Finding the vowels in a word
abschnitte.text: In the German word **“Hund”** (dog) there is only one vowel, the u. H, n and d are consonants. The word **“Esel”** (donkey) begins with the vowel E. Every syllable has a vowel as its core: Ba-na-ne (banana) has three syllables and three a’s. This also helps when clapping syllables.

Vowels can sound **long** or **short**. In the German word “Boot” (boat) the o is long; in a word like “Bott” it would be short. Long vowels are sometimes written double, as in **“Boot”**, **“Meer”** (sea) or **“Haar”** (hair). Sometimes an **h** shows the length too, as in “Kuh” (cow) or “fahren” (to drive).

Two vowels can form a new sound together. They are called **diphthongs** or double sounds: in German **ei**, **ai**, **au**, **eu** and **äu**. Examples are “Eis” (ice), “Mai” (May), “Haus” (house), “heute” (today) and “Häuser” (houses). You say them in one go, like a single sound.

gewusst: The word vowel comes from the Latin “vox”, which means voice.
In German words such as “Typ” (type), the letter Y is pronounced like an ü and is a vowel there.
Most of the letters in the alphabet are consonants.

teile.einleitung: A portmanteau word is created when two words are blended into a new one. Parts of the original words are dropped. A well-known example is “brunch”, from “breakfast” and “lunch”.
wichtigste: A portmanteau word blends two words into one.
Parts of the words are dropped in the process.
“Brunch” was formed from “breakfast” and “lunch”.
Another technical term for it is blend (or contamination).
Portmanteau words often appear in advertising and in everyday speech.

abschnitte.text: In a **portmanteau word**, two words are pushed together so that only parts of them remain. From “breakfast” you keep “br”, from “lunch” you keep “unch”, and together that gives **brunch**. The name comes from the picture of a suitcase into which you pack two things. Experts also speak of a **blend** or contamination. Unlike in a normal compound such as “front door”, the parts are not kept complete.

Many portmanteau words come from English. **Smog** is a mixture of “smoke” and “fog”. **Motel** combines “motor” and “hotel”. There are such words in German too, for example **“Denglisch”** from “Deutsch” (German) and “Englisch” (English), or **“jein”** from “ja” (yes) and “nein” (no). Words like these are often funny and get to the point quickly.

The English term “portmanteau” for such words was coined by the writer **Lewis Carroll**. In his book “Through the Looking-Glass”, a character explains invented words in which two meanings are packed as if in a suitcase. A “portmanteau” was a travelling case with two compartments in those days. This gave rise to the German name “Kofferwort” (suitcase word).

gewusst: Many brand names and advertising words are portmanteau words, because they are short and catchy.

teile.einleitung: Poetic realism is a period of German-language literature in the second half of the 19th century. The writers wanted to show reality, but in a beautiful, artistic form. Two of the most important writers were Swiss: Gottfried Keller and Conrad Ferdinand Meyer.
wichtigste: Poetic realism lasted from about 1848 to 1890.
The writers portrayed reality, but in a condensed and artistic way.
The novella was especially popular.
Important Swiss writers are Gottfried Keller and Conrad Ferdinand Meyer.
Meyer wrote the novel “Jürg Jenatsch” and the poem “The Roman Fountain”.
Theodor Storm wrote the novella “The Rider on the White Horse” (1888).

abschnitte.text: After the revolution of 1848, many writers turned to **reality**. They told of the lives of middle-class people and farmers and of everyday life in town and country. Unlike later in **Naturalism**, however, they did not show ugliness in every detail. Reality was to be presented **poetically**, condensed with artistry. **Humour** often plays a part.

**Conrad Ferdinand Meyer** came from Zurich. His novel **“Jürg Jenatsch”** is set in the Grisons at the time of the Thirty Years’ War. It is about the Grisons pastor and politician **Georg Jenatsch**. Meyer also wrote poems. In the thing poem **“The Roman Fountain”**, water flows from basin to basin. Meyer revised this short poem many times.

**Gottfried Keller** was also from Zurich. He wrote the novel **“Green Henry”** and the collection of novellas **“The People of Seldwyla”**. It contains the well-known novella **“Clothes Make the Man”**, in which a poor tailor is taken for a count. Keller worked for many years as **state secretary** of the canton of Zurich. Jeremias Gotthelf is also often counted among the Swiss storytellers of this period.

In northern Germany, **Theodor Storm** wrote novellas about life on the coast. In **“The Rider on the White Horse”** (1888), the dyke reeve **Hauke Haien** builds a new dyke despite opposition from the villagers. **Theodor Fontane** portrayed society in Berlin and Prussia in his novels. The **novella**, a medium-length story centred on one special event, was especially popular in this period.

gewusst: Keller, Meyer and Gotthelf together are regarded as the great Swiss storytellers of the 19th century.
Gottfried Keller first wanted to become a painter and went to Munich as a young man to do so.

teile.einleitung: Comparison means grading adjectives. Many adjectives can be put into higher degrees in order to compare things with each other, for example fast, faster, fastest. There are three degrees of comparison.
wichtigste: The three degrees are called positive, comparative and superlative.
The positive is the basic form, for example “schön” (beautiful).
In German the comparative usually ends in “-er”: gross, grösser (big, bigger).
The German superlative is often formed with “am ... sten”: am schnellsten (fastest).
Some adjectives are compared irregularly: gern, lieber, am liebsten (gladly, rather, most of all).
Adjectives such as “tot” (dead) cannot be compared.

abschnitte.text: The first degree is the **positive**, the basic form, for example “schön” (beautiful). The second degree is the **comparative**: “schöner” (more beautiful). The third degree is the **superlative**, the highest degree: “am schönsten” (most beautiful). When comparing, you say “Lisa ist grösser als Tom” (Lisa is taller than Tom) and “Lisa ist die Grösste in der Klasse” (Lisa is the tallest in the class). The word comparison comes from the Latin word for “to compare”.

In German the **comparative** is usually formed with the ending “-er”: klein, kleiner (small, smaller). The **superlative** is formed with “am” and the ending “-sten” or “-esten”: am kleinsten (smallest), am heissesten (hottest). Often an **umlaut** is added: gross, grösser, am grössten (big, bigger, biggest) or alt, älter, am ältesten (old, older, oldest). With adjectives ending in “-el”, the e drops out in the comparative: dunkel, dunkler (dark, darker), edel, edler (noble, nobler).

Some common words are compared **irregularly**. You have to learn them by heart. Examples are gut, besser, am besten (good, better, best) and viel, mehr, am meisten (much, more, most). Gern, lieber, am liebsten (gladly, rather, most of all) also belongs here. With “nah” (near), a c is added in the superlative: nah, näher, am nächsten (near, nearer, nearest). The same goes for “hoch” (high): hoch, höher, am höchsten.

Some adjectives describe a state that does not come in degrees. They are called **absolute adjectives**. Examples are “tot” (dead), “leer” (empty), “rund” (round) or “einzig” (only). You cannot be “deader”. Colours such as “schwarz” (black) are normally not compared either in careful use, but in everyday life you sometimes hear “schwärzer” (blacker).

gewusst: As well as adjectives, some adverbs can be compared too, such as oft, öfter (often, more often).
Advertising likes to use double superlatives such as “allerbeste” (very best of all): the prefix “aller-” strengthens the superlative.

teile.einleitung: The Song of Hildebrand is one of the oldest works of German literature. It is the only heroic song in Old High German that has come down to us. It has survived only as a fragment.
wichtigste: The Song of Hildebrand was written down in the 9th century.
It is the only surviving heroic song in Old High German.
It is written in alliterative verse.
It tells of the meeting between Hildebrand and his son Hadubrand.
The end of the story is missing because the text breaks off.

abschnitte.text: The **Song of Hildebrand** was written down in the **9th century**, probably in the monastery of Fulda. Two monks wrote it on the blank pages of a religious manuscript. The text is in **Old High German**, the oldest stage of the German language. Today the manuscript is kept in **Kassel**. After the Second World War it disappeared for a time and later came back.

The song tells of **Hildebrand**, who returns home after many years in foreign lands. Between two armies he meets a young warrior: his son **Hadubrand**. Hildebrand reveals who he is, but Hadubrand does not believe him. He takes him for a cheat, because he has been told that his father is dead. So it comes to a duel, and at this point the text breaks off.

The Song of Hildebrand does not rhyme at the end of the lines. Instead, important words begin with the same sound. This is called **alliterative verse**. One example from it is “Hiltibrant enti Hadubrant” (Hildebrand and Hadubrand). This form was common among the Germanic peoples and helped with learning by heart, because heroic songs were passed on only by word of mouth for a long time.

gewusst: The Song of Hildebrand does not reveal how the fight between father and son ends, because the text stops in the middle of the action.
The language of the song mixes forms from different old dialects.

teile.einleitung: Some words look the same or sound the same but mean something completely different. This is called homonymy. A well-known German example is “Kiefer”: a pine tree and a bone in the face (the jaw).
wichtigste: Homonyms are words that sound the same but have different meanings.
With homonymy, the meanings have no recognisable connection.
The two German words “Kiefer” go back to different old words.
With polysemy, on the other hand, the meanings of one word are connected.
Words that only sound the same are called homophones, such as “sea” and “see”.

abschnitte.text: The word **homonymy** comes from Greek and means something like “having the same name”. **Homonyms** are words that sound the same but mean different things. In German, “Kiefer” can be a pine tree or the jawbone. The two words only happen to have the same form; they go back to **different Old High German words**. Another example is “Ton”: clay for pottery or a sound. In English, “bat” can be a flying animal or something you hit a ball with.

This is different from **polysemy**, when a single word has several meanings. With the German “Birne”, meaning both a pear and a light bulb, you can see a connection: the bulb is shaped like a pear. Here one word has several related meanings. With homonymy there is no such connection. The line is not always easy to draw, so people speak of a “common way of dividing them”.

abschnitte.titel: Sounding the same, spelt the same
abschnitte.text: Some words only **sound** the same but are spelt differently, like the German “Meer” (sea) and “mehr” (more), or “Lerche” (lark) and “Lärche” (larch). They are called **homophones**. Others are spelt the same but stressed differently, like “modern” with the stress at the front (to rot) and “modern” with the stress at the end (modern). They are called **homographs**. In English, “lead” can be a metal or what you do when you go first. Usually the context in the sentence helps you understand the right word.

gewusst: Jokes and riddles love to play with homonyms, because you first understand a word the wrong way.

teile.einleitung: The Dictionary of Variants of German (Variantenwörterbuch des Deutschen) is a reference book that came out in 2004. It shows which words in the standard language only apply in particular countries or regions. That way you can see that good Standard German in Switzerland can be different from that in Germany or Austria.
wichtigste: The Dictionary of Variants of German came out in **2004**.
It was edited by **Ulrich Ammon** and other experts.
It lists national and regional **standard variants** of German.
It covers Germany, Austria, Switzerland and other areas.
Typically Swiss standard words are called **Helvetisms**.

abschnitte.text: German is spoken in several countries. That is why it is called a **pluricentric language**: there is not just one single correct Standard German. In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, words of their own have developed that are completely correct there. The Dictionary of Variants collects these differences and shows where each word applies.

In Switzerland, even in the standard language, people say **“Velo”** instead of “Fahrrad” (bike), **“parkieren”** instead of “parken” (to park) and **“Trottoir”** instead of “Gehsteig” (pavement). In Austria, January is often called **“Jänner”**. Words like these are not dialect but belong to the Standard German of each country. The dictionary helps teachers, translators and anyone who wants to know what is correct.

gewusst: In Switzerland, for example, “grillieren” (to grill) is correct, while in Germany people usually say “grillen”.
Typically Austrian words are called Austriacisms, and typically German ones Teutonisms.

teile.einleitung: The subjunctive is a special form of the verb that expresses possibilities, wishes and other people’s statements. While the indicative says what really is, the subjunctive shows what could be or what someone has said. German has two forms: subjunctive I and subjunctive II.
wichtigste: The subjunctive is a mood of the verb.
Subjunctive I is used mainly for reported speech.
The subjunctive I of “er hat” (he has) is “er habe”.
Subjunctive II expresses things that are not real, wishes and politeness.
The subjunctive II of “sie kommt” (she comes) is “sie käme”.
If subjunctive I sounds like the indicative, you use subjunctive II.
The form with “würde” (would) helps when subjunctive II sounds like the simple past.

abschnitte.text: Verbs can be in different **moods**. The **indicative** is the form for reality: Ich habe Zeit (I have time). The imperative is the form for commands: Komm her! (Come here!) The **subjunctive** is the form for possibility and shows that something is not certain, not real or only being reported.

**Subjunctive I** is used mainly for **reported speech**. It is formed from the stem of the verb and endings with e: er habe, sie sei, er komme (he has, she is, he comes). Anna says: “Ich bin müde” (I am tired). In reported speech this becomes: Anna sagt, sie sei müde (Anna says she is tired). Newspapers use subjunctive I to show neutrally that they are only passing on what someone has said.

abschnitte.titel: Subjunctive II for dreams and wishes
abschnitte.text: **Subjunctive II** expresses what is unreal or only imagined. It is often formed from the simple past, frequently with an umlaut: “sie kam” (she came) becomes “sie **käme**”, “er hatte” (he had) becomes “er hätte”. Typical uses are unreal wishes such as “Wenn ich doch Zeit hätte!” (If only I had time!) and conditions such as “If it weren’t raining, we would go swimming.” Polite requests use it too: “Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen?” (Could you help me, please?)

Sometimes subjunctive I sounds exactly like the indicative, for example with “sie haben” (they have). Then you use subjunctive II in reported speech: Sie sagen, sie hätten Hunger (They say they are hungry). The other way round, if subjunctive II sounds like the simple past, as with “sie kauften” (they bought), the form with **würde** (would) helps: sie würden kaufen (they would buy). In everyday life, many people use the würde form very often.

In old recipes you read sentences such as “Man nehme 200 Gramm Mehl” (Take 200 grams of flour). This is a **subjunctive I** that expresses an instruction. Fixed phrases such as “Es lebe die Freundschaft!” (Long live friendship!) or “Gott sei Dank” (Thank God) also contain this subjunctive. In maths people say something similar: “Gegeben sei ein Dreieck” (Let there be a triangle).

begriffe.erklaerung: The way a verb presents a statement, for example indicative or subjunctive.
The verb form for reality.
Passing on what someone has said, without quotation marks.
Not real, only imagined.

gewusst: In Swiss German the subjunctive is still very much alive; people say, for example, “er heig” for “er habe” (he has).
The phrase “Man nehme” (take) in recipes is one of the few places where subjunctive I still turns up in everyday life.
The word subjunctive (in German “Konjunktiv”) comes from the Latin “modus coniunctivus”, which means joining mood.

teile.einleitung: The trochee is a metrical foot, a small building block in the rhythm of poems. It is made of a stressed and an unstressed syllable. Many children’s songs and ballads have this rhythm.
wichtigste: A trochee has the pattern **stressed, unstressed** (Xx).
The stressed syllable is called the **lift**, the unstressed one the **dip**.
The trochee is the counterpart of the **iamb** (xX).
The name comes from the ancient Greek “trochaios”, meaning roughly “running”.
Goethe’s “The Sorcerer’s Apprentice” is written mainly in trochees.

abschnitte.text: Many German words are a trochee all by themselves: **“Sonne”** (sun), **“Mutter”** (mother), **“Wasser”** (water) or **“Katze”** (cat). You stress the first syllable, and the second is weak. When several trochees follow one another, a falling rhythm is created, which often sounds lively. The German children’s song “Alle meine Entchen” (All my little ducklings) begins like this: AL-le MEI-ne ENT-chen.

Goethe wrote the ballad **“The Sorcerer’s Apprentice”** in 1797. The first line is “Hat der alte Hexenmeister” (Now the old sorcerer has). If you say it aloud, you hear: HAT der AL-te HE-xen-MEI-ster. Four lifts alternate regularly with dips. This is called **trochaic tetrameter**.

In the **iamb** it is exactly the other way round: first unstressed, then stressed, as in the German word “Gedicht” (poem). Other metrical feet are the **dactyl** (stressed, unstressed, unstressed) and the **anapaest** (unstressed, unstressed, stressed). When people examine a poem, they often tap or clap along to the stresses to find the metrical foot.

gewusst: Because many German words are stressed on the first syllable, trochees sound especially natural in German.
Many counting-out rhymes also have a trochaic rhythm.

teile.einleitung: “The sun is smiling down from the sky” or “The wind is howling round the house”: here things do something that really only people can do. This figure of speech is called personification. It makes texts lively and vivid.
wichtigste: In personification, things, animals or ideas are given human qualities.
One example is “The sun is smiling down from the sky”.
In fables, animals talk and act like people.
Death is often shown as the Grim Reaper.
Justitia is the Roman personification of justice.
Helvetia is the personification of Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: In **personification**, objects, animals, natural events or ideas are given **human qualities** or actions. Really only a person can smile. But when “the sun is smiling”, it seems cheerful and friendly. “The stream chatters over the stones” is also a personification: the sound of the water is like a conversation. The word comes from the Latin “persona”, person.

In **fables**, animals talk to each other and act like people. The fox is often clever, the raven vain and the lion powerful. In this way fables show human strengths and weaknesses and usually end with a **lesson**. Famous fable writers are the Greek **Aesop** and the Frenchman **Jean de La Fontaine**. Animals talk in many fairy tales and comics too.

**Abstract ideas**, which you cannot touch, are also often shown as a person. In fairy tales and poems, death appears as the **Grim Reaper** or Godfather Death. Nature is called “Mother Nature”. This makes something invisible easier to imagine. Children also know such figures from picture books and films.

**Justitia** is the Roman personification of **justice**. She carries scales and often wears a blindfold, because she is supposed to treat everyone equally. Her statues stand on many fountains in Swiss towns, for example on the Fountain of Justice in Bern. Switzerland itself is shown as a woman called **Helvetia**. You can find her, for example, on the one- and two-franc coins.
