gewusst: Advertising likes to use personification, for example when a product is given a face and talks.
Sayings such as “Time is running out” or “Luck is smiling on us” are personifications too.

teile.einleitung: The Song of the Nibelungs (Nibelungenlied) is one of the most famous works of medieval German literature. It tells of the hero Siegfried, of loyalty, quarrels and revenge, and of the downfall of the Burgundians. An important manuscript is kept in the Abbey Library of St Gallen.
wichtigste: The Song of the Nibelungs was written around 1200 in the Danube region, probably in the circle of the Bishop of Passau.
It is written in Middle High German.
The poet is unknown, as is usual with heroic epics.
Siegfried can be wounded in only one place, between his shoulder blades.
Hagen von Tronje kills Siegfried and sinks the Nibelung treasure in the Rhine.
Kriemhild later marries Etzel, King of the Huns, and takes revenge on the Burgundians.
Manuscript B is kept in the Abbey Library of St Gallen.

abschnitte.text: The **Song of the Nibelungs** was written down around 1200 in the **Danube region**, probably in the circle of the Bishop of **Passau**. But it draws on much older **legends** from the time of the great migrations. The language is **Middle High German**, which was spoken from about 1050 to 1350. The poet’s name is not known. This is typical of **heroic epics**, which have come down to us anonymously.

**Siegfried** comes from Xanten on the Lower Rhine. He killed a dragon and bathed in its blood, which made his skin invulnerable. But a **linden leaf** fell between his **shoulder blades**, and only there did he remain vulnerable. He also owns the treasure of the Nibelungs, the **Nibelung hoard**, and a **cloak of invisibility**. In Worms on the Rhine he woos **Kriemhild**, the sister of King Gunther.

Siegfried helps Gunther to win the strong Queen **Brünhild**. Later Kriemhild and Brünhild quarrel fiercely about who has the nobler husband. To avenge the insult to Brünhild, **Hagen von Tronje** kills Siegfried during a hunt. Afterwards Hagen sinks the treasure in the **Rhine** so that Kriemhild cannot use it. Kriemhild later marries **Etzel**, King of the Huns. At his court she takes her revenge, and the Burgundians perish in a great battle.

The work is written in **stanzas**. A **Nibelung stanza** is made of **four long lines** that rhyme in pairs and are divided by a pause. More than 30 manuscripts and fragments have survived. The three most important are called A, B and C. **Manuscript B** is kept in the **Abbey Library of St Gallen**. Since 2009 the manuscripts have been part of the **UNESCO Memory of the World**.

gewusst: Ever since the legend, the Nibelung treasure has been considered lost, and people have searched for it along the Rhine again and again.
The composer Richard Wagner used the story for his great cycle of operas “The Ring of the Nibelung”.

teile.einleitung: A word family is a group of words that all have the same stem. “Play”, “player” and “playground”, for example, are relatives, just like the members of a real family. If you know word families, you can understand new words more easily and spell them correctly.
wichtigste: All the words in a word family have the same stem.
With prefixes and suffixes, many new words are made from one stem.
The German word family of “spielen” (to play) includes Spiel (game), Spieler (player) and Spielplatz (playground).
The German word “Erzählung” (story) contains the stem “zähl”.
Sometimes a vowel in the stem changes, as with the German “kalt” (cold) and “Kälte” (coldness).
Words that sound alike, such as the German “Glück” (luck) and “glatt” (smooth), do not automatically belong to the same family.
Word families help with correct spelling.

abschnitte.text: A **word family** is made up of words that go back to the same **stem**. The stem is the core that carries the basic meaning. For example, the German words “Bild” (picture), “bilden” (to form) and “Bildung” (education) form a word family. The words can belong to different word classes, so they can be nouns, verbs or adjectives.

New words are made by attaching building blocks to the stem. At the front there are **prefixes** such as ver-, er- or be-, at the back **suffixes** such as -ung, -heit or -lich. So the German “fahren” (to drive) gives, for example, “verfahren” (to proceed), “Fahrer” (driver) or “fahrbar” (mobile). The word “Erzählung” (story) contains the prefix “er”, the stem “zähl” and the suffix “ung”.

In German you can easily put words together. “Spiel” (play) and “Platz” (place) become **“Spielplatz”** (playground), and “Spiel” and “Zeug” (stuff) become “Spielzeug” (toys). Words like these belong to the word families of both parts. That is why German has very long words such as “Fussballweltmeisterschaft” (football World Cup).

Sometimes the vowel in the stem changes a little. A becomes ä, as with “kalt” and “Kälte” (cold, coldness) or “Hand” and “Hände” (hand, hands). This change is called **umlaut**. With some verbs the vowel changes even more, as with “fahren”, “fuhr” and “Fuhre” (drive, drove, cartload).

Word families are an important trick for **spelling** in German. If you are not sure whether “Kälte” is written with e or ä, you think of the related word “kalt”. With “Bäcker” (baker), the word “backen” (to bake) helps. That way you can avoid many mistakes without having to learn every word by heart.

Not every word that sounds similar belongs to the same family. The German words “Glück” (luck) and “glatt” (smooth) both begin with “gl”, but they have different stems. So you have to pay attention to the **meaning**. If words really belong together, they also have something in common in their meaning.

begriffe.erklaerung: The core of a word, which carries the basic meaning.
A building block before the stem, for example the German ver- or be-.
A building block after the stem, for example the German -ung or -lich.
The letters ä, ö and ü, which often appear in related words.

gewusst: From a single stem such as the German “fahr” you can make dozens of words, from “Fahrrad” (bicycle) to “Abfahrt” (departure).
Other languages have word families too, for example “play”, “player” and “playground” in English.
Language researchers can use word families to show which words belonged together centuries ago.

teile.einleitung: A consonant is one of the two kinds of letters. The letters of our alphabet are divided into vowels and consonants. Consonants such as B, M or S only really sound right when a vowel is added.
wichtigste: In German, consonants are also called “Mitlaute” (sounds that go along).
Vowels are A, E, I, O, U.
All the other letters are consonants, for example B, M, R and S.
“Mama” has two consonants: the two M’s.
Almost every syllable needs a vowel.

abschnitte.text: The **vowels** are A, E, I, O and U. In German there are also the umlauts Ä, Ö and Ü. All the other letters are **consonants**, for example B, D, M, R or S. You can sing a vowel for a long time: “aaaa”. With a consonant this usually does not work so well; it only sounds right together with a vowel.

The word **consonant** comes from Latin and means “sounding together”. With a consonant, the air in your mouth is stopped or squeezed, for example by your lips for M or your tongue for T. That is why a consonant sounds best together with a vowel: “ma”, “to”, “su”. So almost every syllable needs a vowel.

In the word “**Mama**”, the two M’s are consonants and the two a’s are vowels. The German word “**Sonne**” (sun) begins with S, so with a consonant. Words such as “Apfel” (apple), “Esel” (donkey) or “Igel” (hedgehog), on the other hand, begin with a vowel. If you can tell consonants and vowels apart, you also understand spelling rules better, for example when to double a consonant, as in “Sonne”.

gewusst: There are many more consonants than vowels in the alphabet.
The German word “Strumpf” (sock) has only one vowel and six consonants.

teile.einleitung: Spelling, also called orthography, sets out how words are written correctly. Thanks to shared rules, everyone who reads German can understand texts quickly and without misunderstandings. Switzerland has a few special features here; for example, people always write “ss” instead of the Eszett.
wichtigste: The technical word for spelling is orthography.
In Switzerland “Strasse” (street) and “Fuss” (foot) are written with “ss”.
In German, nouns such as “Schule” (school) are written with a capital letter.
After a short, stressed vowel, the consonant is often doubled, as in “Kamm” (comb).
Words from the same family are spelt alike, so “Bäume” (trees) because of “Baum” (tree).
A long i is usually written “ie”, as in “Biene” (bee).
The last big spelling reform came into force in 1998.

abschnitte.text: **Spelling** is the set of rules for writing correctly. It decides which letters you use, when you write capital or small letters, when you join words together and how you split them at the end of a line. Without shared rules, everyone would write the way they speak, and texts would be much harder to read. For German, largely the same rules apply in Germany, Austria, Switzerland and Liechtenstein.

A special feature of German is that nouns are written with a **capital letter**. So you write “die Schule” (the school), “der Vater” (the father) and “die Freude” (the joy) with capitals. Verbs and adjectives also get a capital when they are used as nouns, for example in “Beim Lesen vergisst er alles” (When reading he forgets everything). In addition, every sentence begins with a capital letter. In most other languages nouns are written with small letters.

Many rules depend on whether a vowel is pronounced short or long. After a short, stressed vowel there is often a **double consonant**, for example in “Kamm” (comb), “Sonne” (sun) or “Hütte” (hut). Instead of “kk” you write “ck”, as in “Zucker” (sugar), and instead of “zz” usually “tz”, as in “Katze” (cat). A long i is usually written as “ie”, as in “Biene” (bee). In foreign words such as “Maschine” (machine), however, there is often just a single i.

In Switzerland the **Eszett** (the special letter for a sharp s) does not exist. The canton of Zurich stopped teaching it in primary schools from 1938, and the other cantons followed one by one. The “Neue Zürcher Zeitung” gave it up in 1974, as one of the last big newspapers to do so. That is why here people write “Strasse” (street), “Fuss” (foot) and “gross” (big). Swiss keyboards do not have a key for the Eszett either.

In 1880 the teacher **Konrad Duden** published a dictionary that became the basis for standard German spelling. To this day the Duden is the best-known reference book for it. In 1996 the German-speaking countries agreed on a **spelling reform**, which came into force in 1998. Since then, for example, “Schifffahrt” (shipping) has been written with three f’s. Today the Council for German Orthography watches over the rules.

begriffe.erklaerung: The technical word for spelling, from the Greek for “correct writing”.
The letter sharp S, which is replaced by “ss” in Switzerland.
Two identical consonants in a row, like “mm” in “Kamm” (comb).
The rule that related words are spelt alike, such as “Baum” and “Bäume” (tree, trees).

gewusst: The German word “Rechtschreibung” (spelling) contains a little trap itself: it has “ch” and “sch” right next to each other.
Before the reform of 1996, “Schiffahrt” was written with only two f’s when a vowel followed.
Today many computer programs check spelling automatically and underline mistakes in red.

teile.einleitung: The iamb is a metrical foot, a small building block of rhythm in poems. It is made of an unstressed and a stressed syllable. Many famous poems and plays are written in iambs.
wichtigste: An iamb is made of an unstressed and a stressed syllable.
The German word “Gedicht” (poem) forms an iamb on its own: ge-DICHT.
The rhythm of the iamb feels rising.
The number of stressed syllables decides whether a line has four beats, five beats and so on.
Blank verse is unrhymed iambic pentameter.
Shakespeare’s sonnets are mostly written in iambic pentameter.

abschnitte.text: In the study of verse, a group of stressed and unstressed syllables is called a **metrical foot**. In an **iamb**, an unstressed syllable comes first, then a stressed one. You can think of it as “da-DUM”. German words such as “Gedicht” (poem), “Verstand” (mind) or “Gebet” (prayer) are iambs by themselves, because the second syllable is stressed. Words such as “Sonne” (sun) or “Tiger” do not fit, because they are stressed on the first syllable. The reverse foot, stressed then unstressed, is called a **trochee**.

A stressed syllable is called a **beat** (lift), an unstressed one a **dip**. A line with four iambs is an **iambic tetrameter**. It has eight syllables if the line ends on a stressed syllable. This ending is called a **masculine ending**. If the line ends with an extra unstressed syllable, it is called a **feminine ending**, and then there are nine syllables. In the same way, an iambic pentameter has ten or eleven syllables.

**Blank verse** is iambic pentameter without rhyme. It comes from English drama; Shakespeare often used it in his plays. Since Lessing’s “Nathan the Wise”, it has shaped classical German drama. Schiller and Goethe also mostly wrote their verse plays in blank verse. The verse sounds almost like spoken language, but still feels solemn and orderly.

A **sonnet** is a poem of 14 lines. William Shakespeare wrote a famous collection of sonnets. Their lines are mostly made of five iambs, so ten syllables with a rising rhythm. In English this metre is called **iambic pentameter**, literally “iambic five-measure”. To this day it is one of the best-known metres in English poetry.

gewusst: The iamb is one of the most common metres in German and English poetry.
You can best hear whether a line is iambic by reading it aloud and tapping along.

teile.einleitung: In a text analysis you look closely at how a text is built, what it says and what means it uses to have an effect. People analyse stories, poems, plays and also newspaper articles. Text analysis is an important part of German lessons, especially in the upper years and at grammar school.
wichtigste: A text analysis asks about the content, structure, language and effect of a text.
An authorial narrator knows the inner life of all the characters and comments on events.
Free indirect speech gives thoughts in the third person and in the past tense.
In time compression, the discourse time is shorter than the story time.
A sonnet has 14 lines made of two quatrains and two tercets.
The iamb has the stress pattern unstressed, stressed.
A commentary expressly gives the writer’s opinion.

abschnitte.text: A **text analysis** breaks a text down into its parts in order to understand it better. It usually begins with an introduction giving the title, author, type of text and topic. Then you briefly sum up the content and examine the structure, language and stylistic devices. Finally you interpret the text and explain what effect it has. Here you distinguish between the three great **genres**: narrative, poetry and drama.

With novels and short stories you first ask who is telling the story. An **authorial narrator** knows everything, sees inside all the characters and comments on events. A figural narrator tells the story from the point of view of a single character, and a first-person narrator is part of the story. A character’s thoughts are often given in **free indirect speech**, for example “Tomorrow she would tell him”. The relationship between discourse time and story time is also important, for example in time compression.

With poems you examine the lines, stanzas, rhyme and rhythm. The **metre** comes from the stressed and unstressed syllables. The iamb follows the pattern unstressed, stressed; the trochee the pattern stressed, unstressed. Rhymes following the scheme abba are called enclosed rhymes. If a sentence runs on past the end of a line, this is called **enjambement**.

The **sonnet** is a strict form of poem with 14 lines, divided into two quatrains and two tercets. It comes from Italy and became famous through the poet Petrarch in the 14th century. With plays, on the other hand, you analyse the dialogues, the characters and the structure in acts and scenes. Well-known works by Swiss authors, such as “The Visit” by Friedrich Dürrenmatt, are often analysed at school.

You can also analyse newspaper texts and non-fiction texts. A news story or a report should inform as objectively as possible and answer the most important W questions. A **commentary**, on the other hand, expressly gives the writer’s personal opinion. With advertising and political texts, you ask what means are used to persuade the readers. That way you learn to read texts critically and spot intentions.

begriffe.erklaerung: The angle from which a story is told.
The pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in verse.
A sentence runs on past the end of a line into the next line.
The time needed to read or tell a story.
A large group of texts: narrative, poetry or drama.

gewusst: A single chapter can cover a whole century or describe just one minute over many pages.
William Shakespeare wrote more than 150 sonnets.
The word “analysis” comes from Greek and means “loosening” or “breaking up”.

teile.einleitung: A short form is a shorter version of a long word. Instead of “omnibus” people say “bus”, and in German instead of “Universität” (university) they say “Uni”. Depending on which part of the word is left, there are different kinds of short forms.
wichtigste: A short form is a shortened version of a longer word.
With a front clipping, the beginning is kept: “Uni” from “Universität”.
With a back clipping, the end is kept: “Bus” from “Omnibus”.
Initialisms are made of initial letters, for example SBB or AHV (old-age insurance).
Short forms are used like normal words.

abschnitte.titel: Keeping the front or the end
abschnitte.text: With a **front clipping**, the first part of the long word is kept. “Universität” becomes **“Uni”**, and “Automobil” becomes **“Auto”** (car). With a **back clipping**, on the other hand, the last part is kept: “Omnibus” becomes **“Bus”**. The long word is also called the full form. Short forms are handy because you can say and write them more quickly.

There are other kinds too. **Initialisms** are made of the first letters of several words, for example **SBB** for Swiss Federal Railways (Schweizerische Bundesbahnen) or **AHV** for old-age and survivors’ insurance. **Syllable words** are made from syllables, for example the German “Kita” from “Kindertagesstätte” (day nursery). Some initialisms are spoken letter by letter, others like a whole word.

We use many short forms so often that we have almost forgotten the long word. Who still says “Automobil” today? The German “Kino” (cinema) is also a short form, namely of “Kinematograph”. Short forms have their own gender and their own plural: der Bus, die Busse (the bus, the buses). So they are real words and not just abbreviations in writing.

gewusst: First names are shortened too: “Lisa” is a short form of “Elisabeth”.

teile.einleitung: Legends are old stories that used to be passed on by word of mouth. They are set in real places but also contain made-up things such as dragons, devils or ghosts. Switzerland has a particularly large number of legends.
wichtigste: A legend is set in a real place and used to be told by word of mouth.
At the Devil’s Bridge in the canton of Uri, the people of Uri trick the devil with a billy goat.
William Tell has to shoot an apple off his son’s head.
According to legends, dragons are said to have lived on Mount Pilatus.
Bern is said to have been named after the bear.
The basilisk is the mythical creature of Basel.

abschnitte.text: A **legend** is an old story that was passed on **by word of mouth** for a long time. Unlike a fairy tale, it is set in a **real place**, often at a particular time too. Even so, invented beings such as dwarves, ghosts, dragons or the devil appear in it. Many legends explain how a place, a name or a striking rock is supposed to have come about.

In the **Schöllenen Gorge** in the canton of Uri, building a bridge was very difficult. According to the legend, the **devil** helped, but in return he demanded the first soul to cross the bridge. The clever people of Uri sent a **billy goat** across. Furious, the devil wanted to destroy the bridge with a huge boulder, but he dropped it. This **Devil’s Stone** lies near **Göschenen** today.

abschnitte.titel: William Tell and the Rütli oath
abschnitte.text: The bailiff **Gessler** puts a **hat on a pole** in **Altdorf**, and everyone is supposed to salute it. **William Tell** does not salute it. As a punishment he has to shoot an **apple** off his son’s head. Tell hits it, and nothing happens to the child. According to the legend, men from Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden swore loyalty to each other on the **Rütli** meadow by Lake Uri. Whether Tell really existed has not been proved.

There are many **dragon legends** about **Mount Pilatus** near Lucerne: dragons are said to have lived in the mountain’s caves. In **Bern**, the Duke of Zähringen is said to have decided to name the town after the first animal killed in the hunt. That was a **bear**. In **Basel**, the **basilisk** is a symbol of the city, a mythical creature with a cockerel’s head and a dragon’s tail. You can see it on many of the city’s fountains.

gewusst: The bear is still on the coat of arms of the city and canton of Bern today.
Many Swiss legends were collected and written down in the 19th and 20th centuries so that they would not be lost.

teile.einleitung: Concrete poetry is a kind of poetry in which letters, words and the way they are arranged on the page become the work of art themselves. What the text looks like is just as important as what it says. A well-known example is shape poems.
wichtigste: In concrete poetry, the form and arrangement of the words play a big role.
In a shape poem, the words form the shape of an object.
Concrete poetry began in the 1950s.
An important founder was the Swiss poet Eugen Gomringer.
The Austrian Ernst Jandl is also known for it.

abschnitte.text: In **concrete poetry**, language itself becomes the material, rather like paint in a picture. The poets play with letters, sounds, repetition and the empty space on the page. Often a few words are enough. How they are arranged gives the poem its meaning. So you do not just have to read poems like this, you also have to look at them.

In a **shape poem**, the words are arranged so that they make a **picture**, for example a tree, a raindrop or a staircase. Poems like this are much older than concrete poetry: they already existed in ancient times and in the Baroque period. The Frenchman Guillaume Apollinaire called his picture poems “Calligrammes”. At school it is easy to make your own shape poems.

**Eugen Gomringer** is regarded as one of the founders of concrete poetry. He was born in Bolivia in 1925 and was Swiss. In the 1950s he published poems that he called “Constellations”. In his poem “schweigen” (silence), the word appears many times, but it is missing in the middle, and this gap shows the silence. The Austrian **Ernst Jandl** also became known for word games, for example in the poem “lichtung” (clearing), in which he swaps the letters l and r.

gewusst: Many concrete poems are written entirely in small letters.

teile.einleitung: Johanna Spyri was a Swiss writer. She wrote the story of “Heidi”, the girl from the mountains of the Grisons. Heidi is still one of the best-known characters in children’s literature all over the world.
wichtigste: Johanna Spyri lived from 1827 to 1901.
She came from Hirzel in the canton of Zurich.
The Heidi books came out in 1880 and 1881.
The story is set in the mountains near Maienfeld in the Grisons and in Frankfurt.
Heidi has been translated into many languages and filmed many times.

abschnitte.text: Johanna Spyri was born Johanna Heusser in **Hirzel** in the canton of Zurich in 1827. Her father was a doctor, and her mother Meta Heusser wrote poems. After her marriage, Johanna Spyri lived in the city of **Zurich**. She only began writing as an adult and published many stories, mainly for children. She died in Zurich in 1901.

The orphan **Heidi** goes to live with her grandfather, the **Alm-Uncle**, on an Alpine pasture above Maienfeld. There she makes friends with Peter the goatherd and loves life in the mountains. Later Heidi has to go to **Frankfurt**, where she is to keep the sick girl Clara company. In the city Heidi becomes terribly homesick. Back on the Alpine pasture, Clara visits her, and the mountain air does her good. The two volumes are called “Heidi’s Years of Learning and Travel” and “Heidi Makes Use of What She Has Learned”.

Heidi has been translated into a great many languages and is one of the most widely read books from Switzerland. There are many **film versions**, including a well-known Japanese cartoon series from the 1970s. For many people abroad, Heidi is a picture of Switzerland with mountains, meadows and goats. Today “Heidiland” around Maienfeld recalls the story.

gewusst: Johanna Spyri wrote the Heidi books when she was already over 50.
The Japanese Heidi cartoon series also made the character very well known in Asia.

teile.einleitung: “William Tell” is a play by Friedrich Schiller from 1804. It tells the legend of the marksman Tell and of the people of Central Switzerland fighting for freedom against the bailiffs. To this day the play shapes many people’s picture of how Switzerland was founded.
wichtigste: Friedrich Schiller wrote the play in **1804**; it had its first performance in **Weimar**.
Schiller himself never went to Switzerland.
The bailiff is called **Gessler**, and Tell’s son is called **Walter**.
Tell shoots an apple off his son’s head with a **crossbow**.
In the **Hohle Gasse** (sunken lane) near Küssnacht, Tell hits the bailiff with his arrow.
In **Interlaken** the play has been performed in the open air since 1912.

abschnitte.text: In Altdorf, the bailiff **Gessler** has a hat put on a pole. Everyone is supposed to salute it as if it were the bailiff himself. Tell walks past with his son and does not salute. As a punishment, Gessler demands that Tell shoot an **apple** off the head of his son **Walter**. Walter trusts his father and stands perfectly still.

abschnitte.titel: The apple shot and the sunken lane
abschnitte.text: Tell is a skilled **crossbowman** and hits the apple. But he had a second arrow ready, and Gessler has him arrested. Tell manages to escape and hides in the **Hohle Gasse near Küssnacht**. There he says the famous line: “Through this sunken lane he has to come.” He hits the bailiff with his arrow, and the rule of the bailiffs comes to an end.

Schiller relied on old **chronicles**, especially the one by Aegidius Tschudi. The play also includes the **Rütli oath**, at which men from Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden join together. Whether Tell really existed has not been proved. Today the story is regarded as a **legend**, but it is an important part of how Switzerland remembers its past.

In 1829 the Italian composer **Gioachino Rossini** wrote the opera **“William Tell”** (Guillaume Tell), based on Schiller’s play. The fast final part of its overture is world famous. Since **1912** amateur actors have performed the **Tell Play in Interlaken** in the open air, even with real horses.

In 1971 the Swiss writer **Max Frisch** wrote “William Tell for Schools”. In it he retells the story ironically and from the bailiff’s point of view. In this way he questions the Swiss national myth. To this day people like to discuss what Tell means for Switzerland.

gewusst: The crossbow is still a symbol of the Tell legend and was long a sign of Swiss quality.
In Altdorf there is a well-known Tell monument showing Tell with his son.
Many lines from Schiller’s “Tell” have become well-known sayings.

teile.einleitung: Languages lend each other words and meanings. In a semantic loan, the word stays the same but takes on an extra meaning from a foreign language. One example is the German “realisieren” in the sense of “to notice”.
wichtigste: In a semantic loan, a familiar word gets a new meaning from a foreign language.
The word itself is not newly formed.
The German “realisieren” originally only meant “to make real”.
Under English influence it is also used for “to notice”.
The computer “Maus” (mouse) is also an example of a semantic loan.

abschnitte.text: In a **semantic loan**, no new word is invented. A word that already exists takes on an **extra meaning** from another language. In German, the word “realisieren” originally only meant “to make real”, as in “einen Plan realisieren” (to carry out a plan). The English “to realise” also means “to notice” or “to recognise”. Under this influence, people in German now also say “Ich habe zu spät realisiert, dass der Zug weg ist” (I realised too late that the train had gone).

A well-known example is the computer **mouse**. The German word for the animal, “Maus”, got a new meaning based on the English “mouse”. Semantic loans belong to the **borrowings**, as do loan translations and loan renderings. People often hardly notice them, because the word sounds familiar. Some people criticise new semantic loans, while others see them as a natural development of language.

gewusst: Many semantic loans from earlier centuries come from Latin and no longer stand out to anyone today.

teile.einleitung: Poetry is literature in verse, the world of poems. Poems are usually short, have a special sound and express feelings, images and thoughts. In German, poetry is called “Lyrik”, a name that comes from a musical instrument of ancient Greece.
wichtigste: Alongside narrative and drama, poetry is one of the three great genres of literature.
The German name comes from the lyre, a Greek stringed instrument.
Poems are made of lines of verse, which are grouped into stanzas.
Many poems have rhymes and a regular rhythm.
The voice that speaks in a poem is called the lyrical I.
The lyrical I is not simply the same as the poet.

abschnitte.text: In ancient Greece, poems were often sung to the **lyre**. That is where the word **lyric** comes from. So poems and music belonged together from the very beginning. Even today, many song lyrics are really poems. A famous early poet was **Sappho**, who lived on the island of Lesbos.

A line in a poem is called a **verse line**. Several lines together form a **stanza**. If two words sound similar at the end, like house and mouse, this is called a **rhyme**. Common kinds of rhyme are **couplets** (aabb), **alternate rhyme** (abab) and **enclosed rhyme** (abba). The pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables is called the **metre**.

In many poems someone says “I”. This voice is called the **lyrical I**. It is a kind of character that the poet creates. That is why you must not simply assume that everything in the poem really happened like that. If no “I” speaks in the poem, the voice is often called the **lyrical speaker**.

There are very different forms of poem. The **sonnet** has exactly 14 lines. The Japanese **haiku** has three lines with 5, 7 and 5 syllables. The **ballad** tells an exciting story. Modern poems often do without rhyme and a fixed metre. In Switzerland, for example, Conrad Ferdinand Meyer and Gottfried Keller wrote well-known poems, and Mani Matter sang songs in Bernese German.

gewusst: A haiku is so short that it often captures just a single image from nature.
Rap lyrics also work with rhymes, rhythm and lines, just like classical poems.

teile.einleitung: Stylistic devices are special forms that make language more effective. Poets, advertising writers and speakers use them to make a text more exciting, more beautiful or more convincing. Many stylistic devices have Greek or Latin names, because they were already described in ancient times.
wichtigste: Stylistic devices are also called rhetorical figures.
In alliteration, words begin with the same sound, as in the German “Milch macht müde Männer munter” (Milk makes tired men lively).
Anaphora repeats the same word at the beginning of sentences or lines.
An oxymoron joins opposites, as in “bittersweet”.
Hyperbole is an exaggeration, such as “told you a thousand times”.
In personification, things act like people: “The wind whispers”.
A climax builds up step by step, as in “seconds, minutes, hours”.

abschnitte.text: **Stylistic devices** are language tricks that go beyond pure information. They draw attention, stir feelings or make an idea vivid. You find them in poems, novels, speeches and advertising slogans, but also in everyday language. When you analyse a text, you look for stylistic devices and ask what **effect** they have. Many of them were already described in ancient rhetoric.

In **alliteration**, several words begin with the same sound, as in the German “Milch macht müde Männer munter” or “Haus und Hof” (house and home). **Anaphora** repeats a word at the beginning of sentences that follow each other, for example “We want to learn. We want to play.” Repetitions like these make texts rhythmic and easy to remember. That is why advertising likes to use them too.

An **oxymoron** joins two ideas that really contradict each other, such as “bittersweet” or “eloquent silence”. In **chiasmus**, parts of a sentence are arranged crosswise: “I sleep by day, by night I work.” The name comes from the Greek letter chi, which looks like an X. Antithesis places two opposites side by side, for example “The sky is bright, the earth is dark”.

**Hyperbole** is a strong exaggeration, for example “I’ve told you that a thousand times”. The opposite is **litotes**, an understatement through negation: “That’s not bad” actually means “That’s good”. In a climax, a list builds up, as in “Seconds, minutes, hours went by”. The word climax comes from Greek and means ladder.

Many stylistic devices work with **images**. In personification, things or animals are given human qualities: “The wind whispers in the trees.” A simile links two things with “like” or “as”, for example “as strong as a bear”. A metaphor leaves out the “like” and transfers the meaning directly, as in “She is an angel”. Onomatopoeia belongs here too, where words imitate sounds, such as “hiss” or “cuckoo”.

begriffe.erklaerung: Several words begin with the same sound.
Repeating a word at the beginning of sentences that follow each other.
A figurative expression without “like”, for example “She is an angel”.
Things or animals act like people.
A strong exaggeration.

gewusst: The word “oxymoron” is itself an oxymoron, because in Greek it means something like “sharply foolish”.
Even children use hyperbole when they say: “I’ve been waiting for ages!”
In ancient times there were lists of more than a hundred different rhetorical figures.

teile.einleitung: Words are put together from smaller building blocks. The smallest building block that has a meaning or a grammatical job is called a morpheme. With morphemes you can understand how words are built.
wichtigste: A morpheme is the smallest unit of language that carries meaning.
The German word “Unfreundlichkeit” (unfriendliness) is made of four morphemes: un, freund, lich, keit.
Free morphemes can stand alone as a word, such as “Haus” (house) or “grün” (green).
Bound morphemes only occur together with others, such as “-heit” or “un-”.
The smallest sound unit that distinguishes meaning, by contrast, is called a phoneme.
The study of how words are built is called morphology.

abschnitte.text: A **morpheme** carries a meaning or a grammatical function and cannot be broken down any further into meaningful parts. The German word “Unfreundlichkeit” (unfriendliness) is made of **“un”**, **“freund”** (friend), **“lich”** and **“keit”**. If you split “freund” further, you are left only with sounds that have no meaning of their own. The science of how words are built is called **morphology**.

**Free morphemes** can stand alone as a word, for example “Haus” (house), “grün” (green) or “schnell” (fast). **Bound morphemes** only appear together with others. They include beginnings such as **“un-”** or **“ver-”**, which are called **prefixes**. Endings such as **“-heit”**, **“-lich”** or **“-ung”** are also bound; they are called **suffixes**.

Some morphemes carry the content of a word, such as “spiel” (play) in “spielen” (to play). Others show grammatical features. In “du spielst” (you play), the ending **“-st”** shows that the second person is meant. In “Kinder” (children), **“-er”** shows the plural. Endings like these are called **inflectional morphemes**. Morphemes used to form new words are called **word-formation morphemes**.

The morpheme is easily confused with the **phoneme**. A phoneme is a sound that distinguishes words but has no meaning itself. So “Hund” (dog) and “Mund” (mouth) differ by only one phoneme. A morpheme, on the other hand, means something. The word “Velofahrerin” (female cyclist), for example, can be broken down into “Velo” (bike), “fahr” (ride), “er” and “in”.

gewusst: Some linguists even speak of a zero morpheme: a grammatical function with no audible form at all.
Long German words such as “Kantonsschullehrerin” (female teacher at a cantonal secondary school) are made of many morphemes strung together one after another.

teile.einleitung: A limerick is a short, funny poem from England. It has exactly five lines and a fixed rhyme scheme. Limericks often tell a nonsensical little story with a witty punchline.
wichtigste: A limerick has five lines.
The rhyme scheme is aabba.
The first, second and fifth lines are longer, the third and fourth shorter.
The limerick was made popular by the Englishman Edward Lear.
Limerick is also the name of a city in Ireland.

abschnitte.text: A **limerick** is a **comic poem** with exactly **five lines**. The **rhyme scheme** is **aabba**: lines 1, 2 and 5 rhyme, and so do lines 3 and 4. The first, second and fifth lines are longer, the third and fourth shorter. A limerick often begins with a person and a place, such as “There was an old man from ...”. The last line brings the surprising punchline.

The limerick was made popular by the Englishman **Edward Lear**. He was a painter and poet and in the 19th century published his “Book of Nonsense”, a book of nonsense poems and funny drawings. It contains many limericks about strange old men and women. Lear did not invent the form, but it was through him that it became very popular.

**Limerick** is also the name of a city and a county in **Ireland**. Exactly where the name of the poem comes from has not been settled for certain. Today people all over the world write limericks, in German too. Because the form is so simple, it is good for making up poems of your own.

gewusst: Edward Lear drew funny pictures himself for many of his limericks.

teile.einleitung: A climax is a figure of speech in which words or parts of a sentence build up step by step. It makes a statement more powerful and more exciting. You find it in poems, speeches and also in everyday life.
wichtigste: A climax is a step-by-step build-up.
One example is “He cried, he sobbed, he screamed”.
The word comes from Greek and means “ladder” or “staircase”.
The reverse, a weakening, is called an anticlimax.
Climax often appears in speeches and in advertising.

abschnitte.text: In a **climax**, several expressions are arranged so that their effect grows from one to the next. In the sentence “He cried, he sobbed, he screamed”, the feeling gets stronger and stronger. The word comes from **Greek** and means “ladder”. As on a ladder, you climb higher rung by rung. Often there are three parts in a row, because that sticks in the mind well.

The counterpart is the **anticlimax**. Here the effect decreases, or something big is suddenly followed by something small. An example: “He lost his house, his fortune and his umbrella.” The last part comes as a surprise and is often funny. That is why writers like to use the anticlimax for humour and irony.

The climax is a popular figure of speech in **speeches**, because it builds up tension and carries the audience along. A famous example is the saying “I came, I saw, I conquered”, which is attributed to Julius Caesar. Poems and advertising also work with build-ups, such as “good, better, best”. If you recognise a climax, you understand better how a text is trying to work.

gewusst: In English, “climax” also means the high point of a story or a film.

teile.einleitung: Conversion is one way of forming new words. A word changes its word class without a new ending or prefix being added. In German, for example, the verb “lesen” (to read) becomes the noun “das Lesen” (reading).
wichtigste: In conversion, a word changes its word class.
No affix, that is no prefix or ending, is added.
A typical case in German is turning verbs into nouns: “lesen” (to read) becomes a noun meaning “reading”.
Adjectives can also become nouns: “grün” (green) becomes a noun meaning “the colour green”.
In German, converted nouns are written with a capital letter.

abschnitte.text: In **conversion**, a word is moved into a different word class. Unlike **derivation**, no **affix** is added, so no prefix like “ver-” and no ending like “-ung”. “Lesen” (to read) becomes “das Lesen” (reading), and “schwimmen” (to swim) becomes “das Schwimmen” (swimming). The word looks almost the same but is used differently. You can spot the new noun by the article in front of it.

Turning **infinitives into nouns** is especially common in German: you can make almost any verb into a noun this way, for example “das Laufen” (running) or “beim Essen” (while eating). **Adjectives** become nouns too: “grün” (green) becomes “das Grün” (the green), “ernst” (serious) becomes “der Ernst” (seriousness). Even small words can be converted, as in the saying “ohne Wenn und Aber” (with no ifs and buts). Because they are then nouns, they are written with a **capital letter**.

gewusst: Conversion is very common in English: “to drink” is a verb, while “a drink” is a noun.

teile.einleitung: Reading comprehension means that you can not only read a text but really understand it. This includes finding the most important information, recognising connections and also understanding what is only written between the lines. You need good reading comprehension in every school subject and throughout your life.
wichtigste: If you understand a text, you can put its main message into your own words.
The main message is the most important thing a text tells you.
You often have to draw conclusions that are not stated directly in the text.
Someone who packs a towel and swimming goggles is probably going to the swimming pool.
Fairy tales often begin with “Once upon a time”.
In fables, animals usually talk, and at the end there is a lesson.
Reading strategies help you understand difficult texts better.

abschnitte.text: **Reading comprehension** means grasping the meaning of a text. There are several levels: first you find information that is stated directly in the text. Then you link this information and recognise causes and effects. If it says, for example, “The train to Bern was cancelled. That is why Mr Keller was late”, you understand why he was late. At the highest level you judge a text and think about it.

Many texts do not say everything directly. The reader has to draw **conclusions**. If Lena sighs, lets her shoulders droop and stares at her test, she is probably disappointed, even though the word appears nowhere. If Tim walks to the station without an umbrella in heavy rain, he probably got wet. Reading like this is also called reading **between the lines**.

It helps to know what **type of text** you are reading. Fairy tales often begin with “Once upon a time” and tell of magic, kings and talking animals. The best-known collection is by the Brothers Grimm, who published the first volume of their Children’s and Household Tales in 1812. In **fables**, animals act like people, and at the end there is a lesson. The Greek Aesop was already telling fables like this in ancient times.

With **reading strategies** you can understand difficult texts too. Before reading, you look at the title, pictures and subheadings and think about what it might be about. While reading, you mark key words and clear up words you do not know. After each section, you sum up in one sentence what you have found out. Finally you put the main message into your own words.

Reading and understanding are among the most important aims of the subject German in the **Lehrplan 21**, the curriculum used in the German-speaking cantons. Since 2000 the international **PISA** study has regularly examined how well 15-year-olds can read, and Switzerland takes part in it. The results show that good reading comprehension has a lot to do with reading regularly. That is why libraries, reading nights and class readers are meant to encourage a love of reading.

begriffe.erklaerung: The most important thing a text wants to tell you.
Something you work out yourself from the clues in the text.
The kind of text, for example a fairy tale, a fable, a report or a letter.
A method that helps you understand a text better.

gewusst: Practised readers often take in whole groups of words at once when reading, rather than single letters.
Many of Aesop’s fables are more than 2500 years old and are still told today.
If you read texts aloud, you often notice straight away where you have not understood something.

teile.einleitung: Highest Alemannic is a group of Swiss German dialects. It includes above all Valais German. These dialects have kept many old forms and are often hard for other German-speaking Swiss to understand.
wichtigste: Highest Alemannic is a subgroup of Alemannic.
It mainly includes the dialects of the Upper Valais and parts of the Bernese Oberland.
The dialects of the Walser people belong to it too.
These dialects keep many old forms.
Other German-speaking Swiss often find them hard to understand.

abschnitte.text: Most dialects in German-speaking Switzerland belong to **Alemannic**. Experts divide it into groups: Low Alemannic, for example in Basel, High Alemannic in most of German-speaking Switzerland, and **Highest Alemannic** in the south. The name has nothing to do with “especially good”. It describes the fact that these dialects are spoken mainly in high, remote mountain valleys.

The best-known Highest Alemannic area is the **Upper Valais** with **Valais German**. Highest Alemannic is also spoken in parts of the **Bernese Oberland**. In the Middle Ages, people from the Valais moved away and founded settlements in other mountain valleys. They are called the **Walser** and live, for example, in the Grisons, in northern Italy and in Vorarlberg. Their dialects belong to Highest Alemannic as well.

In remote valleys, language often changes more slowly. That is why Highest Alemannic dialects have kept many **old forms** that have disappeared elsewhere. These include, for example, fuller word endings. To people from Zurich or Bern, Valais German therefore often sounds strange. Some understand it only with difficulty, even though it is Swiss German too.

gewusst: The Walser have kept their dialect for many centuries, even in valleys far away from the Valais.

teile.einleitung: We often say one thing but mean something else as well. “Can you close the window?” is really a question, but what is meant is a request. Statements like this are called indirect speech acts.
wichtigste: In an indirect speech act, one action is carried out in the form of another.
“Can you close the window?” is formally a question, but what is meant is a request.
Indirect speech acts often seem more polite than direct orders.
The term was made known mainly by the philosopher John Searle.
To understand them you need the context and the situation.

abschnitte.titel: What is said and what is meant
abschnitte.text: In a **direct speech act**, form and intention match: “Please close the window!” is a request. In an **indirect speech act**, the sentence has a different form from the real intention. “Can you close the window?” asks about ability, but what is meant is a request. “There’s a draught in here” can also mean: shut the window. Nobody answers it only with “Yes, I can.”

Indirect speech acts often seem **more polite**. A question seems to leave the other person a choice and sounds less strict than an order. That is why in a restaurant you say “Could I have another glass of water?” rather than “Bring me water!” Which forms count as polite differs from language to language and from culture to culture. The American philosopher **John Searle** studied indirect speech acts more closely.

To understand an indirect speech act you need the **context**. Listeners notice that the literal meaning alone does not fit and look for the intended purpose. Usually this happens in a flash and without thinking. Misunderstandings arise when someone takes the sentence only literally. Some jokes are based on exactly that.

gewusst: When asked “Have you got a watch?”, people usually answer with the time, even though they were only asked about the watch.

teile.einleitung: With reported speech you pass on what someone has said without quoting them word for word. In German you mainly need the subjunctive I for this. It shows that you are passing on someone else’s statement.
wichtigste: Direct speech goes in quotation marks; in Switzerland these are often angle-shaped marks.
In German reported speech the verb is in the subjunctive I, for example “er habe” (he has).
The pronouns are changed: “I” becomes “he” or “she”.
Yes/no questions are introduced with “ob” (whether).
Requests are reported with “sollen” (should): “Ben solle das Fenster schliessen” (Ben should close the window).
The part “said Mum” is called the reporting clause.

abschnitte.text: In **direct speech** you give the exact words and put them in **quotation marks**: Tom says: “I’m hungry.” In Switzerland, angle-shaped marks that point outwards are often used for this. The part “Tom says” is called the **reporting clause**; it names the speaker and can come before, after or in the middle of the speech. In **reported speech** the quotation marks disappear: Tom says that he is hungry, in German “Tom sagt, er habe Hunger”.

In German reported speech the verb is in the **subjunctive I**. “Ich spiele” (I play) becomes “sie spiele”, and “ich habe” (I have) becomes “er habe”. From “können” (can) you get “er könne”, while “er könnte” is subjunctive II. For the past you use “sei” or “habe” with the past participle: “Ben sagt, er **sei** gewandert” (Ben says he went hiking). If the subjunctive I looks the same as the normal form, you switch to the subjunctive II: “Sie sagen, sie **hätten** Zeit” (They say they have time).

The **pronouns** change too: “I” or “you” becomes “he” or “she”. A **yes/no question** is introduced with **“ob”** (whether): Lea asks Tim whether he is coming along. With questions that have a question word, the word stays: she asks when he is coming. A **request** is reported with “sollen” (should): the teacher says that Ben **should** close the window, in German “Ben **solle** das Fenster schliessen”.

Reported speech is especially important in **newspapers** and the news. When a federal councillor explains something, for example, the paper writes: the federal councillor said the situation was serious. That way the paper makes clear that it is passing on a statement and not claiming it itself. It also often appears in reports and minutes. In everyday speech, people usually use the normal indicative or “würde” (would) instead.

gewusst: The subjunctive I has become rare in everyday life, but you can read it in the paper almost every day.
Swiss German has its own subjunctive forms, such as “er heig” for “er habe” (he has).

teile.einleitung: The voice of a verb, in Latin “genus verbi”, shows from which point of view a sentence is told. In the active, the focus is on who does something. In the passive, the focus is on whom or what something happens to.
wichtigste: There are two voices: active and passive.
In German grammar the active is also called the “doing form”, the passive the “suffering form”.
In German, the process passive is formed with “werden” and the past participle.
In the past tense, for example, it is “The dog was fed”, in German with “wurde”.
The person doing the action is added with “von” (by) or left out.
When you change a sentence, the tense stays the same.

abschnitte.text: The term **genus verbi** comes from Latin and means something like “kind of verb”. In the **active**, the person doing the action is the subject: “The children are building a sandcastle.” In the **passive**, the thing that something happens to becomes the subject: “The sandcastle is being built.” That is why in German the active is also called the **doing form** and the passive the **suffering form**. This does not mean pain, but that something happens to someone.

In German the **process passive** is made of a form of **“werden”** and the **past participle**. Examples are “Das Fenster wird geöffnet” (The window is being opened) or “The lawn is being mown”. In the past tense it uses “wurde”: “The dog was fed.” In the perfect it is “The dog has been fed”, in German with “ist ... worden”. There is also the **state passive** with “sein” (to be): “The window is open” describes the result.

“Der Hund beisst den Briefträger” (The dog bites the postman) becomes “Der Briefträger wird vom Hund gebissen” (The postman is bitten by the dog) in the passive. The object of the active sentence becomes the subject, and the one doing the action is added with **“von”** (by). The other way round, “The letter is written by Anna” becomes “Anna writes the letter” in the active. Important: the **tense** stays the same when you change the sentence. A sentence in the present stays in the present.

The passive is useful when the person doing the action is unimportant or unknown. In “The road is being repaired”, you do not have to say who is working. You often find the passive in newspapers, instructions and laws. Local council newsletters, too, say things like “The rubbish bags are collected on Tuesday”. But too many passive sentences make a text heavy, so it is best to mix both forms.

gewusst: Not every verb has a passive: you cannot make a personal passive from “schlafen” (to sleep) or “regnen” (to rain).
There are also passive sentences without a subject, such as the German for “No smoking here”, which word for word means “Here is not smoked”.

teile.einleitung: Languages are always changing. Words disappear, new ones are added, and forms and meanings change. This process is called language change.
wichtigste: Every living language changes over time.
After “wegen” (because of), the dative often replaces the genitive in everyday German.
Many strong verbs become weak ones, for example “buk” becomes “backte” (baked).
Words can change their meaning.
Rudi Keller describes language change with the image of the “invisible hand”.
Language change is usually not planned by anyone.

abschnitte.text: If you read a text from 500 years ago, there is a lot you can hardly understand. This is because of **language change**. Pronunciation, vocabulary, grammar and meanings change slowly but steadily. New things need new words, such as “smartphone”. Other words are forgotten because people no longer need the thing they stand for.

A well-known German example concerns the **cases**. In standard German, “wegen” (because of) is followed by the **genitive**: “wegen des Regens” (because of the rain). In spoken German, however, you often hear the **dative**: “wegen dem Regen”. The genitive is becoming rarer in many areas. In the Swiss German dialects there is hardly any genitive left at all.

**Strong verbs** form the past with a change of vowel: “singen, sang” (sing, sang). **Weak verbs** simply add “-te”: “spielen, spielte” (play, played). Over time, many strong verbs have become weak ones. In the past people said “er buk” (he baked), but today usually **“er backte”**. The regular form is easier to learn and therefore often wins out.

The **meaning** of words changes too. The German **“billig”** used to mean “fair” or “proper”; today it means “cheap”. A **“Hochzeit”** (today: wedding) was originally any high festival. Changes like these happen slowly and are often only noticed in hindsight.

The linguist **Rudi Keller** explains that language change comes from many individual actions by speakers. Nobody plans it, and yet the language changes in a particular direction. Keller calls this a **phenomenon of the third kind**, steered by an **“invisible hand”**. A path worn across a meadow comes about in a similar way: many people take the same shortcut without agreeing to.

gewusst: The example of the path across the meadow comes from Rudi Keller himself.
Swiss German is changing too: young people pronounce some words differently from their grandparents.

teile.einleitung: Many poems have an even rhythm, almost like music. This regular pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables is called metre. If you know the metre, you hear a poem more precisely.
wichtigste: Metre is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line of verse.
Stressed syllables are called lifts, unstressed syllables dips.
Small repeating building blocks are called metrical feet, for example the iamb or the dactyl.
The hexameter has six feet and was the metre of the ancient epics.
A distich is made of two lines: a hexameter and a pentameter.
The alexandrine was the main metre of German Baroque poetry.
The cadence describes how a line ends: masculine or feminine.

abschnitte.text: When you say a word aloud, you stress some syllables more strongly. A stressed syllable is called a **lift**, an unstressed one a **dip**. A capital X is often written for stressed and a small x for unstressed. If a pattern repeats regularly, this creates the **metre**. When reading, it is best to tap the beat quietly as you go.

A **metrical foot** is the smallest building block of metre. The **iamb** goes xX, as in “today”. The **trochee** goes Xx, as in “sunny”. The **dactyl** goes Xxx, as in “wonderful”. Its name comes from the Greek word for finger, which has one long and two short joints. The **anapaest** goes xxX.

The **hexameter** is made of six feet, because “hex” means six in Greek. Homer wrote his great epics in this metre. A **distich** is a pair of lines made of a hexameter and a **pentameter**. Goethe and Schiller used it to write their mocking short poems, the **“Xenien”**.

The **alexandrine** is an iambic line with six lifts. After the third lift it has a pause, the **caesura**. This divides the line into two halves, which suits contrasts well. Andreas Gryphius often used it in the **Baroque** period. How a line ends is called the **cadence**: if it ends unstressed, it is **feminine**; if it ends stressed, it is **masculine**.

gewusst: The alexandrine is named after an old French poem about Alexander the Great.
Many nursery rhymes and counting-out rhymes also follow a fixed metre, which is why you can clap along to them so well.

teile.einleitung: A Helvetism is a word, phrase or form that is typical of Swiss Standard German. Helvetisms are not dialect, but correct standard language in Switzerland. In Germany or Austria people often say something different instead.
wichtigste: Helvetisms are special features of standard German in Switzerland.
In Switzerland people say “parkieren” (to park), in Germany “parken”.
The “Trottoir” is the pavement beside the road.
In Switzerland it is “das Tram” (the tram), in Germany usually “die Tram”.
People say “ich bin gestanden” (I stood) with “sein”, as in Austria and southern Germany.
The “Znüni” is a small snack in the middle of the morning.

abschnitte.text: German is a **pluricentric language**. That means there are several equally valid forms, for example in Germany, Austria and Switzerland. The special features of Switzerland are called **Helvetisms**, after “Helvetia”, the Latin name for Switzerland. They are correct standard German and are also listed in the Duden dictionary. They should not be confused with dialect words.

Many Helvetisms are words of their own. People say **“parkieren”** instead of “parken” (to park) and “grillieren” instead of “grillen” (to grill). The **“Trottoir”** comes from French and means the pavement. “Velo” for bicycle and “Glace” for ice cream also belong here. Many of these words come from French because Switzerland is multilingual.

There are Helvetisms in grammar too. In Switzerland people say **“das Tram”**, with a neuter article, while in Germany it is usually “die Tram”. With “stehen” (to stand), “sitzen” (to sit) and “liegen” (to lie), the perfect is formed with **“sein”** (to be): “Ich bin gestanden.” This is also usual in Austria and southern Germany. In northern Germany, on the other hand, people say “ich habe gestanden”, with “haben” (to have).

The **“Znüni”** comes from “zu neun” (at nine) and is the snack at about nine in the morning. In the afternoon people eat the **“Zvieri”** (at four). Both words come from dialect but are also used in Swiss Standard German. Another Swiss feature shows up in writing: the **Eszett** (the special German letter for a sharp s) is not used; instead people always write “ss”. That is why in Switzerland you see “Strasse” (street) and “gross” (big).

gewusst: There is a special dictionary that collects the differences between Germany, Austria and Switzerland: the Variantenwörterbuch des Deutschen (Dictionary of Variants of German).
In Switzerland people also use angle-shaped quotation marks that point outwards like little arrows, similar to French.

teile.einleitung: The word “foot” means a part of the body, but also the bottom part of a mountain. When a word has several meanings that are connected with each other, this is called polysemy. It is very common in every language.
wichtigste: Polysemy means that a word has several connected meanings.
One example is “foot” as a part of the body and as the foot of a mountain.
Other examples are “mouse”, the German “Birne” (pear and light bulb) and “wing”.
New meanings often arise through figurative transfer.
With homonymy, on the other hand, words that sound the same have no connection.

abschnitte.text: The word **polysemy** comes from Greek and means “having many meanings”. A **polysemous** word has several meanings that are related to each other. The **foot of a mountain** is called that because it is at the bottom, like a person’s foot. The computer **mouse** is like the little animal in its shape and cable. The German word for light bulb, **“Glühbirne”**, gets its name from the shape of the fruit, the pear (Birne).

A new meaning often arises through a **figurative comparison**, a so-called **metaphor**. A **wing** belongs first to a bird, but then also to a building or a football team, and in German a grand piano is called a “Flügel” (wing) too. It is always about something that sticks out at the side. That is why the meanings of a word are often numbered in the dictionary. The **context** tells you which one is meant.

Not every word with several meanings is polysemous. With **homonymy**, two words sound the same but have no connection. A well-known German example is **“Kiefer”**: the pine tree and the jawbone. The two words have completely different origins. Sometimes, though, the line is hard to draw, and experts do not always agree.

gewusst: Polysemy is one reason why jokes and puns work: you expect one meaning and get the other.

teile.einleitung: Everyday situations are moments when you really need a foreign language: when shopping, in a restaurant, at the station or when you get to know someone. With a few fixed sentences in French and English you can already get a long way. Polite expressions such as please, thank you and sorry are especially important.
wichtigste: With a few fixed sentences you can manage many everyday situations.
“Je voudrais un croissant, s’il vous plaît.” means “I would like a croissant, please.” (in Swiss German a croissant is a “Gipfeli”).
In a restaurant you ask for the bill with “L’addition, s’il vous plaît.”
In English, the polite answer to “Thank you!” is “You’re welcome.”
In French you say “Enchanté” when you meet someone.
If you have not understood something, you ask “Can you say that again, please?”
You can apologise with “I’m sorry” or “Je suis désolé”.

abschnitte.text: In a bakery in French you say “Je voudrais un croissant, s’il vous plaît.” That means “I would like a croissant, please”, or in Swiss German a “Gipfeli”. In English you say “I would like a croissant, please” or simply “Can I have ...?”. You ask the price with **“How much is it?”** or **“Combien ça coûte ?”**.

In a restaurant you often order with “I’d like ...” or “Je prends ...”. At the end you ask for the bill with **“L’addition, s’il vous plaît.”** or in English “The bill, please.” In the USA people usually call it “the check”. If you cannot eat something, you can say “I’m allergic to nuts.”

When you meet someone in French, you say **“Enchanté”**; a girl or woman writes “Enchantée”. In English you say “Nice to meet you.” Then you ask the person’s name or where they come from. When saying goodbye, “À bientôt !” or “See you soon!” fits well.

Politeness opens doors in every language. In English you answer “Thank you!” with **“You’re welcome.”**, in French with “De rien.” If someone sneezes, you say “Bless you!” in English and “À tes souhaits !” in French. If you arrive late, you apologise with “I’m sorry, I’m late.”

It is completely normal not to understand everything straight away. Then it helps to ask **“Can you say that again, please?”** In French you say “Vous pouvez répéter, s’il vous plaît ?” You can also ask whether someone could speak more slowly: “Could you speak more slowly, please?”

At the station or in the street you ask the way with “Where is the station?” or “Où est la gare ?”. At big stations in Switzerland you hear announcements in several **national languages** and often in English too. If you are lost, you say “I’m lost.” A smile and a friendly “Excuse me” always help.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particularly polite way of addressing someone; in French with “vous”.
A fixed expression that you learn as a whole, for example “You’re welcome”.
An exercise in which you act out an everyday situation as in a play.
The Swiss German word for the pastry called “croissant” in French.

gewusst: The word “croissant” actually means “growing” in French, like the waxing moon, whose shape it resembles.
In French-speaking Switzerland people often say “Santé !” (Good health!) when someone sneezes.
Many language textbooks begin with everyday situations, because these are the sentences you need most often.

teile.einleitung: Signifier and signified are two terms from the Swiss linguist Ferdinand de Saussure. They describe the two sides of a language sign: its form and its content.
wichtigste: Ferdinand de Saussure came from Geneva and is regarded as the founder of modern linguistics.
A language sign has two sides: the signifier and the signified.
The signifier is the side of expression, the sound image.
The signified is the side of content, the idea.
The link between the two is arbitrary.

abschnitte.text: For **Ferdinand de Saussure**, every language sign is made of two parts that belong together like the two sides of a coin. The **signifier** is the **side of expression**, the sound image, for example the sounds in the word “tree”. The **signified** is the **side of content**, the idea of a tree in our head. In short: the signifier is the form, the signified the content.

Saussure stressed that the link between signifier and signified is **arbitrary**. Experts speak of **arbitrariness**. There is no natural reason why a tree is called “tree”. In French it is “arbre”, in German “Baum”. The meaning arises through **agreement** within a language community. A small exception are words that imitate sounds, such as “cuckoo”.

Ferdinand de Saussure taught at the University of **Geneva**. His best-known work, the “Course in General Linguistics”, only came out in **1916**, after his death. His students had put it together from notes of his lectures. His ideas shaped linguistics throughout the 20th century.

gewusst: The terms come from French: “signifiant” means “signifying”, “signifié” means “signified”.
Saussure is regarded as the founder of structuralism in linguistics.

teile.einleitung: A good text does not appear all at once. It is made in several steps, which together are called the writing process: planning, writing and revising.
wichtigste: The writing process has three main stages: planning, writing, revising.
When planning, you collect and sort ideas.
A mind map helps you sort ideas around a topic.
The first version is called the draft or rough version.
In a writing conference, pupils give each other feedback.
The neat final version is called the fair copy.

abschnitte.text: First you think: what am I writing about, for whom and why? Then you **collect** ideas. The **mind map** is very popular: the topic is in the middle, and branches with subtopics and ideas go out from it. That way you can see everything at a glance. Then you **sort** the ideas and decide on an order, for example introduction, main part and ending.

With the plan in mind, you write a **draft**, also called a **rough version**. It can still have mistakes and gaps. What matters is getting your thoughts onto paper first. It helps to keep looking back at your plan while you write. That way you do not lose the thread.

When **revising**, you read the text through critically. You correct the **spelling**, unclear sentences and the **wording**. If repeated words are a problem, **synonyms** help, words with a similar meaning, such as “go”, “walk” or “stroll”. It is often worth reading the text aloud or leaving it for a day.

In a **writing conference**, classmates read the text. First they say what has worked well, and then what could be improved. Anyone giving feedback should be friendly and precise. Afterwards the author decides for themselves which suggestions to take on.

Finally you copy out the improved text neatly and without corrections. This version is called the **fair copy**. On a computer it is the finished version that you print or hand in. The fair copy is what others read in the end.

gewusst: Famous writers also often revise their texts many times.
The three stages take turns: while writing, you sometimes notice that you need to plan again.

teile.einleitung: A syllable is a speaking building block of a word that you say in one go. If you clap along while saying the German word “Ba-na-ne” (banana), you hear exactly three syllables. Syllables help with learning to read, with splitting words and with writing poems.
wichtigste: Words are made of one or more syllables.
The German “Hund” (dog) has one syllable, “Blume” (flower) two and “Banane” (banana) three.
“Schokolade” (chocolate) has four syllables: Scho-ko-la-de.
“Schmetterling” (butterfly) has three syllables too: Schmet-ter-ling.
Every syllable contains a vowel or a double vowel sound.
In German, words are split at the end of a line by syllables, such as Kat-ze (cat) or Son-ne (sun).
You can make syllables audible by clapping or swinging your arm.

abschnitte.text: A **syllable** is the smallest group of sounds that you form naturally when speaking slowly. Every syllable has a core, and that is almost always a **vowel** such as a, e, i, o, u or a double vowel sound such as au or ei. Consonants stand around this core. So a word has as many syllables as it has vowel cores. “Hund” (dog) has only one vowel and therefore only one syllable.

The easiest way to count syllables is to say the word slowly and clap at the same time. In many Swiss schools this is also called **swinging** syllables, because you make an arc with your arm. “Blu-me” gives two arcs, “Scho-ko-la-de” four. You can also put your hand under your chin, because with every syllable your mouth opens and your chin moves. Children practise this at nursery school and in their first year at school.

When a word no longer fits at the end of a line, in German you split it by syllables with a **hyphen**. With double consonants you split between the two letters: Kat-ze, Son-ne, Mut-ter (mother). Since the spelling reform, “ck” stays together, so you split it as Zu-cker (sugar). “Ch” and “sch” are never split either. You do not split off single letters at the beginning or end of a word.

If a syllable ends with a vowel, it is called an **open syllable**, like the “Ba” in “Banane”. If it ends with a consonant, it is a closed syllable, like “Hund”. In every word with several syllables, one is pronounced especially strongly: this is the **stressed syllable**. In German the stress usually falls on the first syllable of the word stem. But with many foreign words such as “Schokolade”, it falls further back.

When **learning to read**, syllables help you break long words down into small bites. That is why some early reading books print the syllables in two alternating colours. Syllables also play an important part in poetry, because the rhythm depends on stressed and unstressed syllables. The Japanese haiku, for example, is a short poem of three lines with five, seven and five syllables.

begriffe.erklaerung: The vowel or double vowel sound in the middle of a syllable.
Splitting a word at the end of a line by syllables.
A syllable that ends with a vowel.
The syllable of a word that is pronounced most strongly.

gewusst: The German word “Strumpf” (sock) has seven letters but only a single syllable.
In Japanese there are written characters that each stand for a whole syllable.
Before the spelling reform, “Zucker” (sugar) was split as “Zuk-ker”.

teile.einleitung: Romanticism is a period in literature, art and music from about 1795 to around 1840. The Romantics sought the mysterious, feeling, nature and a longing for faraway places.
wichtigste: Romanticism lasted from about 1795 to around 1840.
It is divided into early, high and late Romanticism.
Important themes are longing, nature, night, dreams and the uncanny.
In 1812 the Brothers Grimm published the first volume of their “Children’s and Household Tales”.
Joseph von Eichendorff wrote the poem “Moonlit Night” and the novella “Memoirs of a Good-for-Nothing”.
The symbol of Romanticism is the “blue flower” from a novel by Novalis.

abschnitte.text: Before Romanticism, the Enlightenment had stressed **reason**. The Romantics felt that people also need feeling, imagination and dreams. They loved the night, the forest, old castles and the Middle Ages. A central feeling is **longing** for something far away that you never quite reach. This is symbolised by the **blue flower** from the novel “Heinrich von Ofterdingen” by Novalis.

**Early Romanticism** began around 1795 in the town of Jena. From 1798 the brothers August Wilhelm and Friedrich Schlegel published the magazine **“Athenaeum”**. In it, Friedrich Schlegel described the idea of a “progressive universal poetry”, a literature that combines everything. **Novalis**, whose real name was Friedrich von Hardenberg, also belonged to the circle. He died in 1801 at the age of only 28.

In **high Romanticism**, interest in old folk literature grew. Achim von Arnim and Clemens Brentano collected songs and from 1805 published **“The Boy’s Magic Horn”**. Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm collected fairy tales such as “Hansel and Gretel” or “Little Red Riding Hood”. Their **“Children’s and Household Tales”** came out from 1812 onwards and are now part of UNESCO’s Memory of the World.

Romanticism also has a dark side, **Gothic Romanticism**. In **“The Sandman”** (1816), E. T. A. Hoffmann tells of Nathanael, who falls in love with the mechanical doll Olimpia. Adelbert von Chamisso wrote about **Peter Schlemihl**, who sells his shadow for a purse that never runs out of money. Without a shadow, people avoid him. Stories like these play with the line between reality and madness.

The most important poet of **late Romanticism** is **Joseph von Eichendorff**. In his novella “Memoirs of a Good-for-Nothing” (1826), a miller’s son sets out into the world with his violin and travels as far as Italy. His poem **“Moonlit Night”** (1837) begins with “It was as if the sky had kissed the earth so quietly”. Robert Schumann set it to music. Romanticism was also important in painting and music, for example with Caspar David Friedrich and Franz Schubert.

gewusst: Novalis is a pen name; the poet was called Georg Philipp Friedrich von Hardenberg.
Grimms’ fairy tales are among the most translated books in the German language.
Many Romantic poems became songs that are still performed at concerts today.

teile.einleitung: In a loan translation, a word from a foreign language is translated into German part by part, word for word. This is how the English “brainwashing” became the German word “Gehirnwäsche”. Words like this sound German but have a foreign model.
wichtigste: A loan translation translates a foreign word part by part.
“Gehirnwäsche” matches the English “brainwashing” exactly.
“Brain” becomes “Gehirn”, and “washing” becomes “Wäsche”.
“Wochenende” is also a loan translation from the English “weekend”.
Many older loan translations come from Latin.

abschnitte.text: In a **loan translation**, each part of a foreign word is translated **literally**. The English “brainwashing” is made of “brain” and “washing”. In German this became “**Gehirnwäsche**”. In the same way, the English “weekend” became “**Wochenende**” (week end). The new word looks completely German, and you only recognise its foreign origin at second glance.

Loan translations have existed for a very long time. Many come from **Latin**: the German “Halbinsel” (peninsula, literally “half island”) matches the Latin “paeninsula”, which literally means “almost island”. Today many come from **English**, for example “Flutlicht” from “floodlight”. If a foreign word is translated freely rather than quite literally, this is called a **loan rendering**.

gewusst: Other languages also make loan translations: the French “gratte-ciel” translates the English “skyscraper” literally as “sky-scratcher”.

teile.einleitung: Sometimes a word shows a grammatical form without any ending that you can see or hear. One example is the German “die Lehrer” (the teachers). To describe cases like this, linguists speak of a zero morpheme.
wichtigste: A zero morpheme is a grammatical function without any sound form.
One example is the German plural “die Lehrer” (the teachers), which looks the same as the singular.
The zero morpheme is often written with the sign Ø.
Here the difference from the singular only shows in the article.
Not all experts think the term is necessary.

abschnitte.text: Most German nouns get an ending in the plural: “Hund” (dog) becomes “Hunde”, “Blume” (flower) becomes “Blumen”. With some words, though, everything stays the same: ein **Lehrer** (one teacher), zwei **Lehrer** (two teachers). Even so, “Lehrer” in “die Lehrer” is clearly plural. So people say that the plural is expressed here by a **zero morpheme**, an ending you cannot hear.

In specialist books the zero morpheme is often written with the sign **Ø**. The plural “Lehrer” is then broken down as “Lehr-er-Ø”. Other German examples are **“Wagen”** (car), **“Messer”** (knife) or **“Zeichen”** (sign).
