Whether singular or plural is meant can be seen from the **article** or the verb: “Der Wagen fährt” (The car drives), but “Die Wagen fahren” (The cars drive).

The term helps to describe word forms in a uniform way: every plural then has a plural morpheme, sometimes simply an empty one. But some linguists find this solution unnecessary. They say you should only describe what can actually be heard. The term **morpheme** itself means the smallest unit of a language that carries meaning.

gewusst: English has cases like this too: “sheep” means one sheep and several sheep at the same time.

teile.einleitung: Many hundreds of years ago, people said “mîn niuwez hûs” in German. Today we say “mein neues Haus” (my new house). This sound change is called New High German diphthongisation, and it explains why Swiss German says “Huus” while Standard German says “Haus”.
wichtigste: In New High German diphthongisation, long vowels became double sounds.
Middle High German î became ei, û became au, and iu became eu or äu.
A double sound made of two vowels is called a diphthong.
The change began in the south-east of the German-speaking area and spread from there.
Most Swiss German dialects did not take part in it: “Huus” (house), “Iis” (ice), “Ziit” (time).

abschnitte.text: In **Middle High German**, the language of around 1200, there were long vowels such as **î**, **û** and **iu**. Over time these turned into **diphthongs**, that is double sounds. “Mîn” became “mein” (my), “hûs” became “Haus” (house) and “niuwez” became “neues” (new). This change is called **New High German diphthongisation**. It is one of the changes that separate Middle High German from the German of today.

The change began in the south-east of the German-speaking area, in what is now Austria. From there it spread north and west over the centuries. With printing and the new written language, the double sounds became established in the **standard language**. But not all dialects joined in, including the Low German dialects in the north.

Most **Swiss German dialects** have kept the old long vowels. That is why people say “Huus” instead of “Haus” (house), “Iis” instead of “Eis” (ice), “Ziit” instead of “Zeit” (time) and “Lüüt” instead of “Leute” (people). So on this point, Swiss German speakers sound older than Standard German. This shows that dialects are not wrong language but have a history of their own.

gewusst: Another old sound has also survived in Swiss German: Middle High German “guot” became Standard German “gut” (good), but in Swiss German people still say “guet” today.

teile.einleitung: Umlauts are the German sounds ä, ö and ü, as well as the double sound äu. When writing German, it is often unclear whether to write ä or e, äu or eu. A simple trick helps: you look for a related word.
wichtigste: The umlauts in German are **ä**, **ö** and **ü**, plus **äu**.
You write **ä** if a related word has an **a**: Hand, Hände (hand, hands).
You write **äu** if a related word has an **au**: Haus, Häuser (house, houses).
If there is no related word with a, you usually write **e**.
Some words with ä just have to be remembered, for example “Bär” (bear) or “Käse” (cheese).

abschnitte.text: If you do not know whether a German word is written with ä or e, you look for a **related word**. “Gläser” (glasses) comes from “Glas” (glass), so you write ä. “Kälte” (cold) comes from “kalt” (cold), and “Bäcker” (baker) comes from “backen” (to bake). With “Äpfel” (apples), the word “Apfel” (apple) helps. This method is called **deriving**.

Äu and eu sound exactly the same. Here you ask: is there a related word with **au**? “Häuser” (houses) comes from “Haus” (house), “Zäune” (fences) from “Zaun” (fence) and “Bäuche” (bellies) from “Bauch” (belly). “Läuft” (runs) is also written with äu, because it comes from “laufen” (to run). For words such as “heute” (today) or “Leute” (people) there is no such word, so you write eu.

In the past, people wrote a small **e** above a, o and u to show the changed sound. Over time this e got smaller and smaller, and it turned into the two **dots**. That is why ä, ö and ü can also be written as ae, oe and ue instead, for example when a keyboard has no umlauts.

Not every ä can be derived. Words such as **“Bär”** (bear), **“Käse”** (cheese), **“Säge”** (saw) or **“spät”** (late) simply have to be remembered. The other way round, “Eltern” (parents) is written with e, even though it is related to “alt” (old). In cases like these, the dictionary helps.

gewusst: In the plural the sound often changes: “Maus” becomes “Mäuse” (mice), “Buch” becomes “Bücher” (books), “Fuss” becomes “Füsse” (feet).
Linguists also call this sound change umlaut.
Many Swiss place names contain umlauts, such as Zürich or Mönchaltorf.

teile.einleitung: In the theatre, people act out stories on a stage in front of an audience. Theatre has existed since ancient times, and to this day many people like going to a play, an opera or a ballet. Switzerland also has a rich theatre tradition.
wichtigste: The word theatre comes from the Greek “theatron”, which means a place for watching.
A play is divided into **acts** and **scenes**.
A **tragedy** ends sadly, a **comedy** happily.
The first public performance is called the **premiere**.
Props are the objects used on stage.
Friedrich Dürrenmatt and Max Frisch are famous Swiss playwrights.

abschnitte.text: Theatre as we know it arose in **ancient Greece**. There were large open-air theatres with semicircular rows of seats on a hillside. The actors wore masks. The two most important genres date from this time: **tragedy**, a sad play, and **comedy**, a funny play. In a tragedy, the main character ends up in a conflict they cannot get out of.

A play is divided into **acts**, and each act is made of scenes. When two or more characters talk to each other, that is a **dialogue**. When one character speaks alone and shows their thoughts, it is called a **monologue**. The text of a play is also called a drama.

Many people work on a performance. The **director** decides how the play will be performed. Set designers build the scenery, and others look after lighting, sound, costumes and **props** such as cups, letters or swords. The **prompter** sits hidden and whispers the lines if someone forgets them. Before the **premiere** there is usually a dress rehearsal.

Not every kind of theatre needs language. In **mime**, the performers tell a story only through movement and facial expressions. In **opera** people sing, in **ballet** they dance. Puppet theatre and improvised theatre are also popular forms.

In 1956 the Swiss writer Friedrich Dürrenmatt wrote the play **“The Visit”**. In it, the rich Claire Zachanassian returns to her impoverished home town of Güllen. Max Frisch also wrote well-known plays such as “Andorra”. Many towns have theatres, such as the Schauspielhaus Zürich, and in summer open-air plays are performed in many places.

gewusst: In German the prompter is called a “Souffleuse”, from the French “souffler”, which means to breathe or whisper.
In ancient Greece, men played the women’s parts too, wearing masks.
Instead of “Good luck”, many theatre people in German-speaking countries say “Toi, toi, toi” before a performance, a bit like “Break a leg” in English.

teile.einleitung: A circumfix is a two-part word building block that wraps round a word stem from both sides. In German it is known above all from the past participle, as in “gespielt” (played). One part comes at the front, the other at the back.
wichtigste: An **affix** is a word building block that is attached to a word stem.
If it comes at the front it is called a **prefix**; if it comes at the back, a **suffix**.
A **circumfix** is made of two parts and surrounds the stem.
Example: **ge-** and **-t** in the German “gespielt” (played).
The name comes from the Latin “circum”, which means “around”.

abschnitte.titel: At the front and the back at once
abschnitte.text: In the past participle of weak German verbs, **ge-** comes before the stem and **-t** after it: “spielen” (to play) becomes **ge-spiel-t**, and “machen” (to make) becomes **ge-mach-t**. With strong verbs it is often **ge-** and **-en**, as in “gesungen” (sung) or “gefahren” (driven). Both parts belong together and form the new form together. Just one of them on its own would not give a correct form.

Linguists disagree about whether “ge-...-t” is really a true circumfix. Some experts prefer to describe it as a prefix and a suffix that appear together. Other languages in the world have circumfixes too. For school it is enough to know: a circumfix surrounds the word stem from the front and the back.

gewusst: With German verbs such as “studieren” (to study), the ge- is missing: it is “studiert”, not “gestudiert”.

teile.einleitung: Irony is a stylistic device in which you say something but clearly mean the opposite. If someone shouts “Lovely weather today!” in pouring rain, they are being ironic. Irony can be funny, cheeky or even hurtful, and it is an important tool in literature and everyday life.
wichtigste: With irony, you clearly mean the opposite of what you say.
One example is the sentence “Lovely weather today!” in pouring rain.
Sarcasm is biting, hurtful mockery.
With dramatic irony, the audience knows more than the character.
Socratic irony is named after the philosopher Socrates.
Situational irony is when an event contradicts what was expected in an absurd way.
Around 1800, Friedrich Schlegel developed the theory of Romantic irony.

abschnitte.text: **Irony** means saying something while meaning the opposite. The word comes from Greek and means roughly pretence. For irony to work, the listener has to notice that something is not meant seriously. Clues are often the tone of voice, a wink or the situation, for example when someone says in pouring rain: “Lovely weather today!”

Irony can be friendly and humorous. **Sarcasm**, on the other hand, is biting, hurtful mockery that wants to show someone up. The word comes from the Greek “sarkazein”, which means something like “to tear flesh”. Because you cannot hear irony well in text messages, it is often misunderstood there, which is why some people add an emoji.

In plays and films there is **dramatic irony**: the audience knows more than the character on stage. For example, you know that a potion only brings sleep, but the character thinks it is poison, as in Shakespeare’s “Romeo and Juliet”. **Situational irony** is when an event contradicts what was expected in an absurd way. One example would be a fire station burning down.

The Greek philosopher **Socrates** lived in Athens in the 5th century BC. In conversations he deliberately pretended not to know anything and asked lots of questions. This way he got the people he was talking to to think about their own opinions and spot contradictions. Today this way of playing dumb is called **Socratic irony**.

Around 1800, the poet **Friedrich Schlegel** developed the theory of Romantic irony in early Romanticism. In it, the author plays with his work and shows that it is all made up. Many writers use irony to criticise wrongs in society without saying so directly. The Swiss author Friedrich Dürrenmatt also used a lot of irony and black humour in his plays.

begriffe.erklaerung: A language tool that makes a text more effective.
Biting, hurtful mockery.
The audience knows more than the character.
An event contradicts what was expected in an absurd way.

gewusst: Young children often do not understand irony yet and take ironic sentences literally.
In the past, scholars even suggested a special punctuation mark for irony, but it never caught on.
The Greek word “eironeia” means pretence or make-believe.

teile.einleitung: A summary gives the most important ideas of a text in brief. It helps with learning and shows whether you have understood a text. A special form is the plot summary for stories.
wichtigste: A summary is **much shorter** than the original text.
You write it **in your own words**.
It stays **factual** and contains no opinion of your own.
Characters’ statements are given in **reported speech**.
**Minor details** are left out.
The opening sentence names the **title, author, type of text and topic**.

abschnitte.text: Before you write, you read the text carefully, ideally twice. As you do so, you **mark** the **key words** and important passages. Then you divide the text into sections and give each one a short heading. The **W questions** help: who, what, when, where, how and why?

A **plot summary** begins with an opening sentence. It names the title, the author, the type of text and the topic, for example: “The short story ... by ... is about ...”. Then comes the main part with the most important events in the right order. It is usually written in the **present tense**.

A summary gives the content **neutrally**. Suspense, embellishments and your own opinions do not belong in it. If the task asks for an evaluation, you write it in a clearly separate final part. Direct speech is turned into **reported speech**: “He says he will come tomorrow.”

A **retelling** tells a story again in detail and in a lively way, with suspense and direct speech. A **plot summary**, on the other hand, is brief and factual. If you only copy sentences from the original, you do not show that you have understood the text. That is why in a summary you put everything in **your own words**.

gewusst: A good summary can be understood even without knowing the original text.
In science, many articles begin with a short summary called an abstract.

teile.einleitung: “Schellen-Ursli”, known in English as “A Bell for Ursli”, is one of the best-known Swiss picture books. It came out in 1945 with words by Selina Chönz and pictures by Alois Carigiet and tells the story of a brave boy from the Engadine.
wichtigste: The picture book came out in 1945.
Selina Chönz wrote the text, and Alois Carigiet painted the pictures.
The story is set in the village of Guarda in the Lower Engadine.
Ursli does not want to walk in the Chalandamarz procession with the smallest bell.
He fetches a big bell from the Maiensäss, a high summer hut.
The book has been translated into many languages and also made into a film.

abschnitte.text: On **Chalandamarz**, 1 March, the children in the Engadine go through the village with bells to drive the winter away. Ursli only gets the **smallest bell** and is laughed at. He remembers a **big bell** hanging in the **Maiensäss**, a hut higher up the mountain. On his own he trudges up through the snow and spends the night there. His parents are terribly worried. The next day Ursli is allowed to lead the procession with the big bell.

**Alois Carigiet** came from the Grisons and was a painter and graphic artist. His colourful pictures show the Engadine houses with their decorated walls, the mountains and village life. For his work as an illustrator he received the **Hans Christian Andersen Award** in 1966, one of the most important prizes for children’s books. Many people first get to know the Engadine through his pictures.

The story is set in **Guarda** in the **Lower Engadine**, in the canton of the Grisons. Today many visitors come to see Ursli’s village. Selina Chönz wrote more books about the family, for example about Ursli’s sister **Flurina**. In 2015 a feature film about Ursli came out in cinemas.

gewusst: The book has been translated into many languages, including English and Japanese.
Chalandamarz is still celebrated in the Engadine today, with bells, songs and traditional costumes.

teile.einleitung: The case shows what role a noun plays in a sentence. German has four cases: nominative, genitive, dative and accusative. Depending on the case, the article and sometimes the noun itself change.
wichtigste: The German language has four cases.
The nominative answers the question “Who or what?”; the subject is in it.
The genitive answers the question “Whose?”.
The dative answers the question “To whom?”.
The accusative answers the question “Whom or what?”.
The genitive of “das Haus” (the house) is “des Hauses”.
Many verbs and prepositions decide which case follows.

abschnitte.text: **Casus** is the Latin word for case. The case shows what job a noun does in a sentence. In “Der Hund beisst den Briefträger” (The dog bites the postman), it is clear who bites and who is bitten, thanks to the forms “der” and “den”. The way nouns, articles and adjectives change depending on the case is called **declension**.

The **nominative** is the “who” case. The subject is in it, the person or thing doing something: “Der Löwe schläft” (The lion is sleeping). The **accusative** is the “whom” case and answers “Whom or what?”. In the sentence “Im Zoo sehe ich den Löwen” (At the zoo I see the lion), “den Löwen” is in the accusative. Many verbs such as sehen (see), kaufen (buy) or lieben (love) need the accusative.

The **dative** is the “to whom” case. In the sentence “Ich helfe dem Lehrer” (I help the teacher), “dem Lehrer” is in the dative, because you ask: whom am I helping? The **genitive** is the “whose” case and usually shows who something belongs to: “das Dach des Hauses” (the roof of the house). In the genitive the noun often gets an ending, so “das Haus” becomes “des Hauses”.

Prepositions also decide the case. After “mit” (with), “bei” (at) and “von” (from) comes the dative; after “für” (for), “ohne” (without) and “durch” (through) comes the accusative. The preposition “wegen” (because of) needs the genitive in standard German, so “wegen des Regens” (because of the rain) is correct. Some prepositions, such as “in” and “auf” (on), take the dative when it is about a place and the accusative when it is about a direction.

Not all languages have the same number of cases. English and French have almost no cases left in their nouns. Latin had six cases, and Russian also has six. Finnish even has about 15 cases. In Swiss German the genitive has almost disappeared: people tend to say “em Vater sis Huus” (the father his house) rather than “das Haus des Vaters” (the father’s house).

begriffe.erklaerung: The grammatical form of a noun that shows its role in the sentence.
The “who” case, in which the subject stands.
The “whom” case.
The “to whom” case.
The “whose” case, which often shows ownership.

gewusst: The book “Der Dativ ist dem Genitiv sein Tod” (roughly “The dative is the genitive’s death”) by Bastian Sick made the question of the right case very well known in Germany.
Finnish has about 15 cases, almost four times as many as German.
Words such as “Löwe” (lion) or “Bär” (bear) get the ending -en in almost every case except the nominative.

teile.einleitung: An idiom is a fixed group of words whose meaning you must not take literally. In German, someone who has “tomatoes on their eyes” has no vegetables on their face; they are failing to see something obvious. Idioms make language vivid and lively.
wichtigste: Idioms are fixed expressions with a figurative meaning.
The German “jemandem einen Bären aufbinden” (to tie a bear on someone) means to tell someone a lie.
“Den Nagel auf den Kopf treffen” means to hit the nail on the head, to say exactly the right thing.
Someone who “steps into the little fat pot” (ins Fettnäpfchen treten) says something tactless.
“Being on the wood path” (auf dem Holzweg sein) means being wrong.
“Pouring someone pure wine” (reinen Wein einschenken) means telling them the truth.
Many idioms come from everyday life in past centuries.

abschnitte.text: An **idiom** is made up of several words that together take on a new meaning. You cannot work out the meaning from the individual words. The German “die Katze im Sack kaufen” (to buy the cat in the sack) has nothing to do with cats; it means to buy something without checking it, like the English “to buy a pig in a poke”. Linguists call fixed expressions like these **idioms** or phraseologisms. Unlike a proverb, an idiom is usually not a whole sentence but is built into a sentence.

Many idioms have their origins in old trades and customs. A **“Holzweg”** (wood path) used to be a path along which wood was fetched from the forest. It ended in the middle of the forest and did not lead to the next village, so anyone who took it was going the wrong way. With “pouring pure wine”, people think of innkeepers who sometimes used to water down their wine. An honest innkeeper, on the other hand, served wine that had not been tampered with.

In old farmhouses there was often a bowl of fat next to the stove, used for greasing boots. Anyone who stepped in it by mistake made the floor dirty and got the housewife cross. This gave rise to the German idiom **“ins Fettnäpfchen treten”** (to step into the little fat pot), meaning to put your foot in it. For the cat in the sack, people say that cheats at markets put a cat in a sack instead of a piglet. But the origin of not every idiom is known for certain.

Swiss German also has many idioms of its own. Someone who wants “de Füfer und s Weggli” (the five-centime coin and the bread roll) wants two advantages at once, both the money and the roll, like “having your cake and eating it”. Some expressions exist in all German-speaking countries, others only in **dialect**. French and Italian, which are also spoken in Switzerland, have their very own images too. That is why, when you learn a language, you often have to learn idioms one by one.

Idioms make texts and conversations **vivid** and sometimes funny. With a picture you can often express more than with a plain description. But you should use them where they fit, because too many idioms one after another seem overdone. If you understand idioms, you also read books and newspapers better, because they appear there often.

begriffe.erklaerung: The technical word for a fixed expression with a figurative meaning.
A meaning that is not meant literally but lies in the picture.
In the past, a forest track for fetching wood that led nowhere.
The regional spoken language, for example Swiss German.

gewusst: In English, people say it is raining cats and dogs when it is pouring with rain.
The German idiom “ins Fettnäpfchen treten” has existed for several hundred years.
Translation programs often have great difficulty with idioms because they take them literally.

teile.einleitung: A metaphor is an image in language in which a word is used in a transferred sense. Anyone who says “Life is a journey” does not mean a real journey, but compares life with a path. Metaphors make language vivid, lively and often shorter too.
wichtigste: A metaphor is a shortened comparison without a comparing word such as “like”.
The area the image comes from is called the image source (vehicle).
In “Life is a journey”, the journey is the image source.
Metaphors such as “table leg” are hardly noticed as images any more; they are called dead metaphors.
A mixed metaphor happens when two images are combined in a way that does not fit.
Related stylistic devices are allegory, metonymy and synaesthesia.
Metaphors appear all the time in poems, advertising and everyday life.

abschnitte.text: The word **metaphor** comes from Greek and means transfer. You transfer a word from one area to another because there is a similarity. If you say of a brave person “He is a lion”, you do not mean the animal but his courage. Unlike a **simile**, a metaphor does without a comparing word such as “like”: “He fights like a lion” is a simile, “He is a lion” is a metaphor.

Every metaphor links two areas. The **image source** supplies the picture, and the image receiver is what you are actually talking about. In “Life is a journey”, the journey is the image source and life is the image receiver. What they have in common is, for example, a beginning, a goal, detours and crossroads.

We use many metaphors without noticing. A **table leg** is not a real leg, the neck of a bottle is not a real neck, and the foot of a mountain does not walk. Images like these are called **dead metaphors**, because people hardly notice them as images any more. Expressions such as the German “Rabeneltern” (raven parents, meaning uncaring parents), “earworm” or “information superhighway” are also metaphors.

An **allegory** presents an abstract idea as a figure, for example justice as a woman with a blindfold and scales, Justitia. In **metonymy**, a word is replaced by another that is closely linked to it: “The Federal Palace has decided” means the government in Bern. In synaesthesia the senses are mixed, as in “a screaming red”, because you cannot actually hear colours.

If you mix two images that do not fit together, you get a **mixed metaphor**, also called catachresis. A funny German example is “Das schlägt dem Fass die Krone ins Gesicht” (That hits the barrel’s crown in the face). It mixes up three German sayings: “knocking the bottom out of the barrel”, “putting the crown on everything” and “hitting everything in the face”, which all express that something is outrageous. Good writers make sure their images fit together.

begriffe.erklaerung: A word used in a transferred, figurative sense.
The area from which the image of a metaphor comes.
Showing an abstract idea as a figure or picture.
Replacing a word with a closely related word.
Combining two images in language that do not fit together.

gewusst: Researchers have found that we use a great many metaphors in everyday life without noticing.
In Switzerland, the figure of Justitia with her blindfold stands on many Fountains of Justice, for example in Bern.
Even computers have metaphors in their vocabulary, such as the “mouse” or the “recycle bin”.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland has produced many well-known children’s books. Characters such as Heidi, Ursli with his bell, Globi and Pitschi are known to children all over Switzerland and some of them all over the world.
wichtigste: Heidi is by Johanna Spyri and lives with her grandfather on an Alpine pasture.
Heidi’s friends are Peter the goatherd and Clara.
Ursli lives in Guarda in the Lower Engadine.
On Chalandamarz, 1 March, the children go through the village with bells.
Globi is a blue parrot-man with red and black checked trousers.
Pitschi is a kitten from the book by Hans Fischer.

abschnitte.text: **Johanna Spyri** wrote the story of **Heidi** around 1880. Heidi lives with her grandfather, the Alm-Uncle, on an Alpine pasture above Maienfeld. With the shepherd boy **Peter**, Peter the goatherd, she takes the goats out to graze. For a while she has to live with a rich family in the city of Frankfurt. There she makes friends with **Clara**, who uses a wheelchair. Heidi is one of the best-known books in the world.

The picture book **“A Bell for Ursli”** by Selina Chönz, with pictures by Alois Carigiet, came out in 1945. Ursli lives in **Guarda** in the Lower Engadine. For **Chalandamarz** he fetches a big bell from the Maiensäss, a high summer hut. On this day the children ring the winter out with bells. Selina Chönz also wrote the book **“Florina and the Wild Bird”** about Ursli’s sister.

**Globi** is a parrot-man with a blue body, a yellow beak and **red and black checked trousers**. He wears a cap on his head. He was created in the 1930s as an advertising character for the Globus department store. Since then he has had funny adventures in many books, travelled round the world and tried out all sorts of jobs.

In 1948 the artist **Hans Fischer** drew the book **“Pitschi”**. It tells of a kitten that always wants to be something else, for example a cockerel or a goat. In the end it realises that being a cat is best. Today Swiss authors still write many children’s books, for example Franz Hohler.

gewusst: “Heidi” has been translated into a great many languages and filmed several times, including as a Japanese cartoon series.
In Maienfeld in the canton of the Grisons there is a “Heidi Village” that many visitors from all over the world come to see.

teile.einleitung: The parts of a sentence are its building blocks. They are made of one or more words that always stay together when you rearrange the sentence. The most important parts of a sentence are subject, predicate, object and adverbial.
wichtigste: A part of a sentence can be made of one word or several words.
With the shifting test you find out which words belong together.
You find the subject by asking “Who or what?”.
The predicate is the verb; it can be in two parts, such as “have seen”.
With “Whom or what?” you ask about the accusative object, with “To whom?” about the dative object.
Adverbials say when, where, how or why something happens.
In “Lea feeds the dog”, “the dog” is the accusative object.

abschnitte.titel: What is a part of a sentence?
abschnitte.text: A **part of a sentence** is a piece of the sentence that does a particular job. In the German sentence “Am Morgen trinkt meine Schwester Tee” (In the morning my sister drinks tea) there are four parts: “Am Morgen” (in the morning), “trinkt” (drinks), “meine Schwester” (my sister) and “Tee” (tea). “Meine Schwester” is made of two words but is a single part. You can tell because the two words always stay together when you rearrange the sentence.

With the **shifting test** you rearrange a sentence without changing its meaning. For example, “Am Sonntag besuchen wir Oma” (On Sunday we visit Grandma) becomes “Wir besuchen am Sonntag Oma”. The words that move together form one part of the sentence. In a German statement the finite verb always stays in second place. This test was made known by the Swiss linguist **Hans Glinz**.

The **subject** is the person or thing that does something or that the sentence is about. You find it by asking “Who or what?”, and in German it is always in the nominative. The **predicate** is the verb and says what happens. In “Wir haben im Zoo Pinguine gesehen” (We saw penguins at the zoo), the predicate is made of “haben” and “gesehen”. Subject and predicate match each other in person and number: “ich spiele” (I play), but “wir spielen” (we play).

Many verbs need something more, the **object**. You ask about the accusative object with “Whom or what?”, for example “Lea feeds the dog”. You ask about the dative object with “To whom?”, for example “Yesterday Grandpa gave me a book”. In this sentence, “a book” is also an accusative object. The verb decides which objects are needed.

**Adverbials** describe the circumstances. The adverbial of time answers “When?”, for example “on Sunday”. The adverbial of place answers “Where?”, for example “in the garden”. There are also adverbials of manner (How?) and of reason (Why?). In many Swiss school books they are also called “Umstandsbestimmungen” (words of circumstance).

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of the sentence that says who or what does something.
The verb in the sentence, which says what happens.
An addition you ask about with “Whom or what?”.
An addition you ask about with “To whom?”.
A part of the sentence that gives the time, place, manner or reason.

gewusst: In a German statement you can put almost any part of the sentence at the beginning; only the verb has to stay in second place.
A whole subordinate clause can be a part of a sentence, for example “Whoever is late” in “Whoever is late misses the bus”.
In English the order of the parts of a sentence is much stricter than in German.

tipoync.t: Loss of the simple past in Upper German

teile.einleitung: In Standard German people say “ich ging” (I went) or “ich war” (I was). But in most Swiss German dialects this tense hardly exists. This disappearance of the simple past in the south of the German-speaking area is called the loss of the preterite in Upper German.
wichtigste: The preterite is the simple past form, such as “ich ging” (I went).
It is largely missing from most Swiss German dialects.
Instead the perfect is used: “ich bi gange” (I have gone).
The preterite has largely disappeared from Upper German since the 16th century.
In written Standard German, Swiss people also use the preterite.

abschnitte.text: **Upper German** is the name for the dialects in the south of the German-speaking area. They include **Alemannic**, to which almost all Swiss German dialects belong, and **Bavarian** in Bavaria and Austria. In these dialects the **preterite** has largely disappeared since the **16th century**. This is called the **loss of the preterite**.

abschnitte.titel: How people tell stories in Swiss German
abschnitte.text: When you talk about yesterday in Swiss German, you use the **perfect**. People say “ich bi gange” (I have gone) instead of “ich ging” (I went) and “ich ha gässe” (I have eaten) instead of “ich ass” (I ate). Even for “ich war” (I was), people usually say “ich bi gsii” (I have been). For an even earlier past, many dialects use a double perfect form, such as “ich ha’s vergässe gha” (I had forgotten it). But forms in the **subjunctive** have survived, such as “ich wär” (I would be) or “ich hett” (I would have).

Why the preterite disappeared has not been fully explained. One well-known explanation has to do with the loss of the final e in the southern dialects. Because of this, forms like “er sagte” (he said) and “er sagt” (he says) sounded almost the same. The perfect was clearer and won out. Other experts suspect further reasons. In the **written language**, on the other hand, the preterite is still the usual tense for telling stories.

gewusst: When someone in Switzerland writes an essay, they usually tell it in the preterite, even though they hardly ever use this tense when speaking.

teile.einleitung: When people speak, they are often doing something: promising, warning, asking a favour or asking a question. This action, carried out by saying something, is called illocution. The term comes from speech act theory.
wichtigste: Speech act theory studies what people do with language.
It was founded by the English philosopher John L. Austin.
The locutionary act is simply saying the words.
The illocutionary act is the action itself, such as a promise or a warning.
The perlocutionary act is the effect on the listener.

abschnitte.text: The philosopher **John L. Austin** noticed that with language we do not only describe things, we also act. If you say “I promise to come tomorrow”, you are making a promise. From this, Austin developed **speech act theory**. His student **John Searle** later developed it further. Today it is one of the foundations of linguistics.

Austin divided a speech act into three parts. The **locutionary act** is simply saying words that have a meaning. The **illocutionary act** is the action you carry out with them: promising, warning, asking, claiming. The **perlocutionary act** is the **effect** on the listener, for example that they get a fright or are pleased. A sentence such as “The dog bites” can be meant as a warning and can lead someone to keep their distance.

abschnitte.titel: How do you recognise the illocution?
abschnitte.text: Sometimes the action is named directly, with verbs such as “promise”, “warn” or “thank”. Often, though, you have to work it out from the context. “I’ll come round tomorrow” can be a promise or an announcement. Tone of voice and the situation also help you understand. Misunderstandings often arise when someone takes the illocution differently from how it was meant.

gewusst: A sentence such as “I hereby open the meeting” changes reality simply by being spoken.

teile.einleitung: A short story is a brief narrative that usually shows only a small slice of life. Typical features are a beginning in the middle of the action and an open ending. Readers have to keep thinking for themselves.
wichtigste: Short stories often begin in the middle of the action.
They usually have an open ending.
They show a short slice of everyday life.
The language is often simple and brief.
The form comes from the American “short story”.
After 1945 the short story became very popular in the German-speaking world.

abschnitte.text: A **short story** is brief and can often be read in a few minutes. It usually has an **abrupt beginning**: there is no long introduction, and you are right in the middle of things straight away. At the end there is often an **open ending**; the story simply stops. There are only a few characters and a short period of time. Often a turning point is at the centre, a moment that changes something.

The language of short stories is often **everyday** and plain. A lot is not said directly but only hinted at. That is why it is worth reading carefully and paying attention to small details. Because the ending is open, you wonder: what happens next? What were the characters thinking? In this way the short story makes you think and discuss.

The German short story was modelled on the English-language **short story**, for example by American writers such as Edgar Allan Poe and Ernest Hemingway. In the German-speaking world it became very popular after the **Second World War**. Authors such as **Wolfgang Borchert** and **Heinrich Böll** wrote short texts about people’s lives in the post-war period. Borchert’s story “The Bread” is well known.

Swiss writers also wrote well-known short stories. In 1969 **Peter Bichsel** published his “Children’s Stories”. They include the story “A Table Is a Table” about an old man who gives all things new names. In the end nobody understands him any more, and he does not understand the others. The story is read in many schools.

gewusst: Many short stories are only one or two pages long.
Short stories are good for lessons because you can read and discuss them in a single lesson.

teile.einleitung: In many sentences the verb needs something more to make the sentence complete. This addition is called the object. In German, depending on the verb, the object is in a particular case.
wichtigste: An object is a part of the sentence that the verb requires.
You find the accusative object by asking “Whom or what?”.
You find the dative object by asking “To whom?”.
The German verb “gehören” (to belong) needs a dative object, “besuchen” (to visit) an accusative object.
Some verbs need two objects, for example “leihen” (to lend).
There are also rare genitive objects and prepositional objects.

abschnitte.text: A sentence is made of **parts of the sentence**. The **subject** says who does something, and the **predicate** says what happens. Many verbs need a further addition: the **object**. In the sentence “I am reading a book”, “a book” is the object. Which object is needed is decided by the **verb**. Information about place, time or manner, on the other hand, is not an object.

The **accusative object** is the most common object. You find it by asking **“Whom or what?”**. Example: “We are visiting our grandmother.” Question: whom are we visiting? Answer: our grandmother. Other German verbs with an accusative object are sehen (see), kaufen (buy) and lieben (love).

You find the **dative object** by asking **“To whom?”**. Example: “The bike belongs to me”, in German “Das Velo gehört mir”. Question: to whom does the bike belong? Answer: to me. The German verbs for help, thank and congratulate also need a dative object. With verbs such as **“leihen”** (to lend) or **“geben”** (to give) there are often two objects: “I’m lending you my book.” Here “you” is the dative object and “my book” the accusative object.

The **genitive object**, which you find by asking “Whose?”, is rare. It occurs mainly in formal language, for example “Wir gedenken der Verstorbenen” (We remember the dead). The **prepositional object**, which is joined to a fixed preposition, is more common: “I’m waiting for the bus.” Here you ask “What am I waiting for?” With the **question test** you can find every object.

gewusst: Whether a verb needs an object, and which one, is called its valency.
In Swiss German the genitive has almost disappeared, so you only hear genitive objects in the written language.

teile.einleitung: Swiss German is the umbrella term for the many dialects spoken in German-speaking Switzerland. In everyday life people speak dialect, but at school they mostly write Standard German.
wichtigste: Mundart is another word for dialect.
There are many different dialects in German-speaking Switzerland.
Almost all Swiss German dialects belong to Alemannic.
At school people mostly write Standard German.
Typical words are “Chuchichäschtli”, “Zmorge”, “Rüebli” and “Finke”.
“Schmöcke” means to smell and “gumpe” means to jump.

abschnitte.text: A **dialect** (Mundart) is the language people speak in everyday life in a particular area. In German-speaking Switzerland almost everyone speaks dialect, children and adults alike. But at school and in newspapers and books, people mostly **write** in **Standard German**. Having dialect and Standard German side by side like this is typical of German-speaking Switzerland. In text messages and chats, though, many people also like to write in dialect.

Swiss German is not one uniform language. You can hear whether someone comes from Basel, Bern, Zurich, St Gallen or the Valais. Almost all these dialects belong to the **Alemannic** group of dialects. Alemannic dialects are also spoken in Alsace, Baden, Vorarlberg and Swabia. One exception is **Samnaun** in the Grisons, where people speak a Bavarian-Tyrolean dialect.

Many words only exist in Switzerland. A **“Chuchichäschtli”** is a small kitchen cupboard. **“Zmorge”** is breakfast, and the Znüni is the mid-morning break. A **“Rüebli”** is a carrot, and **“Finke”** are warm slippers. People from Germany often do not understand these words.

Some dialect words sound similar to Standard German words but mean something different. In many dialects, **“schmöcke”** means **to smell**, not to taste, like the Standard German “schmecken”. Someone who **“gumpt”** is hopping or **jumping**, for example on a trampoline. So when you write Standard German, you should watch out for words like these.

gewusst: People from abroad are often asked to repeat the word “Chuchichäschtli” because it sounds so difficult.
There is a big dictionary of the Swiss German dialects, the Schweizerisches Idiotikon.

teile.einleitung: A compound is a word made up of other words. It is formed when you join two or more words into a new one, for example the German “Hand” (hand) and “Schuh” (shoe) into “Handschuh” (glove). In German you can form a great many new words this way.
wichtigste: A compound is made of at least two words.
The last word is called the base word, the word in front of it the modifier.
The base word decides the word class and the article: “der Baum” (the tree), so “der Apfelbaum” (the apple tree).
Sometimes a linking sound is needed, like the n in “Sonnenblume” (sunflower).
In German, compound nouns are written as one word with a capital letter.
The plural of compound (Kompositum) is Komposita.

abschnitte.text: In German, “Regen” (rain) and “Schirm” (shade) become **“Regenschirm”** (umbrella), and “Zahn” (tooth) and “Bürste” (brush) become **“Zahnbürste”** (toothbrush). A word like this is called a **compound**. Usually the new word almost explains itself: a Regenschirm is a shade that protects you from rain. You can also join three or more words, for example “Fussballschuh” (football boot). This is how new words keep appearing in German.

The **last word** of a compound is called the **base word**. It says what the thing is: a “Haustür” (front door) is a “Tür” (door). The word in front is called the **modifier**; it describes the base word more precisely. The base word also decides the **word class** and the **gender**. That is why it is “die Haustür”, even though it is “das Haus” (the house). In the same way: “das Tier” (the animal), so “das Haustier” (the pet); “der Baum” (the tree), so “der Apfelbaum” (the apple tree).

Sometimes a small extra bit is needed between the parts, a so-called **linking element**. “Sonne” (sun) and “Blume” (flower) become **“Sonnenblume”** (sunflower); here an n is added. In “Geburtstag” (birthday) an s is added, and in “Hundehütte” (dog kennel) an e. These linking sounds make the word easier to say. There is no simple rule for them; you learn them best through reading and speaking.

In German, compound nouns are written **as one word** with a **capital first letter**, for example “Schulhaus” (school building) or “Fussball” (football). A compound can also be made of other word classes, such as “Schreibtisch” (desk) from a verb (to write) and a noun (table). With very long words you may use a hyphen to make them easier to read, for example “Kaffee-Ersatz” (coffee substitute).

gewusst: The word “Donaudampfschifffahrtsgesellschaftskapitän” (Danube steamship company captain) is a famous example of a very long compound.
Since the spelling reform, “Schifffahrt” (shipping) has been written with three f’s, because “Schiff” (ship) and “Fahrt” (journey) come together.

teile.einleitung: A copulative compound is a compound word in which both parts are equally important. Something “süsssauer” (sweet and sour), for example, is sweet and sour at the same time. This kind of compound is fairly rare in German.
wichtigste: In a copulative compound, both parts are of equal rank.
“Süsssauer” means sweet and sour at the same time.
You can imagine an “and” between the parts.
In the more common determinative compound, on the other hand, one part describes the other more precisely.
“Nasskalt” (cold and wet) is another example.

abschnitte.text: The word **copulative** comes from the Latin word for “to join”. In a **copulative compound**, two parts stand side by side as equals. You can imagine an “and” between them: **“süsssauer”** means “sweet and sour”, **“nasskalt”** means “wet and cold”. Neither part is subordinate to the other. By the way, “süsssauer” has three s’s because both words are kept complete.

abschnitte.titel: The difference from the determinative compound
abschnitte.text: Most German compounds are **determinative compounds**. In them, the first part describes the second more precisely: a **“Haustür”** (front door) is a door, not a house. A copulative compound is different: both parts contribute equally to the meaning. Number words such as “dreizehn” (thirteen), that is three and ten, are also often explained as copulative compounds.

gewusst: Hyphenated names such as “Baden-Württemberg” are also given as examples of copulative compounds.

teile.einleitung: In L-vocalisation, an l is pronounced like a vowel, for example like a u. That is why in Bernese German people say “Miuch” instead of “Milch” (milk). This sound feature is typical of western Swiss German dialects.
wichtigste: In L-vocalisation, an l becomes a vowel such as u.
This happens mainly before consonants or at the end of a syllable.
Bernese German “Miuch” for “Milch” (milk) is a well-known example.
The feature is typical of Bernese German and other western dialects.
L-vocalisation also exists in other languages.

abschnitte.text: A **vowel** is a sound like a, e, i, o or u. In **L-vocalisation**, an l is not pronounced as an l but as a vowel, usually like a **u**. This happens mainly when the l comes **before a consonant** or **at the end of a syllable**. So in Bernese German “Milch” (milk) becomes “Miuch”. In a similar way, “viel” (much) sounds like “viu” and “Stall” (stable) like “Stau”.

L-vocalisation is seen as a mark of **Bernese German**. It also occurs in other western dialects of German-speaking Switzerland, for example in parts of the cantons of Fribourg, Solothurn and Aargau. In Zurich or eastern Switzerland, on the other hand, people say “Milch” with a clear l. This often lets you hear which area someone comes from.

L-vocalisation does not only exist in Switzerland. In **French** it happened a long time ago: “cheval” means horse, and the plural is “chevaux”. In **English**, too, the l is no longer pronounced in words such as “walk” or “talk”. Linguists call changes like these **sound change**.

gewusst: For speakers of Bernese German, L-vocalisation is so natural that they often do not even notice it.

teile.einleitung: A radio play is like theatre for your ears. Several speakers play the parts, and there are sound effects and music too. That way the story takes shape entirely in the listener’s head.
wichtigste: A radio play has several speakers, sound effects and music.
In an audiobook, usually just one person reads a text aloud.
Radio plays began in the 1920s for the radio.
Foley artists create sounds such as footsteps or creaking doors.
The “atmos” are background sounds that let you hear where you are.
In Switzerland, the Kasperli radio plays with Jörg Schneider became very well known.

abschnitte.text: In an **audiobook**, usually one person reads a text aloud. A **radio play** is different: the parts are shared out among several speakers, and there are **sound effects** and **music**. You hear doors slamming, horses galloping or rain pattering. Because you cannot see anything, everyone makes their own picture. This really gets your imagination going.

Radio plays began in the **1920s**, when **radio** first appeared. Soon many radio stations were broadcasting their own radio plays. Later came records, cassettes, CDs and streaming. In 1938, **Orson Welles** in the USA staged “**The War of the Worlds**” as a radio broadcast with acted news reports. Some listeners are said to have believed the Martian invasion was real, but how great the panic really was is disputed.

abschnitte.titel: How a radio play is made
abschnitte.text: In the studio, actors record their parts. **Foley artists** create sounds with everyday objects. Footsteps in the snow, for example, are made with cornflour. Then there is the **atmos**, short for atmosphere. These are background sounds such as birdsong or traffic noise that show where the scene takes place.

In the series “**The Three Investigators**”, **Jupiter, Pete and Bob** solve crimes in the invented town of Rocky Beach. In German these radio plays have been coming out since 1979. The talking elephant **Benjamin Blümchen** has been on air since 1977. In Switzerland, the actor **Jörg Schneider** told many **Kasperli** stories in Swiss German. Generations of children have listened to them.

gewusst: There are well over 200 episodes of “The Three Investigators” in German; the series is one of the most successful radio plays ever.
For the sound of fire, Foley artists often scrunch up paper or plastic film in front of the microphone.

teile.einleitung: The Schweizerisches Idiotikon is the great scholarly dictionary of the Swiss German dialects. It collects and explains the vocabulary of German-speaking Switzerland from the late Middle Ages until today.
wichtigste: The Schweizerisches Idiotikon is a dictionary of the dialects of German-speaking Switzerland.
Work on it began in 1862.
Since 1881 it has been coming out in separate instalments.
It shows the vocabulary from the late Middle Ages to the present.
Today you can also look things up in the dictionary on the internet.

abschnitte.text: The **Schweizerisches Idiotikon** was started in **1862**. At that time the dialects were changing a lot, and people wanted to record the old words before they disappeared. Since **1881** the work has been published in separate parts, the **instalments**. It contains not only today’s dialect words but also words from old writings since the **late Middle Ages**. Work on it continues to this day.

The word **“Idiotikon”** comes from Greek. It means a dictionary that collects the **special words** of an area or dialect. It has nothing to do with the insult “idiot” used today. For every word, the Idiotikon explains what it means, where it is used and where it comes from.

The volumes are thick, and the system of order is not easy for non-experts. But today you can also search the Idiotikon **online**. That way you can find out what an old word means or how a family name might have come about. The dictionary is an important source for research into **Swiss German**.

gewusst: The Idiotikon is one of the largest dialect dictionaries in the whole German-speaking world.
The words are not simply in alphabetical order but follow a special system based on the consonants.

teile.einleitung: In many songs there is a part that comes back after every verse and that everyone can sing along to. This repeated line or group of lines is called the refrain, or in German “Kehrreim”. You find it in songs, poems and ballads.
wichtigste: A refrain is a line or group of lines that comes back after every verse.
The German word for it is “Kehrreim” (returning rhyme).
The word “refrain” comes from French.
There are refrains in folk songs, ballads, poems and pop songs.
A refrain helps you remember and sing along.

abschnitte.text: A song or poem is often made of several **verses** or stanzas. Each verse tells something new. The **refrain**, on the other hand, stays the same and is repeated after every verse. The German word for it is **“Kehrreim”**, because the rhyme keeps coming back. The refrain can be just one line long or take up several lines.

abschnitte.titel: From folk song to pop song
abschnitte.text: You find refrains in **folk songs**, in **ballads**, in children’s songs and in **pop songs**. In pop music it is often called the **chorus**. It frequently contains the title of the song. Because it comes up so often, it soon sticks in your head. That is why the refrain is usually the part that the audience sings along to at the top of their voices at a concert.

The refrain gives a song a fixed **structure**: verse, refrain, verse, refrain. It highlights the most important part and links the verses together. Thanks to the **repetition**, you can easily learn it by heart. In the past, when many people could not read, this helped songs to be passed on by word of mouth. In poems, a refrain can also strengthen a mood.

gewusst: Chants in football stadiums work like a refrain too: short, catchy and repeated again and again.

teile.einleitung: German is spoken as an official language in several countries. Each of these countries has its own form of the standard language. A language with several equally valid standard forms is called pluricentric.
wichtigste: A pluricentric language has several equally valid national standard varieties.
German has standard varieties in Germany, Austria and Switzerland.
None of these varieties counts as the only correct one.
Typical Swiss words are called Helvetisms, for example “Velo” (bike) or “Trottoir” (pavement).
In Switzerland the sharp S (Eszett) is not used; people always write ss.
English, French and Spanish are also pluricentric languages.

abschnitte.text: The word **pluricentric** means “with several centres”. German has such centres in **Germany**, **Austria** and **Switzerland**. In each country there is a separate **standard variety**, its own correct Standard German. These forms are **equally valid**. So Swiss Standard German is not wrong German, but a correct form of its own.

Words that are typical of Switzerland are called **Helvetisms**. They include **“Velo”** instead of “Fahrrad” (bike), **“Trottoir”** instead of “Gehsteig” (pavement), **“parkieren”** instead of “parken” (to park) and **“Znüni”** for the mid-morning snack. A special spelling feature is that in Switzerland the **sharp S** (Eszett) is not used; people always write **ss**. Pronunciation and some grammatical forms differ too.

Austria also has its own words, which are called **Austriacisms**. There people say, for example, **“Jänner”** for January and **“Paradeiser”** for tomatoes. Typically German words are called **Teutonisms**. Dictionaries such as the Duden often mark words like these with the country where they are used. This shows that there are several correct forms.

German is not the only pluricentric language. In **English**, for example, there is British, American and Australian English. **French** is spoken in France, Belgium, Canada and French-speaking Switzerland, among other places, each with its own words. **Spanish** and **Portuguese** also have several centres in Europe and the Americas.

gewusst: In French-speaking Switzerland, people usually say “septante” and “nonante” for 70 and 90, while in France they say “soixante-dix” and “quatre-vingt-dix”.
German is also an official language in Liechtenstein, as well as in Luxembourg, South Tyrol and eastern Belgium.

teile.einleitung: In a poetry analysis you examine a poem closely and explain what it can mean. You look at content, form and language and ask how everything works together.
wichtigste: The voice that speaks in a poem is called the lyrical I, or speaker.
You must not simply assume the lyrical I is the poet.
Important rhyme schemes are couplets (aabb), alternate rhyme (abab) and enclosed rhyme (abba).
A ballad tells an exciting story, often with direct speech.
A thing poem describes an object or an animal as precisely as possible.
The Swiss poet Eugen Gomringer is seen as the founder of concrete poetry.

abschnitte.text: First you read the poem several times and briefly sum up the **content**. Then you examine the **form**: how many stanzas and lines are there, what rhyme scheme, what metre? Next you look for **language devices** such as metaphors, similes or repetition. Finally you bring everything together into an **interpretation**. It is important to back up every point with a passage from the text.

In a poem a voice speaks that is called the **lyrical I**. It is not automatically the poet, because a poet can also take on a role. That is why in an analysis you write “the lyrical I feels lonely” and not “Goethe feels lonely”. The term goes back to the writer **Margarete Susman**, who coined it in 1910.

The **rhyme scheme** is written down with letters. In **alternate rhyme** (abab), the first and third lines rhyme, and so do the second and fourth. In couplets (aabb), two neighbouring lines rhyme; in enclosed rhyme (abba), one pair of rhymes wraps round the other. The **metre** describes the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables, for example in the iamb or the trochee.

A **ballad** such as Goethe’s “The Erl-King” tells a dramatic story with characters and direct speech. Goethe called it the “original egg” of literature, because it combines poetry, narrative and drama. A **thing poem** such as Rilke’s “The Panther” presents an object or an animal from within itself. An early example is “The Roman Fountain” by **Conrad Ferdinand Meyer** from Zurich. In **concrete poetry**, words are arranged on the page like picture material.

gewusst: Eugen Gomringer, the founder of concrete poetry, was born in Bolivia in 1925 and is Swiss.
In concrete poetry, the arrangement of the words on the page is sometimes more important than any sentence.

teile.einleitung: The semicolon is a punctuation mark made of a dot above a comma. In German it is also called a “Strichpunkt” (stroke point). It separates more strongly than a comma but less strongly than a full stop.
wichtigste: In German the semicolon is also called a “Strichpunkt”.
It is made of a dot above a comma.
It separates more strongly than a comma and less strongly than a full stop.
It links main clauses that belong closely together.
In German you carry on with a small letter after a semicolon, unless a noun follows.
In long lists it separates groups.

abschnitte.titel: Between a comma and a full stop
abschnitte.text: The **semicolon** (;) is a mark for a **medium pause**. A comma separates only weakly, and a full stop ends the sentence. The semicolon lies in between: it separates clearly but shows that the parts **belong closely together**. Because it is made of a dot and a comma-like stroke, in German it is called a **“Strichpunkt”** (stroke point). Do not confuse it with the raised comma, which is the apostrophe.

The semicolon often goes between two **main clauses of equal rank** that belong together in meaning. An example: “It was raining hard; even so, we went outside.” After the semicolon you carry on with a **small letter**, unless in German the next word is a noun. Often you could also use a full stop or a comma instead of the semicolon. But with the semicolon you show exactly the connection you want.

In long **lists**, the semicolon helps to form **groups**. This is useful when there are already commas within the groups. An example: “In the rucksack there are bread, cheese and apples; a jumper, a hat and gloves; a map and a compass.” That way you can see at once what belongs together.

The word **semicolon** comes from Greek and Latin and means something like “half a limb”. As a punctuation mark it was introduced by printers in **Venice** in the **15th century**, especially by Aldus Manutius. Today the semicolon is used fairly rarely. But if you use it correctly, you can structure texts finely.

gewusst: In the Greek language, the question mark looks exactly like our semicolon.
In programming languages the semicolon often ends a command.

teile.einleitung: As well as their factual meaning, many words have a special undertone. This extra meaning that resonates along with a word, and often carries a judgement, is called connotation. It shows whether a word seems friendly, insulting or posh.
wichtigste: Connotation is the extra meaning that resonates along with a word.
The factual basic meaning is called denotation.
The German words “Ross” and “Gaul” name the same animal as “Pferd” (horse), but sound different.
Connotations can be positive, negative or neutral.
They often depend on region, time and experience.

abschnitte.text: Every word has a **denotation**, a factual basic meaning. The German words “Pferd”, “Ross” and “Gaul” all name the same animal, the horse. And yet they come across differently: “Ross” sounds proud, like “steed”, or in Switzerland completely everyday, while “Gaul” sounds rather insulting, like “nag”. This extra undertone is called **connotation**. It comes from the feelings and ideas that people link with a word.

Connotations can be **positive** or **negative**. “Thrifty” sounds like a good quality and “stingy” like a bad one, even though both describe something similar. In the same way, “dog” seems neutral, while “mutt” is insulting. So anyone who writes or speaks can express an opinion through their choice of words without saying it directly. That is why it is worth paying close attention to words like these in texts.

Connotations are not the same everywhere. A word can sound neutral in one region and insulting in another. The undertone of words also changes over time. Personal experience plays a part too: for someone who is afraid of dogs, “dog” sounds different than it does for a dog owner.

gewusst: In advertising, words are often chosen for their positive connotation, for example “natural” or “fresh”.

teile.einleitung: Naturalism was a movement in literature and art at the end of the 19th century. The Naturalists wanted to show reality as precisely as possible, including poverty and misery. In German literature it reached its peak from about 1880 to 1900.
wichtigste: Naturalism reached its peak from about 1880 to 1900.
It arose as a reaction to industrialisation and misery in the big cities.
Its great model was the French writer Émile Zola.
In the Naturalist view, heredity and environment determine a person.
Arno Holz and Johannes Schlaf invented the “second-by-second style”.
Gerhart Hauptmann was the best-known German Naturalist and received the Nobel Prize in 1912.
His play “The Weavers” shows the Silesian weavers’ uprising of 1844.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century, factories and cities grew fast. Many working families lived in great **poverty**, in cramped flats and with long working days. The Naturalists did not want to make this reality look prettier. They wrote about hunger, illness and need, and about the **social question**. Important centres were Berlin and Munich.

The Naturalists admired the **natural sciences**. They believed that people are determined mainly by **heredity** and **environment**. This view is called **determinism**. Their great model was the Frenchman **Émile Zola**. In his series of novels “Les Rougon-Macquart”, he followed one family over several generations. The Norwegian Henrik Ibsen also influenced the movement.

**Arno Holz** and **Johannes Schlaf** wanted to capture reality exactly. They described events almost in real time, with every sound and every pause. This way of writing is called the **second-by-second style** (Sekundenstil). One example is their story “Papa Hamlet” from 1889. Holz believed that art should come as close as possible to nature.

**Gerhart Hauptmann** was the best-known German Naturalist. In the novella-like study **“Signalman Thiel”** (1888), a railway signalman lives a lonely life in Brandenburg. The play **“The Weavers”** (1892) shows the hardship of home weavers in Silesia, who rebelled against their exploitation in 1844. The first version was called “De Waber” and was written in **Silesian dialect**. The play was banned for a time. In 1912 Hauptmann received the **Nobel Prize in Literature**.

gewusst: The Naturalists often had their characters speak in dialect, because that was how real people talked.
Around 1900 other movements took over from Naturalism, for example Symbolism and later Expressionism.

teile.einleitung: The story arc shows how the tension in a story develops. It rises to the climax and then falls away again. With a few tricks you can tell exciting stories yourself.
wichtigste: The tension rises to the climax and then falls away.
Foreshadowing announces something that will happen later.
Words such as “suddenly” build tension.
Short sentences increase the pace.
When stretching time, you describe a short moment in great detail.
A cliffhanger leaves the tension open at the end.

abschnitte.text: A typical story begins **calmly** in the introduction. You find out who the characters are and where the story is set. In the **main part**, the tension builds up step by step. It reaches the **climax**, the most exciting part. After that the tension **fades away** in the ending, and the story comes to a close. If you draw it, it looks like an arc or a mountain.

With **foreshadowing**, the narrator hints that something is about to happen. An example: “She had no idea yet what was waiting for her behind the door.” This makes readers curious. It is also important not to give away the **outcome** in the introduction. Tension comes from not yet knowing how it will end.

Words such as **“suddenly”**, “all at once” or “then” announce a surprising turn. At the most exciting point, **short sentences** help: “He ran. The door creaked. Silence.” They feel breathless and fast. The characters’ thoughts and feelings, sounds and questions such as “What was that?” also increase the tension.

When you **stretch time** in a story, you describe a moment of just a few seconds in great detail, with lots of details, thoughts and feelings. That way the tension is drawn out for longer. You might describe exactly how the door handle slowly moves and the heart beats faster and faster. It feels almost like slow motion in a film.

A **cliffhanger** is an open ending at the most exciting point, for example at the end of a chapter or an episode of a series. Imagine the heroine hanging from a cliff, and right at that moment the episode ends. That way you really want to keep reading or watching.

gewusst: Many TV series end every episode with a cliffhanger so that you watch the next one too.
Crime novels and even non-fiction books use the story arc to keep readers hooked.

teile.einleitung: A hypernym is an umbrella term. “Flower”, for example, is the hypernym of “rose”, “tulip” and “daisy”. With terms like these, our language sorts the world into groups.
wichtigste: A hypernym is an umbrella term.
The narrower term is called a hyponym.
“Flower” is a hypernym, and “rose” is a hyponym of it.
Terms on the same level, such as “rose” and “tulip”, are called co-hyponyms.
A word can be an umbrella term and a narrower term at the same time.

abschnitte.text: The word **hypernym** comes from Greek: “hyper” means “over” and “onyma” means “name”. So a hypernym is an **umbrella term**. Its counterpart is the **hyponym**, the **narrower term**. “Rose” is a hyponym of “flower”, because every rose is a flower. But the other way round, not every flower is a rose.

Terms can be arranged like a ladder: living thing, plant, flower, rose. Each step is the umbrella term for the next. So “flower” is a hypernym of “rose” and at the same time a hyponym of “plant”. Terms on the same step, such as “rose”, “tulip” and “carnation”, are called **co-hyponyms**. It works for vehicles too: bike, car and tram are all vehicles.

Umbrella terms help with **sorting** and **explaining**. A good definition often names the umbrella term first and then a special feature: “A rose is a flower with thorns.” When you write, umbrella terms help you avoid repetition. Instead of writing “the dog” three times, you can write “the animal” once.

gewusst: Many dictionaries and search engines sort words into umbrella terms and narrower terms like these.

teile.einleitung: Max Frisch was one of the most important Swiss writers of the 20th century. He wrote novels, plays and diaries that are read in many languages. Alongside his writing, he worked for a long time as an architect.
wichtigste: Max Frisch was born in Zurich in 1911 and also died in Zurich, in 1991.
He studied architecture at ETH Zurich and built the Letzigraben open-air swimming pool.
Well-known novels are “I’m Not Stiller” (1954) and “Homo Faber” (1957).
Well-known plays are “The Fire Raisers” (1958) and “Andorra” (1961).
An important theme is the question of one’s own identity.
Frisch also showed how prejudice and cowardice harm people.

abschnitte.text: Max Frisch first studied German literature and then **architecture** at **ETH Zurich**. He ran his own architecture office. His best-known building is the **Letzigraben open-air pool** in Zurich, which opened in 1949. When his books became successful, he gave up the profession and devoted himself entirely to **literature**. He was honoured with many prizes, for example the Georg Büchner Prize in 1958.

The novel **“I’m Not Stiller”** begins with the sentence “I’m not Stiller!” The narrator denies being the missing sculptor Anatol Stiller. With this, Frisch asks whether we are what others see in us. In his diary he wrote the related thought “Thou shalt not make unto thee any image”. What he meant was that you should not pin other people down to a fixed picture.

In the novel **“Homo Faber”**, Walter Faber is an **engineer**. He believes in technology and statistics and has no time for fate or feelings. But a series of coincidences shakes his view of the world. The title is Latin and means roughly “man the maker”. The book is read in many schools.

In **“The Fire Raisers”**, Gottlieb Biedermann takes men into his house who are obviously arsonists. Out of cowardice, he refuses to admit it. In **“Andorra”**, the young Andri is thought to be Jewish and is treated by everyone with **prejudice**, until he comes to believe it himself. Both plays show what happens when people look away or shut others out.

gewusst: Frisch and Friedrich Dürrenmatt are regarded as the two great Swiss authors of the post-war period.
The Andorra in the play is an invented country and has nothing to do with the real microstate.

teile.einleitung: The Hans Christian Andersen Award is regarded as the most important international prize for children’s and young people’s books. It is given to authors and illustrators for their whole body of work. Swiss people have won it too.
wichtigste: The award is named after the Danish fairy-tale writer Hans Christian Andersen.
It is presented by the international organisation IBBY, which is based in Basel.
It is sometimes called the “little Nobel Prize” of children’s literature.
Since 1966 there has also been an award for illustration.
In 1994 the Swiss illustrator Jörg Müller won the award.

abschnitte.titel: An award for a whole body of work
abschnitte.text: The award is named after **Hans Christian Andersen**, who wrote fairy tales such as “The Emperor’s New Clothes”. It is presented by **IBBY**, the International Board on Books for Young People. IBBY was founded in Zurich in 1953 and has its secretariat in **Basel**. The award is given every two years. It does not honour a single book, but the whole body of work of one person.

At first the award was only for authors. Among those honoured are **Astrid Lindgren** and **Erich Kästner**. Since **1966** there has also been an award for **illustration**. The first winner in this category was **Alois Carigiet** from the Grisons, known for the pictures in “A Bell for Ursli”.

In 1994 the Swiss illustrator **Jörg Müller** won the award. He became known for the picture book “**The Changing Countryside**”. In it, he uses several large pictures to show how a landscape changes over the years through building. His books encourage you to look closely and think about the environment.

gewusst: With Alois Carigiet and Jörg Müller, two Swiss illustrators have won this important award.

teile.einleitung: The verb is the word class that says what someone does, what happens or what state something is in. Words such as “jump”, “fly” or “sleep” are verbs. Hardly any sentence manages without a verb, which is why it is one of the most important word classes of all.
wichtigste: In German, verbs are also called “doing words” or “time words”.
A verb says what someone does, for example “jump”.
The basic form is called the infinitive, such as the German “laufen” (to run) for “er läuft” (he runs).
Verbs change their form depending on the person: “du singst” (you sing), “der Vogel fliegt” (the bird flies).
Verbs have different tenses, for example “ich ging” (I went) for yesterday.
In German, verbs are written with a small letter, except at the start of a sentence or when used as nouns.
“Garden” is not a verb but a noun.

abschnitte.text: A **verb** describes an action, a process or a state. Actions are, for example, “jump” or “write”, processes “grow” or “rain”, and states “sleep” or “stay”. At school verbs are often called **doing words**. Because they change with time, in German they are also called time words (Zeitwörter). A test: you can say almost any verb with “I” in front of it, such as “I jump”.

The basic form of the verb is called the **infinitive**. In German it almost always ends in “-en” or “-n”, such as “laufen” (to run), “spielen” (to play) or “wandern” (to hike). In the dictionary you always find verbs in this form. If you want to find the basic form of “er läuft” (he runs), you ask: “What is he doing?” and arrive at “laufen”. Together with “zu” (to), the infinitive is also used in sentences such as “Ich habe Lust, zu spielen” (I feel like playing).

Verbs change their form; this is called **conjugation**. In German the form depends on the person and the number: ich singe, du singst, er singt, wir singen (I sing, you sing, he sings, we sing). The verb also changes with the tense, as in “ich gehe” (I go) and “ich ging” (I went). Weak verbs such as “spielen” form the past regularly, while strong verbs such as “gehen” change their vowel. Commands have a form of their own too, the imperative: “Komm!” (Come!)

The **auxiliary verbs** haben, sein and werden (have, be, become) help to form tenses, as in “Ich bin gegangen” (I have gone). **Modal verbs** such as können, dürfen, müssen, sollen, wollen and mögen (can, may, must, should, want, like) say whether you can, must or would like to do something. They usually go together with another verb: “Ich kann schwimmen” (I can swim). The three most common verbs in German are sein, haben and werden. They are also among the most irregular.

Swiss Standard German has some verbs of its own. People say “parkieren” instead of “parken” (to park) and “grillieren” instead of “grillen” (to grill). Many of these words ending in “-ieren” come from French. When a verb is used as a **noun** in German, it is written with a capital letter, as in “das Schwimmen” (swimming) or “beim Lesen” (while reading). In a German statement, the finite verb always comes in second place.

begriffe.erklaerung: The basic form of the verb, for example the German “laufen” (to run).
The change of the verb according to person, number and tense.
A verb such as can or must, which expresses possibility or obligation.
The command form of the verb, for example “Come!”.

gewusst: The shortest German verb in the infinitive is “tun” (to do), with only three letters.
The Duden lists many thousands of verbs, and new ones keep being added, such as “googeln” (to google) or “chatten” (to chat).
In Latin, “verbum” simply means “word”, because it was regarded as the most important word in the sentence.

teile.einleitung: The tense shows when something happens: in the past, in the present or in the future. German has six tenses, from the present to the future perfect. If you have a sure grasp of them, you can tell stories, describe plans and report on experiences.
wichtigste: The Latin word for tense is “tempus”; the plural is “tempora”.
There are six tenses: present, simple past (preterite), perfect, past perfect, future and future perfect.
“Ich war müde” (I was tired) is in the simple past.
“Sie hatte schon gegessen” (She had already eaten) is in the past perfect.
“Wir werden nach Lugano reisen” (We will travel to Lugano) is in the future.
In the perfect, “Ich gehe” (I go) becomes “Ich bin gegangen” (I have gone).
The past participle of “schwimmen” (to swim) is “geschwommen”.

abschnitte.text: The word **tempus** comes from Latin and means “time”. In grammar it means the form of the verb that places an action in time. The verb changes as it does so: “ich spiele” (I play), “ich spielte” (I played), “ich habe gespielt” (I have played). Some tenses are made of a single word, others of an **auxiliary verb** and another verb form. The German auxiliary verbs for this are haben (have), sein (be) and werden (become).

The **present** describes now, but also things that are always true, such as “The earth turns”. It is often used for the future too: “Tomorrow I’m going to Bern.” In German the **future** is formed with “werden” and the infinitive, as in “Wir werden nach Lugano reisen” (We will travel to Lugano). The future perfect describes something that will be finished in the future: “He will have managed it by tomorrow.” It is used fairly rarely.

There are three tenses for the past. The **simple past**, such as “ich war” (I was) or “er brachte” (he brought), is used mainly in written storytelling, for example in books and fairy tales. The **perfect**, such as “ich bin gegangen” (I have gone), is typical of telling a story in conversation. The past perfect shows that something happened even earlier than another event in the past: “When I came, she had already eaten.”

With **weak verbs**, the simple past is formed regularly with “-te”: spielen, spielte, gespielt (play, played, played). **Strong verbs**, on the other hand, change their stem vowel: schwimmen, schwamm, geschwommen (swim, swam, swum). There are also mixed verbs such as “bringen” (to bring), where the vowel changes and “-te” is still added: er brachte (he brought). You have to learn the forms of the strong verbs by heart, often with the help of a list.

Swiss German has almost no simple past at all. When someone tells you about yesterday in Bernese or Zurich German, they use the **perfect**, for example “Ich bi gsi” (I have been) for “Ich war” (I was). This loss of the simple past also affects dialects in southern Germany and Austria. That is why Swiss children have to practise the simple past especially for writing. In essays and stories, though, it is the most important tense for telling a story.
