begriffe.erklaerung: The form of the verb that shows time; in Latin “tempus”, plural “tempora”.
A past tense, for example “ich ging” (I went).
A past tense formed with haben or sein, for example “ich bin gegangen” (I have gone).
A verb form such as “gegangen” (gone) or “geschwommen” (swum), needed for the perfect and past perfect.
The German verbs haben, sein and werden, which are used to form tenses.

gewusst: Some languages, such as Chinese, do not change their verbs for time at all, but use time words such as “yesterday”.
Whether the perfect is formed with “haben” or “sein” is not the same everywhere; in Switzerland and southern Germany, for example, people say “ich bin gesessen” (I sat).
In everyday life you often hear the future perfect as a guess: “He will have missed the bus.”

teile.einleitung: The semiotic triangle is a model from linguistics. It shows how a word, the idea in our head and the object in the world are connected.
wichtigste: The semiotic triangle links sign, concept and object.
It became known especially through Charles Ogden and Ivor Richards in 1923.
A word does not point directly to an object.
The link runs through the idea in our head.
That is why the base line of the triangle is often drawn as a dotted line.

abschnitte.text: The **semiotic triangle** has three corners. The first is the **sign**, the word as you hear or read it, for example “tree”. The second is the **concept**, the idea in our head. The third is the **object**, a real tree out in the woods. The model became known especially through **Charles Ogden** and **Ivor Richards**, who presented it in **1923** in their book “The Meaning of Meaning”.

The most important part of the model is the **bottom line** between word and object. It is often drawn as a **dotted line**. This means that a word has no direct, natural link to the object. The word “tree” does not look like a tree. It calls up an **idea**, and only this idea refers to the real tree.

Because the link runs through the head, different languages can have different words for the same thing: “Baum”, “arbre”, “albero”, “tree”. Misunderstandings can be explained this way too, when two people think of something different with the same word. The model helps you think more precisely about the meaning of words. It is related to Ferdinand de Saussure’s ideas about the language sign.

gewusst: The word “semiotics” means the study of signs and comes from the Greek word for sign.
Philosophers in ancient times already had similar thoughts about the relationship between word and thing.

teile.einleitung: Jeremias Gotthelf is one of the best-known Swiss writers. He was a pastor in the Emmental in the canton of Bern and wrote novels and stories about the lives of farmers. His most famous story is “The Black Spider”.
wichtigste: Jeremias Gotthelf’s real name was Albert Bitzius.
He lived from 1797 to 1854 and was a Reformed pastor in Lützelflüh in the Emmental.
His works describe farming life in the Emmental.
“The Black Spider” came out in 1842 and tells of a pact with the devil.
Well-known novels are “Uli the Farmhand” and “Uli the Tenant Farmer”.
He took the name Jeremias Gotthelf from the main character of his first novel.

abschnitte.text: Albert Bitzius was born in **Murten** in 1797 and, like his father, became a pastor. From 1832 he worked in **Lützelflüh** in the Emmental. There he got to know the lives of farming families, farmhands and maids very well. He only began writing when he was about 40. His first novel was called “The Farmers’ Mirror” and came out in 1837. Its main character is called Jeremias Gotthelf, and this name became his **pen name**.

Almost all of Gotthelf’s works are set in the **Emmental**. He describes the farms, work, festivals and worries of the people in great detail. In “**Uli the Farmhand**”, a young farmhand becomes a capable man through hard work and honesty. Gotthelf also wanted his books to educate: he showed what he thought was good and what was bad. He often mixed words from Bernese German into his texts.

The novella “**The Black Spider**” from 1842 has a **frame story**: at a christening on a farm, the grandfather tells an old legend. In it, villagers in great need make a pact with the devil. Because the promise is broken, a black spider brings death and plague to the village. The story is regarded as a masterpiece and is still read in schools today.

gewusst: Many of Gotthelf’s works have been filmed, for example “Uli the Farmhand” in the 1950s.
In Lützelflüh a museum remembers Gotthelf and his work.

teile.einleitung: The sonnet is a strict form of poem with exactly 14 lines. It comes from Italy and later became popular all over Europe, including in German literature.
wichtigste: A classic sonnet has 14 lines.
It is usually made of two stanzas of four lines and two stanzas of three lines.
The four-line stanzas are called quatrains, the three-line ones tercets.
The sonnet arose in Italy and became famous through Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch).
The English sonnet after Shakespeare ends with a rhyming couplet.

abschnitte.text: A classic **sonnet** has **14 lines**. They are usually divided into **two quatrains** (stanzas of four lines) and **two tercets** (stanzas of three lines). The lines rhyme according to a fixed pattern. The quatrains often present a theme or a contrast. The tercets then bring a turn or a solution.

The sonnet arose in **Italy** in the 13th century. It became famous through the poet **Francesco Petrarca**, known in English as Petrarch, who wrote many sonnets. From Italy the form spread all over Europe. In England, **William Shakespeare** wrote more than 150 sonnets. His form is a little different: three four-line stanzas and, at the end, a **rhyming couplet**.

In German literature the sonnet was especially popular in the **Baroque** period. **Andreas Gryphius** wrote the well-known sonnet “All Is Vanity” about how everything passes away. Goethe, the Romantics and later **Rainer Maria Rilke** with his “Sonnets to Orpheus” also used this form. To this day the strict form attracts many poets.

gewusst: The word “sonnet” comes from the Italian “sonetto” and means something like “little sound”.
Rainer Maria Rilke wrote the “Sonnets to Orpheus” in the Valais, where he spent the last years of his life.

teile.einleitung: A non-fiction text gives information about facts, explains something or wants to persuade readers of something. Newspaper articles, encyclopedia entries, instructions, tables and advertising are examples of non-fiction texts.
wichtigste: Non-fiction texts deal with reality, not with invented stories.
Karl Bühler distinguished the functions of representation, expression and appeal.
A news story is built like an upside-down pyramid.
A news item answers the W questions: who, what, when, where.
Tables and charts are called non-continuous texts.
Advertising texts above all have an appeal function.

abschnitte.text: In 1934 the linguist **Karl Bühler** presented the **organon model**. According to it, every language sign has three jobs. It **represents** a state of affairs, it **expresses** the attitude of the sender, and it makes an **appeal** to the receiver. In an encyclopedia article, representation is the main thing. In advertising, the appeal comes first, because it wants you to buy something.

A classic newspaper news story follows the principle of the **inverted pyramid**: the most important things come at the beginning, and details follow afterwards. That way the editors can shorten the text from the end without losing anything important. A short **news item** answers the **W questions** who, what, when and where, often also how and why. The source should be named too. The **lead**, also called the standfirst, comes between the headline and the main text and sums up the key points.

As well as the news story and the report, there are other **types of journalistic text**. A **feature** (reportage) describes events vividly, with scenes, impressions and quotations, as if you were there yourself. A **commentary** gives the writer’s opinion. An **interview** is made up of questions and answers. When you read a newspaper, you should be able to tell whether a text is informing you or putting forward an opinion.

Not every text is made of sentences and paragraphs. **Tables, charts, timetables or graphics** are called **non-continuous texts**, because you do not read them from beginning to end. The term became especially well known through the **PISA studies**. An SBB timetable is a good example: you look specifically for the row and column you need.

An **analysis of a non-fiction text** has three parts. In the **introduction** you name the author, title, type of text, where it was published and the topic. In the **main part** you examine the structure, the argument and the language more closely. In the **conclusion** you sum up the results and can give your own assessment.

gewusst: The word “organon” comes from Greek and means tool: Bühler saw language as a tool.
The inverted pyramid helps readers too: if you only read the beginning, you already know the most important things.

teile.einleitung: In German, a “Langohr” (long ear) is not a long ear but a hare. A “Rotkehlchen” (red throat) is a bird with a red throat, the robin. Compound words like these, which name something after one of its features, are called possessive compounds.
wichtigste: A possessive compound names a creature after a feature it has.
“Langohr” (long ear) means an animal with long ears, such as a hare.
Other examples are “Rotkehlchen” (robin), “Dickkopf” (stubborn person) and “Grünschnabel” (greenhorn).
The word “possessive” means showing ownership.
In a normal compound such as “Haustür” (front door), the whole thing is a kind of the last word.

abschnitte.text: A **compound** is a word made of other words. Usually the whole thing is a kind of its last part: a **“Haustür”** (front door) is a door. A **possessive compound** is different. A **“Langohr”** (long ear) is not an ear but an animal that **has** long ears. That is where the name comes from, because the Latin “possidere” means to own. So the word names one striking feature and means the whole creature. English has similar words, such as “redhead”.

Possessive compounds are not rare at all. A **“Rotkehlchen”** (red throat) is a bird with a red throat, the robin. A **“Dickkopf”** (thick head) is a stubborn person, and a **“Trotzkopf”** (defiance head) a defiant child. A **“Grünschnabel”** (green beak) is someone who is still young and inexperienced. The fairy-tale character **“Rotkäppchen”**, Little Red Riding Hood, is also named after her red cap.

Many possessive compounds name **people** or **animals**. They are often meant figuratively and sound joking or slightly insulting, such as “Angsthase” (scaredy-cat, literally fear hare) or “Schlafmütze” (sleepyhead, literally nightcap). The principle is similar to **pars pro toto**, where a part stands for the whole. In linguistics such words are also called **bahuvrihi**, after a term from ancient Indian grammar.

gewusst: The ancient Indian word “bahuvrihi” is itself a possessive compound and means roughly “having much rice”.

teile.einleitung: A zeugma is a figure of speech in which one word belongs to several parts of a sentence. But it fits each part with a different meaning. This often comes across as funny and surprising.
wichtigste: In a **zeugma**, one word refers to several parts of a sentence.
The word has a **different meaning** each time.
A German example: “He smashed the door and set off on the way home”, where both actions are expressed by the one verb “einschlagen”.
Zeugma is often used for **wordplay** and humour.
The name comes from Greek and means something like “yoke” or “joining”.

abschnitte.text: In the German sentence “Er schlug die Tür und den Weg nach Hause ein”, the verb **“einschlagen”** belongs to two things. With the door it means to smash; with the way it means to choose a direction. Because one word has to carry both meanings at the same time, you stumble briefly as you read. It is exactly this surprise that gives the zeugma its charm.

Many humorists like to play with zeugma. A well-known German example is: “Ich heisse nicht nur Heinz, sondern Sie auch herzlich willkommen.” Here “heissen” belongs once to the name (my name is Heinz) and once to the welcome (I bid you welcome). Sentences such as “She lost her umbrella and her patience” are zeugmas too. If you want to build one yourself, look for a word with two meanings.

gewusst: The plural of zeugma is zeugmata or zeugmas.

teile.einleitung: A letter to the editor is a letter to a newspaper or magazine in which someone expresses their opinion. It often refers to an article that was published earlier. In this way readers can take part in public debate.
wichtigste: A letter to the editor often refers to a published article.
It is an opinion text that gives reasons for a personal view.
Newspapers usually require the writer’s full name and place of residence.
A good letter to the editor is short, factual and well reasoned.
At the beginning you name what you are responding to, such as the title and date of the article.
The editors decide which letters appear and may shorten them.

abschnitte.titel: What is a letter to the editor?
abschnitte.text: In a **letter to the editor**, a reader writes to a newspaper. Many letters **respond to an article**: the writer agrees, disagrees or adds something. Other letters take up a current topic from the village, the town or the country. In Switzerland, letters to the editor are very common, for example before **popular votes** and elections.

A letter to the editor puts forward a **personal opinion** and **gives reasons** for it. That is why it counts as an opinion-based, **argumentative** text. If you want to convince people, you give reasons and examples. Feelings may come into it, but insults have no place. So a letter to the editor is similar to a commentary, except that it does not come from the newspaper’s own staff.

At the **beginning** you name what you are referring to, for example the title and date of the article. That way readers understand the context straight away. Then comes your own **opinion** with arguments. At the end there can be a demand or a conclusion. A good letter to the editor is **short, factual and well reasoned** and stays respectful.

abschnitte.titel: With name and place of residence
abschnitte.text: Newspapers normally do **not** publish **anonymous** letters. They require the writer’s **full name** and **place of residence**. If you express your opinion in public, you stand by it. The **editors** choose which letters appear and are allowed to shorten them. Many newspapers set a maximum number of characters.

gewusst: Today many newspapers also accept letters to the editor by email or through a form on their website.
In many newspapers, the letters page is one of the most widely read pages.

teile.einleitung: A simile is a figure of speech that places two things side by side. A comparing word such as “like” or “as” shows clearly that a comparison is being made. Similes make texts vivid and lively.
wichtigste: A simile links two things with a **comparing word**.
Typical comparing words are **“like”**, **“as”** and **“as if”**.
Example: “He is as strong as a bear.”
In a **metaphor** the comparing word is missing: “He is a bear.”
Similes appear in poems, stories and everyday language.

abschnitte.text: A simile has three parts: the thing being described, the image it is compared with, and what they have in common. In the sentence “He is as strong as a bear”, what they have in common is **strength**. This shared quality is called the **tertium comparationis** in technical language, which means “the third thing of the comparison”.

Simile and **metaphor** are closely related. The simile says explicitly: one thing is **like** the other. The metaphor leaves out this word and uses the image directly. “She is as fast as the wind” is a simile. “She is a whirlwind” is a metaphor. You can tell the difference by the comparing word.

We use many similes every day without noticing: **as sly as a fox**, **as white as snow** or **as tired as a dog**. With “as if” you can also compare whole sentences: “He ran as if someone were chasing him.” Images like these help you picture something quickly.

If you are writing a story or a poem, you can create atmosphere with similes. Good similes are surprising but still understandable. Instead of “The lake was calm”, you can write: “The lake lay there like a mirror.” That way the reader sees the picture.

gewusst: The ancient Greek epics of Homer already contain long, detailed similes.
The Latin word for comparison is “comparatio”, which is also where the comparative, as in “bigger”, gets its name.

teile.einleitung: A quotation is a passage from someone else’s text that you take into your own text. If you quote, you have to mark this clearly and give the source. That way everyone knows whose words or thoughts they are.
wichtigste: A **word-for-word quotation** goes in quotation marks; in Switzerland these are **angle-shaped marks**.
A quotation within a quotation goes in **single angle-shaped marks**.
Omissions are marked with **[...]**, and your own additions go in **square brackets**.
With **[sic]** you show that a mistake is already in the original.
An **indirect quotation** also needs a source reference.
Anyone who takes something over without giving the source is committing **plagiarism**.

abschnitte.titel: Word for word or in your own words
abschnitte.text: In a **word-for-word quotation** you take over the text exactly as it is in the original. In an **indirect quotation**, also called a **paraphrase**, you give the content in your own words. In both cases the idea belongs to someone else. That is why you must always say where it comes from, for example with a **footnote**.

If you leave words out of a quotation, you put **[...]** in their place. If you have to add a word so that the sentence fits grammatically, you put it in **square brackets**. That way your own changes can be told apart from the original. The important thing is that the meaning of the quotation must not change as a result.

“Sic” is Latin and means “thus”. With **[sic]** you show that a striking mistake really is in the original like that. In footnotes you often read **“ibid.”** (in German “ebd.”), which means “in the same place”. It refers to the same source as the footnote before. If someone in your quotation is quoting someone themselves, in Switzerland you use the single angle-shaped marks for this.

In Switzerland, quoting is governed by the **Copyright Act**. Under **Article 25 of the Copyright Act (URG)**, you may quote from published works if the quotation serves to explain, refer to or illustrate something. The length must be justified by this purpose, and the quotation and the source must be identified. Anyone who passes off other people’s texts as their own is committing **plagiarism**, which can have serious consequences at schools and universities.

gewusst: The word quotation (in German “Zitat”) comes from the Latin “citare”, which means “to summon”.
Some quotations are so well known that they are called household sayings, for example “Through this sunken lane he has to come” from Schiller’s “Tell”.

teile.einleitung: Poems, novels and plays are very different kinds of text. So that we can talk about them, literature is divided into genres. For a long time three great genres have been distinguished: narrative, poetry and drama.
wichtigste: A literary genre is a group of texts with shared features.
The three main genres are narrative, poetry and drama.
Narrative includes storytelling texts such as the novel, the fairy tale or the short story.
Poetry includes poems with lines of verse and often with rhymes.
Drama includes plays, which are acted out by characters.
Within the genres there are smaller types of text, for example the fable, the sonnet or the comedy.

abschnitte.text: In **narrative** literature, someone tells a story. This voice is called the **narrator**. Narrative includes long texts such as the **novel** and short ones such as the **short story**, the **fable** or the **fairy tale**. The old heroic epics, such as the Song of the Nibelungs, count too. A well-known Swiss storyteller is Jeremias Gotthelf.

**Poetry** is the genre of poems. Typical features are **lines of verse**, **stanzas**, a rhythm and often **rhymes**. Poems are usually short and express feelings, moods or thoughts. The voice that speaks in a poem is called the **lyrical I**. Well-known forms are the sonnet, the ode and the haiku.

**Drama** includes texts that are written for the stage. There is no narrator: the plot develops through the characters’ conversations, the **dialogue**. A play is often divided into **acts** and **scenes**. The most important kinds are **tragedy** and **comedy**. One example from Switzerland is Friedrich Dürrenmatt’s “The Visit”.

Not every text fits neatly into one box. The **ballad** is a poem, but it tells a story and often has dialogue like a play. That is why Goethe called it an “original egg” of literature. Today **non-fiction texts** such as reports or essays are sometimes counted as a further group. So the division is a help for sorting, not a strict law.

gewusst: More than 2300 years ago the Greek philosopher Aristotle was already writing about the rules of tragedy and epic.
Goethe called epic, poetry and drama the three “natural forms of literature”.

teile.einleitung: Speech act theory shows that with language we do not only describe things, we also act. Anyone who makes a promise, opens a meeting or asks for something is carrying out an action with words.
wichtigste: Speaking is a form of acting.
The British philosopher John L. Austin founded speech act theory.
His lectures were published in 1962 as “How to Do Things with Words”.
John Searle developed the theory and distinguished five classes of speech act.
A promise is one of the commissives.
“I hereby declare the meeting open” is a declaration.

abschnitte.text: For a long time people thought that sentences mainly **describe** something and are true or false. The British philosopher **John L. Austin** showed that this is not enough. If you say “I promise to come tomorrow”, you are not describing anything; you are **acting**: you are making a promise. Austin’s lectures were published in **1962** under the title **“How to Do Things with Words”**.

Austin distinguished different sides of a speech act. The **locution** is the saying of the words themselves. The **illocution** is the action you carry out with them, such as warning, asking or promising. The **perlocution** is the effect on the other person, for example that someone gets a fright or is persuaded. The illocution is especially important for the theory.

The American philosopher **John Searle** developed the theory further. He divided illocutionary acts into **five classes**. **Representatives** present something as true, such as a claim. **Directives** are meant to get the listener to do something, for example a request. With **commissives** such as a promise, the speaker commits himself. **Expressives** express feelings, such as thanks. **Declarations** change reality directly by being said.

The sentence **“I hereby declare the meeting open”** is a declaration: afterwards the meeting really is open. But this only works if the person has a suitable **role**, such as chairing the meeting. Speech acts are often **indirect** too. “Can you close the window?” is not really a question about ability, but a request.

gewusst: Verbs such as “promise”, “name” or “declare” are called performative verbs, because you carry out an action with them.
Today speech act theory is also used to improve conversations with computers and voice assistants.

teile.einleitung: If a word no longer fits at the end of a line, you can split it. There are fixed rules for this. The most important one is: in German you split words by spoken syllables.
wichtigste: In German, words are basically split by **spoken syllables**.
Two identical consonants are split: **Was-ser** (water).
The combinations **ck**, **ch** and **sch** stay together: **Zu-cker** (sugar), **la-chen** (to laugh).
Since the spelling reform you may split **st**: **Kas-ten** (box).
A single vowel at the beginning or end of a word is not split off.
Compound words are split between their parts: **Schul-haus** (school building).

abschnitte.text: The easiest way to find the places where you can split a word is to say it slowly and **clap** along. Each clap is a syllable. “Scho-ko-la-de” (chocolate) has four syllables and therefore three places to split. At the end of a line you put a **hyphen** at the split, and the rest goes onto the next line.

If there is only one consonant between two vowels, it goes onto the new line: **Ro-se** (rose). If there are several consonants in between, only the last one goes onto the new line: **Kas-ten** (box), **Fens-ter** (window). With double consonants you split in the middle: **Was-ser** (water), **Bal-lon** (balloon).

Some groups of letters stand for a single sound. That is why **ch**, **sch** and **ck** are never split: “la-chen” (to laugh), “Fla-sche” (bottle), “Zu-cker” (sugar). In the past, ck became k-k when a word was split, but not any more. The old rule “never split st” no longer applies either, since the **spelling reform** was agreed in 1996.

A single vowel at the beginning or end of a word is not split off. That is why “Igel” (hedgehog) is not split at all, because a single I at the end of a line would look odd. With compound words such as **Schul-haus** (school building) or **Haus-tür** (front door), you split at the seam. After that you can split the parts by syllables again.

gewusst: Computer programs often split words automatically, but they sometimes make funny mistakes.
A well-known example of a misleading split is the German “Urin-stinkt” (urine stinks) instead of “Ur-instinkt” (primal instinct).

teile.einleitung: An interview is a conversation in which one person asks specific questions and another answers. You find interviews in newspapers, on the radio, on television and also at school, when you ask someone questions about a topic.
wichtigste: In an interview, the interviewer asks the questions.
Open questions usually begin with a question word such as “how”, “why” or “what”.
Closed questions can often be answered with yes or no.
A good interview is prepared: you find out about the topic and write down questions.
Before recording, you always ask the person for permission.
If you listen well, you can ask fitting follow-up questions.
In writing, questions and answers take turns.

abschnitte.text: The word **interview** comes from English and means something like “questioning”. The person asking the questions is called the **interviewer**. The person being interviewed gives information about themselves, their work or a topic. Journalists use interviews to let experts, sportspeople or politicians have their say. That way the audience hears a person’s opinion or knowledge straight from them.

**Open questions** begin with a question word, for example “How did you get into your hobby?” They invite the person to tell a story and bring out lots of information. **Closed questions** allow only a few answers, often yes or no, for example “Have you been playing football for long?” They are useful for clearing something up exactly. In a good interview you mix both kinds cleverly.

Before the conversation, you find out about the person and the topic. Then you write down questions and put them in a sensible order, from easy to difficult. You agree on a place and time and check whether you may record the conversation. Without **permission** you must not record a conversation. If you are well prepared, you come across as confident and can concentrate fully on the answers.

During the interview, **listening carefully** is especially important. That way you notice where an answer is exciting or unclear. Then you ask a **follow-up question**, for example “Can you explain that in more detail?” So you do not have to stick rigidly to your prepared list. At the end, you thank the person for the conversation.

In the written version, questions and answers **take turns**. Often there are names or initials in front of them, and the questions are printed in bold. The conversation is usually shortened a little and smoothed out, but the meaning must stay the same. In Switzerland it is common for newspapers to have the interviewee **approve** the interview. They read the text before it is published and give it the go-ahead.

gewusst: When approving an interview, the interviewee confirms that their statements have been reported correctly.
Interviews are not only found in the media: researchers also interview people to find out about their lives or opinions.

teile.einleitung: Synonyms are words that mean the same or almost the same, like “fast” and “quick” or “begin” and “start”. With synonyms you can make texts more varied and avoid annoying repetition. Switzerland also has many words of its own that have a synonym in the rest of the German-speaking world.
wichtigste: Synonyms are words with the same or a similar meaning.
The German “schnell” and “rasch” (fast, quick) and “sprechen” and “reden” (speak, talk) are synonyms.
“Schön” and “hübsch” (beautiful, pretty) or “froh” and “glücklich” (glad, happy) also mean almost the same.
The Swiss word “Velo” means the same as “Fahrrad” (bicycle).
In Germany the Swiss “Trottoir” (pavement) is usually called “Gehsteig” or “Bürgersteig”.
The opposite of a synonym is an antonym.
Words that mean exactly the same are rare; they usually differ a little.

abschnitte.text: A **synonym** is a word that means the same or almost the same as another word. The term comes from Greek and means roughly “having the same name”. Examples are “begin” and “start”, or in German “Samstag” and “Sonnabend” (Saturday). Synonyms always belong to the same word class: a verb has a verb as a synonym, an adjective an adjective. Words with opposite meanings, such as “big” and “small”, on the other hand, are called **antonyms**.

Words with completely identical meanings are rare. Synonyms often differ in their **register**: in German “Gesicht” (face) is neutral, “Antlitz” (countenance) sounds solemn and “Visage” (mug) insulting. Sometimes a word only fits in certain combinations: you say “act quickly”, but hardly “a quick-acting car” in the same sense. Feelings play a part too, because “pretty” sounds different from “beautiful”. That is why you always have to check synonyms in context.

Swiss Standard German has its own words, which are called **Helvetisms**. Instead of “Fahrrad” (bicycle), people in Switzerland say “Velo”, instead of “Gehsteig” (pavement) “Trottoir” and instead of “Speiseeis” (ice cream) “Glace”. “Rüebli” for carrot or “parkieren” for to park are also typical. Many of these words come from French, because Switzerland is closely connected with the French-speaking Romandy. In Switzerland they count as correct Standard German and are also in the Duden dictionary.

When people write an essay, they often repeat the same words, especially “say”, “make” or “go”. With synonyms such as “explain”, “whisper” or “shout”, a text becomes much livelier and more precise. A **word field** helps here, a collection of words with similar meanings. You could, for example, make a word field for “go” with stroll, run, hop and stumble. Each of these words describes the movement a little differently.

There are special dictionaries for finding synonyms, which are called a **thesaurus**. The word comes from Greek and means “treasure”. Word processing programs on the computer also suggest synonyms if you want. But you should check the suggestions carefully, because not every synonym fits every sentence. You develop a good feel for language above all by reading a lot.

begriffe.erklaerung: A word with the same or a similar meaning as another.
A word with the opposite meaning, such as “light” and “dark”.
A word or expression that is typical of German in Switzerland.
A dictionary that collects words with similar meanings.

gewusst: German has a large number of slang synonyms for “Geld” (money), such as “Kohle”, “Knete” or the Swiss “Stutz”.
In northern Germany people often say “Sonnabend” for Saturday, while in Switzerland they almost only say “Samstag”.
The word “synonym” has a synonym itself: in German “sinnverwandtes Wort” (word of related meaning).

teile.einleitung: A rhyme happens when two words sound the same at the end, like “house” and “mouse”. You find rhymes in poems, songs, children’s verses and even in rap. They make texts sound good and help you remember them.
wichtigste: In a rhyme, words sound the same from the last stressed vowel onwards.
In German, “Haus” and “Maus” (house, mouse), “Hund” and “Mund” (dog, mouth) and “Tisch” and “Fisch” (table, fish) are rhyming pairs.
“Sonne” and “Tonne” (sun, barrel) or “Katze” and “Tatze” (cat, paw) also rhyme.
When words rhyme at the end of a line, this is called end rhyme.
Rhyme schemes are described with letters such as aabb or abab.
Rhymes help the memory, which is why there are so many rhyming children’s verses.
Alliteration is not end rhyme; there, words begin with the same sound.

abschnitte.text: A **rhyme** is when words sound alike. Strictly speaking, the sounds from the last stressed vowel onwards have to match. In the German “Sonne” and “Tonne” the “-onne” is the same, in “Schnee” and “Tee” (snow, tea) the long “ee”. “Stein” and “Bein” (stone, leg) rhyme too. If the words only sound similar but not quite the same, it is called an **impure rhyme**, as with the German “Höhle” and “Seele” (cave, soul).

Letters are used to show which lines rhyme. In **couplets** (aabb), two lines in a row rhyme. In **alternate rhyme** (abab), every second line rhymes. In enclosed rhyme (abba), one pair of rhymes wraps round another. Tail rhyme follows the pattern aabccb.

In very old Germanic poetry, for example in the Song of Hildebrand from the 9th century, there was no end rhyme yet. Instead people used **alliteration**, in which stressed words begin with the same sound. End rhyme became established in German from the 9th century, among other places in the works of the monk Otfrid of Weissenburg. Since then it has been very widespread in poems and songs. But many modern poems deliberately do without rhymes.

Nursery rhymes, counting-out rhymes and lullabies almost always rhyme. This is because rhymes help the **memory**: the brain stores the sound more easily. Finding rhyming words is also practice in listening carefully to sounds. That is an important preparation for learning to read and write. In Switzerland, too, there are many dialect verses that people recite at nursery school and at home.

We come across rhymes everywhere: in pop songs, in advertising slogans and on greetings cards. Rappers rhyme with special skill, often making several syllables rhyme at the same time. For poets there are even **rhyming dictionaries**, in which words are sorted by their endings. Good rhymes sound natural and fit the content; bad rhymes sound forced.

begriffe.erklaerung: Words sounding alike at the end of lines.
Two lines in a row rhyme, scheme aabb.
Every second line rhymes, scheme abab.
Stressed words begin with the same sound, for example the German “Haus und Hof” (house and home).

gewusst: There is hardly any word that rhymes properly with the German word “Mensch” (human being), just as nothing rhymes with “orange” in English.
Many fixed German expressions rhyme, such as “Sang und Klang” (song and sound) or “mit Rat und Tat” (with advice and help).
Wilhelm Busch wrote his famous story “Max and Moritz” from 1865 entirely in rhyming couplets.

teile.einleitung: Punctuation marks are small signs such as the full stop, comma or question mark that structure a written text. They show where a sentence ends, whether someone is asking or shouting, and who is saying something word for word. Without punctuation, many texts would be hard to understand or even misleading.
wichtigste: At the end of a statement there is a full stop.
A question ends with a question mark.
Exclamations such as “Help, the house is on fire!” end with an exclamation mark.
The comma separates, for example, the words in a list.
Quotation marks show what someone says word for word.
In German there is often a colon before direct speech.
In Switzerland, angle-shaped quotation marks are usually used.

abschnitte.text: **Punctuation marks** help with reading, because they make the pauses and melody of spoken language visible. They show where one thought ends and a new one begins. A famous example shows how important the comma is: “Come on, let’s eat, Grandpa!” is an invitation to Grandpa. Without the second comma the sentence would mean something quite different. So punctuation marks make texts clear.

The **full stop** ends a statement that simply tells something. The **question mark** comes at the end of a question, such as “What time is it?” The exclamation mark comes after exclamations, commands and warnings, for example “Watch out!” These three marks are called end marks. After them, the next sentence begins with a capital letter.

The **comma** is the most common punctuation mark within a sentence. It separates items in lists, such as “apples, pears, bananas”. In German it also goes between a main clause and a subordinate clause, for example before “weil” (because), “dass” (that) or “obwohl” (although). After the greeting in a letter, such as “Dear Tim,”, you put a comma too. In German you then carry on with a small letter on the next line, unless a noun follows.

What someone says word for word goes in **quotation marks**. In German, if a reporting clause introduces the speech, there is a colon before it: Mum says: “Come and eat!” In Switzerland people mostly use the French-style angle-shaped quotation marks, which are called guillemets. In Germany, on the other hand, you often see marks that sit low at the start and high at the end. Other marks are the semicolon, brackets and the apostrophe.

In ancient times people often wrote without punctuation and even without spaces between words. But in ancient Greece the first dots were already invented to show pauses for reading. Many of today’s marks developed in the Middle Ages and became established after the invention of **printing** in the 15th century. The exact comma rules in German were only fixed much later.

begriffe.erklaerung: The full stop, question mark and exclamation mark, which end a sentence.
A mark that separates parts of a sentence from each other.
The angle-shaped quotation marks that are usual in Switzerland.
What a person says exactly as they say it, in quotation marks.

gewusst: In Spanish an upside-down question mark also goes at the beginning of a question.
The word “comma” comes from Greek and originally meant “section”.
In programming, even a single missing punctuation mark can stop a whole program from working.

teile.einleitung: The Linguistic Atlas of German-speaking Switzerland, SDS for short (Sprachatlas der deutschen Schweiz), is a large collection of maps of the dialects of German-speaking Switzerland. Its maps show where which sounds, forms and words are used.
wichtigste: The abbreviation SDS stands for Sprachatlas der deutschen Schweiz.
The atlas shows the dialects on maps.
It is based on surveys in hundreds of places.
You can see on it where which dialect form is used.
The SDS is an important source for research into Swiss German.

abschnitte.text: A **linguistic atlas** is a collection of maps that show language instead of roads or mountains. In the **Linguistic Atlas of German-speaking Switzerland**, each map shows a word, a sound or a grammatical form. Symbols and colours show which variant is said in which place. That way you can spot **borders** between dialects, which often run along mountains, rivers or old territories.

For the SDS, experts in the middle of the 20th century questioned people in **hundreds of places** in German-speaking Switzerland. They asked the same questions everywhere and wrote down the answers in a precise phonetic script. The results were then published in several volumes with many maps. The work was directed at the University of Zurich.

The SDS is an important source for anyone researching **Swiss German**. You can use it to compare how dialects have changed since then. Newer projects and apps build on its data and show the maps to a wide audience too. Together with the Schweizerisches Idiotikon, the SDS is one of the great works of Swiss dialect research.

gewusst: For the SDS, mainly older people who had always lived in a place were questioned, so that the traditional dialect of the place was recorded.
There is also a smaller, easy-to-understand edition with selected maps for non-experts.
